learn.title: shape, size and ndim
learn.body: shape is one number per axis, size is the product of those numbers and ndim is how many axes exist — the three answers every shape error is really about.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)
learn.simple: Shape batata hai array ka dhancha — jaise 2 rows aur 3 columns. Size batata hai total kitne number hain, aur ndim batata hai kitne 'dabbe' (axes) hain: ek line ka ndim 1, table ka 2.
learn.pro: Shape is a tuple of axis lengths, size is their product, and ndim is the count of axes. Printing all three together is the fastest way to catch a transposed or flattened array before it reaches a model.
learn.syntax: a.shape → tuple   |   a.size → int   |   a.ndim → int
steps: Build the 2×3 array and print all three attributes in one call.
Read shape as (rows, columns) and check size is their product.
Count the entries of shape to confirm ndim.
learn.visual:
a.shape = (2, 3)   rows × columns
a.size  = 6        cells
a.ndim  = 2        number of axes
learn.realWorld: A model expects a feature matrix and fails on shape; printing shape, size and ndim first tells you whether the data is transposed or flattened.
mistakes: Reading shape as (columns, rows) and transposing the wrong way.
Using len(a) when the total cell count is what is needed.
revision: shape is the structure, size is the cell count, ndim is the axis count.

learn.title: dtype and itemsize
learn.body: The dtype decides how the bytes are interpreted and itemsize is the bytes per element; together they explain both the values you get and the memory you pay.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize)
learn.simple: Dtype batata hai array me kaise number hain — pure integer ya decimal (float). Itemsize batata hai ek number kitni memory leta hai, jaise int64 ka 8 byte.
learn.pro: dtype fixes the element type and itemsize its width in bytes; nbytes is their product with size. Downcasting to a narrower dtype is a deliberate memory trade that must be checked against the value range.
steps: Build an integer array and print dtype.
Print itemsize and note it is bytes per element, not per array.
Multiply itemsize by size to reach nbytes.
learn.visual:
dtype int64 → itemsize 8 bytes
3 elements  → nbytes 24
learn.realWorld: A million-row column of small integers costs 8 MB as int64 and 1 MB as int8 — the dtype decision is the memory decision.
mistakes: Assuming itemsize changes with array length.
Casting to a smaller dtype without checking the value range.
revision: dtype names the element type; itemsize is its width in bytes.

learn.title: Axis means the direction that is collapsed
learn.body: Reducing along axis 0 collapses rows (one result per column) and axis 1 collapses columns (one result per row); reading the output length tells you which axis was reduced.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=1))
learn.simple: Jis axis ka naam doge, wahi axis gayab ho jaata hai. axis=0 ka matlab rows ko mila do (columns bachenge), axis=1 ka matlab columns ko mila do.
learn.pro: The axis argument names the axis that is reduced away, not the one preserved. A (2, 3) reduction with axis=0 returns three values, one per column, and drops the row dimension.
steps: Sum a 2×2 array with axis=0 and read the result shape.
Sum with axis=1 and compare which values disappeared.
Say out loud which axis vanished in each case.
learn.realWorld: Monthly sales per product: axis=0 totals each product across months, axis=1 totals each month across products.
mistakes: Thinking axis names the direction that stays.
Expecting the same shape back from a reduction.
revision: The named axis is the one removed.

learn.title: len counts the first axis only
learn.body: len() reports the length of axis 0, not the number of elements, so for a (3, 4) array len is 3 while size is 12.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(len(a), a.size)
learn.simple: len(array) sirf pehla axis ginta hai — table me rows. Saare numbers ginne hain to size use karo.
learn.pro: len calls the first axis length, so on a (3, 4) array it returns 3 while size returns 12. Use shape[0] and shape[1] when both counts matter, and never use len as a sample count.
steps: Build a 3×4 array and print len(a).
Compare it with a.size.
Use shape[0] and shape[1] when both counts matter.
learn.realWorld: Counting rows of a table is len(a); counting measured values is a.size — mixing them inflates sample counts.
mistakes: Assuming len gives the cell count.
Using len on a 0-d array and expecting 1.
revision: len is the first axis only.

learn.title: Transpose swaps the shape
learn.body: Transposing reverses the axis order, so a (3, 4) array becomes (4, 3) and every operation that follows reads the new shape.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(a.T.shape)
learn.simple: Transpose rows ko columns bana deta hai. Shape (3, 4) ka transpose (4, 3) ho jaata hai, par numbers ka order wahi rehta hai.
learn.pro: Transpose swaps the axis order, so the shape reverses and the strides swap with it. It returns a view of the same buffer, which is why the operation is free until a consumer demands C-contiguous data.
steps: Build a 3×4 array and print both shapes.
Transpose and print the shape again.
Note that values were not reordered, only the axes were swapped.
learn.realWorld: A CSV read as (features, samples) usually needs .T before a model that expects (samples, features).
mistakes: Believing .T copies the data — it is a view with swapped strides.
Transposing twice and forgetting the data is back to the original.
revision: It is a view until something forces a copy.

learn.title: Mixed literals promote to float
learn.body: One float in the input is enough to make the whole array float64, because a single dtype has to hold every value.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2.5]).dtype)
learn.simple: Agar list me ek bhi decimal hai, poora array float ban jaata hai — integer bhi 1.0 ban jaata hai. Ek dtype hi hota hai poore array ka.
learn.pro: NumPy promotes all elements to a single common dtype, so one float literal converts the integers to float64. That promotion changes memory width and makes exact equality unreliable, so pass dtype deliberately when it matters.
steps: Build an array from an int and a float.
Print the dtype and observe both values became floats.
Pass dtype explicitly when the promotion is unwanted.
learn.realWorld: One decimal in a price column silently turns the whole column into floats, which changes equality and memory behaviour.
mistakes: Expecting the integer to stay an integer in a mixed array.
Relying on exact equality after promotion.
revision: Mixed input promotes to the common type.

learn.title: A zero-dimensional array has no axes
learn.body: `np.array(7)` is a 0-d array: it has one value, ndim 0 and an empty shape tuple, which is how a scalar crosses into array code.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
s = np.array(7)
print(s.ndim, s.shape)
learn.simple: Ek single number ka array bhi array hota hai, par uska koi axis nahi hota (ndim 0, shape khaali). `.item()` se asli Python number milta hai.
learn.pro: A 0-d array holds one value with ndim 0 and shape (); reductions over every axis return one. Use .item() when a plain Python scalar is required, because the object is still an ndarray.
steps: Create an array from a single number.
Print ndim and shape to see () and 0.
Use .item() to get the plain Python scalar back.
learn.realWorld: A reduction over every axis returns a 0-d array; printing it looks like a number but it is still an ndarray.
mistakes: Indexing a 0-d array as if it had axes.
Comparing it to a Python int in a type check.

learn.title: Bytes are shape times itemsize
learn.body: nbytes is size multiplied by itemsize, so a float32 array of six elements costs 24 bytes and a float64 one would cost 48.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=np.float32)
print(a.nbytes)
learn.simple: Total memory = number of elements × ek element ka size. float32 se float64 karoge to memory dugni ho jaayegi.
learn.pro: nbytes equals size multiplied by itemsize, so dtype is the lever on memory: float32 halves a float64 matrix. Account for copies separately, since a copy doubles the live footprint.
steps: Create a float32 array of shape (2, 3).
Print nbytes and square it against size × itemsize.
Repeat with float64 to see the memory double.
learn.realWorld: Choosing float32 for a large feature matrix halves memory and often changes nothing measurable in accuracy.
mistakes: Confusing nbytes with the Python object's overhead.
Forgetting that a copy doubles the count.
revision: dtype width is the multiplier you control.

learn.title: ndim counts the axes
learn.body: `ndim` is how many indices you need to reach a single value; `size` is how many values exist in total.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.ndim, a.size)
learn.simple: Jitne brackets ke andar brackets, utne axes. 3D array me ndim 3 hota hai aur index bhi teen lagte hain.
learn.pro: ndim equals len(shape), and every axis needs its own index. In practice ndim identifies the convention you are holding — (batch, height, width) versus (batch, height, width, channels).
steps: Create a three-axis array.
Print ndim and size, and confirm size is the product of shape.
Index with three positions to see each axis used.
learn.realWorld: An image batch is (batch, height, width) or (batch, height, width, channels) — ndim tells you which convention you are holding.
mistakes: Counting shape entries by eye and getting it wrong.
Assuming a 2-D model accepts a 3-D batch.
revision: Each axis needs its own index.

learn.title: Ten zeros are one dimension
learn.body: A one-dimensional array has a trailing comma in its shape. That is a 1-tuple, not a scalar.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.zeros(10).shape)
learn.simple: `np.zeros(10)` me sirf 10 numbers hain, ek line. `(10, 1)` do axis hain — 10 rows aur 1 column, jo model ke liye column banta hai.
learn.pro: Shape (10,) is one axis while (10, 1) is two; broadcasting treats them differently. A feature matrix needs the explicit column axis, otherwise the vector broadcasts across rows and silently produces the wrong result.
steps: Create ten zeros and print the shape.
Notice the trailing comma: one axis, ten cells.
Compare with np.zeros((10, 1)) which has two axes.
learn.realWorld: A single feature column must be (n, 1) to broadcast as a column; (n,) silently broadcasts as a row.
mistakes: Treating (10,) and (10, 1) as the same shape.
Reshaping to (10,) and losing the column semantics.
revision: A 1-D shape is written with a trailing comma.

learn.title: Shape is a tuple you can index
learn.body: `shape` is data, not a method. Read `shape[0]` for rows and `shape[1]` for columns instead of calling it.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 2))
print(a.shape[0], a.shape[1])
learn.simple: Shape ek tuple hai, isliye shape[0] se rows aur shape[1] se columns nikal sakte ho — badi value hard-code karne ki zarurat nahi.
learn.pro: shape is an immutable tuple, so indexing it gives axis lengths you can reuse in allocations and reshapes. That keeps code correct when the row count changes between runs.
steps: Create a 2×2 array.
Read rows and columns from the tuple by position.
Use those values in a reshape or a loop bound.
learn.realWorld: Building a result array with np.zeros(a.shape[0]) is how code stays correct when the row count changes.
mistakes: Indexing shape[1] on a 1-D array.
Assuming shape is a list and calling .append.

learn.title: A matrix of one row still has two axes
learn.body: Wrapping a list in a list adds an axis even when there is only one element in it. Shape `(1, 2)` is a matrix, `(2,)` is a vector.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[7, 8]]).shape)
learn.simple: `[[7, 8]]` me bahar ka bracket ek extra axis banata hai, isliye shape (1, 2) hota hai. Model ko aksar aisa hi batch chahiye.
learn.pro: Nesting a list adds an axis, so [[7, 8]] is (1, 2) while [7, 8] is (2,). A single-sample batch must keep that leading axis or the model receives a vector instead of a batch.
steps: Build a nested list with one inner list.
Print the shape and note the leading 1.
Compare with np.array([7, 8]) which is 1-D.
learn.realWorld: Batching a single sample for a model needs (1, features); passing (features,) is the classic shape error.
mistakes: Dropping the outer list and losing the batch axis.
Squeezing a batch of one to save memory and breaking the model call.
revision: Batch of one is still a batch.

learn.title: Every attribute of an ndarray
learn.body: shape, ndim, size, dtype, itemsize and nbytes answer different questions about the same buffer, and strides tells you how many elements each axis step moves.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a.shape, a.ndim, a.size, a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes, a.strides)
learn.simple: Ek array ke baare me hum alag-alag sawaal poochh sakte hain: kitni rows aur columns hain (`shape`), kitne total numbers hain (`size`), har number ka type kya hai (`dtype`), aur memory me kitni jagah lagi (`nbytes`). `strides` batata hai ki agla number lene ke liye memory me kitne step aage jaana hai — jaise seedhi ke steps.
learn.pro: shape, ndim, size, dtype, itemsize, nbytes and strides describe different layers of the same allocation: logical axes, element type, buffer bytes and the byte offset each axis step applies. For a C-contiguous (3, 4) int64 array the strides are (32, 8), so every column step moves one 8-byte element and every row step moves four.
learn.syntax: shape · ndim · size · dtype · itemsize · nbytes · strides
steps: Reshape a range into a 3×4 array.
Print all attributes in one line.
Read strides as bytes to step per axis.
learn.visual:
shape (3, 4) · size 12 · dtype int64
strides (32, 8) = 4 elements, then 1
learn.realWorld: Disagreement between shape and strides is how a transposed view keeps the same buffer without copying.
mistakes: Reading strides in elements instead of bytes.
Assuming a reshape always changes strides.
revision: strides are byte steps per axis.
A view shares the buffer; strides differ.

learn.title: np.empty is not filled with zeros
learn.body: empty allocates the buffer without writing values, so whatever was in memory is what you read. Use zeros when you need a known starting value.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
z = np.zeros(3, dtype=np.int64)
print(z, z.dtype)
print(np.zeros((2, 2)).shape)
learn.simple: `np.empty` ek khaali dabba deta hai jisme pehle se kuch bhi likha ho sakta hai — purane numbers, kachra, kuch bhi. Ye zeros nahi deta. Agar tumhe pakka pata ho ki tum turant saare numbers khud bhar doge, tab empty use karo; warna `np.zeros` hi lo.
learn.pro: empty allocates the buffer without initialising it, so the values are whatever the allocator returned — reading them is undefined behaviour for your program. It is only appropriate for a preallocated output that is fully overwritten before any read; zeros trades one memset pass for determinism.
steps: Create zeros to see a known starting state.
Create empty of the same shape and print its dtype and shape only.
Never print or rely on empty's values.
learn.realWorld: Preallocating an output buffer with empty is a legitimate speed trick — as long as every cell is written before it is read.
mistakes: Assuming empty contains zeros.
Reading an unwritten cell and treating garbage as data.
revision: Write every cell before reading it.

learn.title: strides report bytes per axis step
learn.body: strides is a tuple of byte offsets: moving one step along an axis jumps that many bytes. For a C-contiguous int64 matrix the row stride is the row width in bytes.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6, dtype=np.int64).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.strides)
print(a.shape)
learn.simple: Strides batate hain ki ek row aage badhne me kitne bytes jump karne hain. Shape batata hai kitne ghar hain, strides batate hain unke beech ka rasta kitna lamba hai.
learn.pro: `strides` is a tuple of byte offsets, one per axis: advancing one index along an axis adds that many bytes to the pointer. For a C-contiguous int64 matrix the row stride is the row width in bytes, which is why transposing only reverses the strides and never moves data.
learn.syntax: a.strides  # bytes to advance one index on each axis
steps: Create an int64 matrix with `arange` and `reshape`.
Print `a.strides` and `a.shape`.
Move one row and confirm the byte jump matches the row stride.
learn.visual:
shape (2, 3), int64
strides (24, 8)
row step 24 bytes = 3 × 8
learn.realWorld: Memory layout explains why a transpose is free and why some library calls copy.
mistakes: Reading strides as element counts instead of bytes.
revision: Strides are byte offsets per axis.
C-order rows jump by the row width.

learn.title: A transpose keeps the same size
learn.body: Transposing swaps the axes and reverses the strides, but the number of elements is unchanged. That is why a transpose is a view, not a copy.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.shape, a.T.size, a.size)
print(a.T.strides)
learn.simple: Transpose sirf rows aur columns ki jagah badalta hai, cheezein kam ya zyada nahi hotin. Isliye size same rehta hai aur NumPy data copy kiye bina kaam chala leta hai.
learn.pro: Transposing swaps the shape and reverses the strides while leaving `size` and the underlying buffer untouched, so it is a view rather than a copy. Code that mutates a transpose is therefore mutating the source; call `.copy()` when the transposed layout must be independent.
learn.syntax: a.T  # shape and strides swap, size is unchanged
steps: Build a 2×3 array.
Print `a.T.shape` and `a.size`.
Compare the strides of both views.
learn.realWorld: Linear algebra libraries expect a particular orientation, and transpose supplies it without a copy.
mistakes: Mutating a transpose and being surprised the source changed.
revision: Size is the product of the shape and does not change.

learn.title: dtype name versus dtype kind
learn.body: `str(dtype)` gives the full name like `int64`, while `.kind` gives one character such as `i` or `f`. Kind is what you branch on when the width should not matter.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(str(np.array([1]).dtype), np.array([1]).dtype.kind)
print(str(np.array([1.0]).dtype), np.array([1.0]).dtype.kind)
learn.simple: `dtype` poora naam deta hai jaise `int64`, aur `.kind` ek chhota letter jaise `i` ya `f`. Jab width matter na kare to letter se check karo, naam se nahi.
learn.pro: `str(dtype)` reports the exact type including width, while `.kind` collapses it to a one-character category such as `i`, `f`, `b` or `U`. Branch on `kind` when the logic is about the family of values; branch on the full dtype only when byte width or precision is the actual contract.
steps: Create one integer and one float array.
Print the full dtype name for both.
Print `.kind` and compare the single letters.
learn.realWorld: Validation code branches on kind when any integer width is acceptable.
mistakes: Comparing `.kind` with the full dtype string.
revision: The name includes width and precision.
The kind is the type family.

learn.title: size is zero when any axis is zero
learn.body: One empty axis makes the whole array hold nothing, even if the other axes are large. Plotting or reshaping such an array produces an empty result rather than an error.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((0, 5))
print(a.shape, a.size, a.nbytes)
learn.simple: Agar kisi bhi side ki lambai zero hai to poora array khaali hai, chahe doosri side kitni badi ho. Isliye `(0, 5)` ka size zero hota hai, paanch nahi.
learn.pro: An array's `size` is the product of its shape, so one zero-length axis makes the whole array empty regardless of the other dimensions. Reductions over such an array return their empty-result convention rather than an error, which is why a filter that selects nothing can flow through a pipeline without raising.
steps: Create an array with a zero-length axis.
Print shape, size and nbytes.
Reduce it and observe the empty result.
learn.realWorld: A filter that matches no rows still flows through a pipeline as a valid empty result.
mistakes: Assuming the non-zero axis still yields elements.
revision: One zero axis empties the array.

learn.title: flags report the memory layout
learn.body: `flags` answers whether the buffer is C-contiguous, Fortran-contiguous or writeable. Library calls that require a layout look at exactly these flags.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'], a.flags['F_CONTIGUOUS'], a.flags['WRITEABLE'])
learn.simple: `flags` batata hai array memory me kaise rakha hai — C order me, Fortran order me, aur likhne layak hai ya nahi. Jo library layout maangti hai, woh yahi dekhti hai.
learn.pro: `flags` exposes `C_CONTIGUOUS`, `F_CONTIGUOUS` and `WRITEABLE`, the properties compiled code actually queries before choosing a fast path. A transposed view is typically not C-contiguous, so a library that requires that layout will copy; reading the flag first tells you where that copy will happen.
steps: Build a contiguous matrix.
Print its C, Fortran and writeable flags.
Transpose it and print the flags again.
learn.visual:
a     C True  F False
a.T   C False F True
learn.realWorld: A library that needs contiguous input reads these flags before deciding to copy.
mistakes: Ignoring a non-contiguous warning until a copy appears in profiling.
revision: Flags describe the buffer, not the values.

learn.title: base links a view to its source
learn.body: A view's `.base` points at the array that owns the buffer, while an owning array reports None. That single attribute tells you whether a write will be visible elsewhere.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a.base is None)
print(a[1:3].base is a)
learn.simple: View ka `.base` batata hai ki uska maalik kaun array hai. Agar base `None` hai to yeh khud memory ka maalik hai; warna koi doosra array usi memory ko chalata hai.
learn.pro: `.base` points at the array that owns the buffer, while an owning array reports `None`. It is the direct way to answer whether a write through one name can appear in another, and it survives chained views, so checking `base` is more reliable than comparing values or shapes.
learn.syntax: a[1:3].base is a  # True for a view
steps: Create a vector.
Print `a.base` for the owner and for a slice.
Confirm the slice's base is the source array.
learn.realWorld: Debugging a silent data change starts by checking whether two names share a base.
mistakes: Assuming a slice always owns its own data.
revision: A view's base points at the owner.

interview.q: How do you find the number of rows of an array without hard-coding the rank?
interview.answer: Use `arr.shape[0]`. Axis 0 is rows by convention, whatever the rank.

interview.q: Why can a scalar array have `shape == ()` and `ndim == 0`?
interview.answer: It is a single value with no axes: the shape tuple is empty and the rank is zero, which is still a valid ndarray rather than a Python float.

interview.q: What does a dtype tell you that a shape does not?
interview.answer: The shape says how values are arranged; the dtype says what each value is and how many bytes it takes, which decides overflow, precision and the result of arithmetic.

interview.q: How do you read a shape of `(2, 3, 4)` in words?
interview.answer: Two blocks, each holding three rows of four values. Reading right to left gives the fastest-varying axis first.

interview.q: What is `size` in terms of `shape`?
interview.answer: The product of the shape entries. An empty axis makes the product zero.

interview.q: Why is `len(arr)` not the number of elements?
interview.answer: `len` reports the length of the first axis only, so a `(2, 3)` array has `len` 2 and size 6.

interview.q: What does `arr.reshape(2, -1)` do with the second dimension?
interview.answer: It infers that dimension from the element count and raises if the total is not divisible by 2.

interview.q: How do you check that two arrays have the same shape?
interview.answer: Compare `a.shape == b.shape`; shapes are tuples, so the comparison is exact and cheap.

interview.q: What is a 0-d array?
interview.answer: A single value with no axes: its shape is `()` and it still supports NumPy operations.

interview.q: A bug report says an image has shape (0, 256, 3). What does that tell you about the array, and what will happen when you plot it?
interview.answer: The first axis (height) is zero, so the array holds no pixels at all. Plotting or reshaping will fail or render nothing; the bug is upstream where the image was read, not in the plotting call.

followUps.q: Which check in the loader would stop a zero-size image before it reaches the plot?
followUps.answer: Assert every axis is positive (`all(dim > 0 for dim in arr.shape)`) right after reading, and raise with the source path — the failure belongs where the bad data entered.

followUps.q: What does `.size` report for that array?
followUps.answer: Zero, because the product of the axis lengths includes the zero-height axis. A zero size is the fastest way to spot it programmatically.

interview.q: Someone allocates np.empty((1000, 1000)) to save time and sees random huge numbers. Is NumPy broken?
interview.answer: No — empty only allocates the buffer without writing values, so it exposes whatever was in memory. Use np.zeros or np.full when a known starting value is required.

followUps.q: When is `np.empty` actually appropriate?
followUps.answer: When the very next statement writes every element (a preallocated output buffer), so uninitialised garbage can never be read.

followUps.q: Why does NumPy skip zeroing the memory?
followUps.answer: Initialising is a full pass over the buffer; skipping it is a deliberate speed trade for callers who will overwrite the array immediately.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: shape, size and ndim
practice.task: shape is one number per axis, size is the product of those numbers and ndim is how many axes exist — the three answers every shape error is really about.
practice.solution:

a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: dtype and itemsize
practice.task: The dtype decides how the bytes are interpreted and itemsize is the bytes per element; together they explain both the values you get and the memory you pay.

print(a.dtype, a.itemsize)

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Axis means the direction that is collapsed

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: flags report the memory layout
practice.task: `flags` answers whether the buffer is C-contiguous, Fortran-contiguous or writeable. Library calls that require a layout look at exactly these flags.

practice.task: A view's `.base` points at the array that owns the buffer, while an owning array reports None. That single attribute tells you whether a write will be visible elsewhere.

print(a.base is None)

defense.q: Defend checking `shape` before arithmetic in a data pipeline.
defense.answer: Most silent numeric bugs are shape bugs, and a shape check turns a wrong answer into a loud failure at the boundary. It also documents the contract the next stage expects.

defense.q: Two arrays have 6 elements each but will not broadcast. Explain why size is not enough.
defense.answer: Broadcasting compares axes from the right, so `(2, 3)` and `(3, 2)` disagree on both axes even though both hold 6 values. Compatibility is per-axis, not per-total.

defense.q: You can store a vector as `(3,)` or `(3, 1)`. Defend the one you keep in a matrix pipeline.
defense.answer: `(3, 1)` is explicit that it is a column, so it broadcasts across columns the way matrix code expects. `(3,)` aliases to the last axis and silently repeats in the wrong direction.

defense.q: Defend asserting `ndim` at a function boundary.
defense.answer: A function written for 2-D input silently misbehaves on 3-D data by reducing the wrong axis. The assertion turns that into an immediate error.

defense.q: Explain why a 3-D array is not "three lists".
defense.answer: It is one buffer addressed by three strides, so it can be sliced, transposed and broadcast as a single object. Three lists would be three objects with no shared shape.

defense.q: Defend naming axes in comments instead of using bare axis numbers.
defense.answer: `axis=1` is meaningless without the shape in mind, and a wrong axis is a silent wrong answer. A comment such as `# axis 1 = features` is the cheapest guard.

defense.q: Defend asserting `shape` rather than `size` at a function boundary.
defense.answer: A size can match while the layout is wrong, and layout is what every later reduction and broadcast depends on.

defense.q: Explain why `len(arr)` misleads on a 2-D array.
defense.answer: It returns the length of axis 0 only, not the number of elements, so `(2, 3)` reports 2.

defense.q: Defend reading `arr.ndim` instead of trusting a comment about rank.
defense.answer: The attribute cannot drift from the data, while a comment survives refactors that change the shape.

modules.title: Array Creation and Initialization
modules.goal: Create arrays with zeros, ones, full, arange, linspace, eye and diag, and pick the right constructor for a dataset.

topics.title: zeros, ones and full
topics.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))

topics.title: arange and linspace
topics.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))

topics.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
topics.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))

topics.title: zeros_like copies a shape
topics.body: `zeros_like` and `ones_like` take the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is how you allocate an accumulator that lines up with real data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.zeros_like(a), np.ones_like(a, dtype=int))

topics.title: linspace can exclude the endpoint
topics.body: With endpoint=False, linspace still gives you a fixed number of points but stops one step short, which is what periodic sampling needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 4, endpoint=False))

topics.title: arange accepts a fractional step
topics.body: arange happily takes a float step, though repeated float addition can drift; linspace is the safer tool when exact spacing matters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))

topics.title: ones can take an integer dtype
topics.body: The default float dtype is a choice, not a rule: pass dtype=int when you want ones that stay integers in later arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int))

topics.title: full repeats any value
topics.body: full allocates a shape and fills every cell with the value you give, so a constant column or a sentinel matrix is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.full((2, 2), 3, dtype=int))

topics.title: empty allocates without setting values
topics.body: `np.empty` skips initialisation, so it is faster but holds whatever memory was there. Use it only when you overwrite every element next.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.empty(3)
print(a.shape, a.dtype)

topics.title: identity builds an identity matrix
topics.body: `np.identity(n)` is the square identity: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.identity(2))

topics.title: arange counts down with a negative step
topics.body: The stop value is excluded in both directions. A negative step reverses the walk through the range.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(5, 0, -1))

topics.title: linspace controls the step you get
topics.body: `linspace(start, stop, n)` includes the endpoint and spaces `n` values evenly, which `arange` with floats cannot promise.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

topics.title: arange versus linspace
topics.body: arange takes a step and can miss the stop value; linspace takes a count and always includes both ends. For floats, linspace is usually the safer choice.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

topics.title: Identity and eye
topics.body: eye builds an identity of any rectangular shape, while identity requires a square one. Both put ones on the main diagonal.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(3, dtype=int))
print(np.identity(2, dtype=int))

topics.title: diag builds a matrix from a vector
topics.body: `np.diag` turns a vector into a matrix with those values on the diagonal, and given a matrix it extracts that diagonal back out.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.diag([1, 2, 3]).tolist())
print(np.diag(np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)).tolist())

topics.title: tril and triu keep one triangle
topics.body: `tril` zeroes everything above the diagonal and `triu` zeroes everything below it. Both accept an offset to move the boundary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 3), dtype=int)
print(np.tril(a).tolist())
print(np.triu(a, 1).sum())

topics.title: repeat repeats each element
topics.body: `np.repeat` duplicates individual values in place, so `[1, 2]` repeated twice becomes `[1, 1, 2, 2]`. It is different from tiling the whole sequence.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.repeat([1, 2], 2).tolist())
print(np.repeat([1, 2], [3, 1]).tolist())

topics.title: tile repeats the whole block
topics.body: `np.tile` copies the entire sequence as a unit, so a pair tiled twice becomes the pair twice. The output length is the input length times the repeat count.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.tile([1, 2], 2).tolist())
print(np.tile([[1], [2]], (1, 2)).tolist())

topics.title: logspace spaces powers of ten
topics.body: `np.logspace(start, stop, n)` returns values evenly spaced on a log scale, which is how learning rates and frequencies are sampled.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.logspace(0, 2, 3).tolist())
print(np.logspace(0, 1, 3, base=2).round(3).tolist())

topics.title: fromfunction builds from indices
topics.body: `np.fromfunction` calls a function once per index tuple, so a grid can be written as an expression of its row and column numbers.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
grid = np.fromfunction(lambda i, j: i * 10 + j, (2, 3))
print(grid.tolist())

interviewBank.q: When is `linspace` a better choice than `arange`?
interviewBank.answer: When the number of points matters and the endpoints must be exact. `linspace` computes each point from the count, avoiding the floating step error that can add or drop the last element of `arange`.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `zeros` and `empty`?
interviewBank.answer: `zeros` writes every element as 0; `empty` only allocates, so the values are whatever was in memory. Use `empty` only when you will overwrite all of it.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.eye(3, 4)` exist when `np.identity(3)` does?
interviewBank.answer: `eye` allows a rectangular shape and an offset diagonal via `k`; `identity` is only the square case.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.full` take a shape but `np.full_like` does not?
interviewBank.answer: `full_like` copies the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is why it takes that array instead of a shape.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.arange(5).reshape(1, -1)` produce?
interviewBank.answer: A single row with five columns: the `1` fixes the row count and `-1` infers the columns.

interviewBank.q: Why is `np.zeros` slower than `np.empty`?
interviewBank.answer: `zeros` writes every element; `empty` only allocates, leaving whatever bytes were there.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.full_like(a, 7)` reuse from `a`?
interviewBank.answer: Its shape and dtype, so only the fill value is new.

interviewBank.q: How do you build a diagonal matrix from a vector?
interviewBank.answer: `np.diag(v)` places the values on the main diagonal of a square matrix.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.arange(5.0)` produce floats?
interviewBank.answer: The start value is a float, so the inferred dtype is float64 rather than an integer type.

interviewBank.q: A test fixture needs 50 points from 0 to 10 inclusive. Why is np.linspace(0, 10, 50) safer than np.arange(0, 10, 0.2)?
interviewBank.answer: linspace takes a count and always includes both ends; arange takes a step, can include the stop unexpectedly with float steps, and can produce 50 or 51 points depending on rounding. Choose by count when the count is the requirement.

followUps.q: When is `arange` the better call than `linspace`?
followUps.answer: When the step is the requirement — integer ranges and fixed increments where the count is incidental. `linspace` wins when the count is what the test asserts.

followUps.q: How do you confirm the count before relying on it?
followUps.answer: Check `.size` (and the first/last values) on a tiny equivalent range first; float steps are exactly where off-by-one surprises appear.

interviewBank.q: An identity matrix is needed for a 3×4 system, but np.identity(3, 4) raises. What is the right call?
interviewBank.answer: identity only builds square matrices. Use np.eye(3, 4) (rows, columns), which puts ones on the main diagonal of a rectangular shape.

followUps.q: What does the second argument of `np.eye` change?
followUps.answer: The number of columns: `np.eye(3, 4)` is three rows by four columns, with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

followUps.q: How would you build the same rectangular identity without `eye`?
followUps.answer: `a = np.zeros((3, 4)); np.fill_diagonal(a, 1)` — useful when the diagonal value is not 1.

defenseBank.q: Defend using `arange` for indices and `linspace` for plotted ranges.
defenseBank.answer: Integer positions want an exact step and an exclusive stop, which is what `arange` gives. A plotted range wants a fixed count with both ends included, which `linspace` guarantees.

defenseBank.q: Why can `np.arange(0, 1, 0.1)` return eleven values instead of ten?
defenseBank.answer: The step is not exactly representable in binary, so repeated addition lands just below or above 1.0. A `linspace(0, 1, 10)` avoids the ambiguity.

defenseBank.q: Defend choosing the dtype at creation instead of fixing it later.
defenseBank.answer: The dtype decides memory and the arithmetic that follows; converting later copies the whole array and can change results. Declaring it once keeps the intent visible.

defenseBank.q: Defend `linspace` for a fixed number of dashboard points.
defenseBank.answer: The chart needs exactly N points across a closed range, and `linspace` guarantees the count and both endpoints without floating-step drift.

defenseBank.q: Why does `np.eye(3)` print floats?
defenseBank.answer: The default dtype is float64, because an identity is usually used in floating-point algebra. Pass `dtype=int` for an integer one.

defenseBank.q: Defend building an index array once and reusing it.
defenseBank.answer: Positions rarely change while data does, so recomputing them wastes work and risks drift. One array documents the layout the rest of the code assumes.

defenseBank.q: Defend `zeros_like` over an explicit shape when copying a layout.
defenseBank.answer: It keeps shape and dtype in one expression, so they cannot drift apart when the source changes.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `np.empty` is not a shortcut for zeros.
defenseBank.answer: It leaves whatever bytes were in memory, so values are arbitrary until written.

defenseBank.q: Defend computing an index grid once and reusing it.
defenseBank.answer: The positions do not depend on the data, and recomputing them only adds work and a chance to drift.

learn.title: zeros, ones and full
learn.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))
learn.simple: Zeros se sab 0 wala array, ones se sab 1 wala, aur full se kisi bhi number se bhara array banta hai. Shape dena zaruri hai.
learn.pro: Each takes the shape first: zeros and ones fill with 0 and 1 (float64 by default), full fills with any value. They are the three constructors for a known-shape buffer before real data arrives.
steps: Create a length-3 zeros array and print its dtype.
Create a 2×2 ones array and confirm the shape.
Fill a length-3 array with 7 using full.
learn.realWorld: A results buffer starts as zeros, a mask starts as ones, and a default price list starts as full — all three are one call with a known shape.
mistakes: Forgetting the shape argument needs a tuple for 2-D.
Expecting full to infer the dtype from the value.

learn.title: arange and linspace
learn.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))
learn.simple: arange me step dete hain ('har 2 kadam'), linspace me count dete hain ('mujhe 5 number chahiye'). Dono ke apne use hain.
learn.pro: arange fixes the step and derives the count; linspace fixes the count, includes both endpoints and derives the step. Choose by which quantity your problem actually specifies.
learn.syntax: np.arange(start, stop, step) · np.linspace(start, stop, count)
steps: Create a range with a step of 2 and read the values.
Create three evenly spaced values from 0 to 1.
Count both results to see which argument controls the length.
learn.realWorld: Axis ticks are linspace (a count), while index arithmetic is arange (a step).
mistakes: Using arange with a float step and getting an extra element.
Expecting arange to include the stop value.
revision: arange takes a step; linspace takes a count.
linspace includes both ends by default.

learn.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
learn.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))
learn.simple: Identity matrix me diagonal par 1 aur baaki 0 hote hain. diag se list ko diagonal matrix bana sakte hain, aur matrix se diagonal nikal bhi sakte hain.
learn.pro: eye and identity build matrices with ones on the main diagonal; diag is overloaded — given a vector it builds a diagonal matrix, given a matrix it extracts the diagonal. Read the argument type before trusting the result.
steps: Create a 2×2 identity and read the diagonal.
Build a diagonal matrix from a list.
Compare np.diag on a matrix (extracts) with a vector (builds).
learn.realWorld: Identity matrices appear in ridge regression and in one-hot encodings; diag builds covariance from variances.
mistakes: Assuming diag always builds a matrix.
Forgetting eye is float by default.
revision: eye is square identity; diag is context-dependent.
Pass dtype=int when the values are counts.

learn.title: zeros_like copies a shape
learn.body: `zeros_like` and `ones_like` take the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is how you allocate an accumulator that lines up with real data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.zeros_like(a), np.ones_like(a, dtype=int))
learn.simple: `zeros_like(a)` wahi shape aur dtype deta hai jo `a` ka hai, isliye shape hard-code karne ki zarurat nahi padti.
learn.pro: The _like constructors copy shape and dtype from an existing array, so an output buffer cannot drift when the input shape changes. Override dtype explicitly when the buffer must hold a different type.
steps: Create a source array and print its shape.
Call zeros_like and confirm the shape matches.
Override dtype with ones_like to get integer ones.
learn.realWorld: An output buffer that must match an input uses zeros_like, so the shape never drifts when the input changes.
mistakes: Assuming zeros_like copies the values.
Forgetting it copies the dtype too.

learn.title: linspace can exclude the endpoint
learn.body: With endpoint=False, linspace still gives you a fixed number of points but stops one step short, which is what periodic sampling needs.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 4, endpoint=False))
learn.simple: `endpoint=False` se aakhri value nahi aati — aur isse step bhi badal jaata hai, sirf last number nahi hatta.
learn.pro: With endpoint=False the range covers [start, stop) and the step becomes the full span divided by the count, not by count − 1. Both the values and the spacing change, which matters for bin edges.
steps: Create four points including the endpoint.
Repeat with endpoint=False and compare.
Note the step becomes the full range divided by the count.
learn.realWorld: Histogram bin edges exclude the last endpoint when the range is cyclic, such as angles or phase.
mistakes: Assuming endpoint=False keeps the same step.
Using it and then expecting the maximum value to appear.
revision: Excluding it changes the spacing, not just the last value.

learn.title: arange accepts a fractional step
learn.body: arange happily takes a float step, though repeated float addition can drift; linspace is the safer tool when exact spacing matters.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))
learn.simple: arange me 0.25 jaisa decimal step bhi de sakte hain, par float galti se ek extra ya kam number aa sakta hai.
learn.pro: Fractional steps work but accumulate binary floating-point error, so the length can differ from the arithmetic expectation and the stop is never included. For a required count, linspace is the safer constructor.
steps: Create the range with a 0.25 step.
Count the values and compare with the expected four.
Check the last value against the stop.
learn.realWorld: Sampling a signal at a fractional interval is arange, but accumulated float error is why linspace is preferred for fixed counts.
mistakes: Expecting 1.0 to be included.
Trusting float steps to land exactly on the stop.
revision: Fractional steps work but accumulate error.

learn.title: ones can take an integer dtype
learn.body: The default float dtype is a choice, not a rule: pass dtype=int when you want ones that stay integers in later arithmetic.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int))
learn.simple: `np.ones(3)` float deta hai; agar pure integer chahiye to `dtype=int` likhna padta hai.
learn.pro: ones defaults to float64 regardless of the literal 1, so counters and masks need dtype=int. Leaving them float drags floating arithmetic and rounding into code that should stay integral.
steps: Create ones without a dtype and read the float dtype.
Repeat with dtype=int and read the values.
Use the integer version where counts must stay integral.
learn.realWorld: A counter array or a one-hot mask should be integer so later arithmetic does not drag floats through the pipeline.
mistakes: Assuming the dtype is inferred from the value 1.
Mixing float ones with integer counts in comparisons.
revision: dtype is an argument, not a guess.

learn.title: full repeats any value
learn.body: full allocates a shape and fills every cell with the value you give, so a constant column or a sentinel matrix is one call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.full((2, 2), 3, dtype=int))
learn.simple: `np.full((2, 2), 3)` do-ka-do array banata hai jisme har jagah 3 hota hai. Shape pehle, value baad me.
learn.pro: full(shape, value) is the general constant constructor, and dtype can be forced. It replaces the pattern of building zeros and then adding a scalar to every cell.
steps: Create a 2×2 array filled with 3.
Print the dtype to see it follows the value or the argument.
Use full for a constant baseline array.
learn.realWorld: A default discount table or a sentinel-filled buffer is one full call with a shape.
mistakes: Passing the value before the shape.
Forgetting the shape must be a tuple for 2-D.

learn.title: empty allocates without setting values
learn.body: `np.empty` skips initialisation, so it is faster but holds whatever memory was there. Use it only when you overwrite every element next.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.empty(3)
print(a.shape, a.dtype)
learn.simple: `np.empty(3)` sirf 3 jagah banata hai, number nahi daalta. Isme purani memory ka kachra dikh sakta hai.
learn.pro: empty performs allocation only, so the contents are undefined until written. It saves the zeroing pass in tight loops, at the cost of a real bug if any cell is read before assignment.
steps: Create empty of length 3 and print shape and dtype only.
Compare with zeros of the same shape.
Write every cell before reading it in real code.
learn.realWorld: A tight loop that fills a preallocated buffer uses empty to skip a pointless zeroing pass.
mistakes: Treating the values as zeros.
Shipping code that reads uninitialised cells.

learn.title: identity builds an identity matrix
learn.body: `np.identity(n)` is the square identity: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.identity(2))
learn.simple: `np.identity(2)` 2×2 ki identity deta hai — diagonal par 1. Ye sirf square (barabar rows-columns) ke liye hota hai.
learn.pro: identity(n) is the square special case of eye, so it accepts exactly one dimension. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication and a standard way to test a matmul implementation.
steps: Build a 2×2 identity and print it.
Compare with eye(2) and note they agree for square shapes.
Use eye when the matrix is rectangular.
learn.realWorld: Identity is the neutral element in matrix multiplication, used to initialise and to test a multiplication routine.
mistakes: Expecting identity to accept two dimensions.
Comparing identity to an integer matrix with == and getting False.

learn.title: arange counts down with a negative step
learn.body: The stop value is excluded in both directions. A negative step reverses the walk through the range.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(5, 0, -1))
learn.simple: Negative step dene se range ulti chalti hai — `arange(5, 0, -1)` 5 se 1 tak deta hai, 0 nahi aata.
learn.pro: A negative step walks downward and still excludes the stop, so arange(5, 0, -1) yields 5 through 1. A sign mismatch between start, stop and step produces an empty array rather than an error.
steps: Create the descending range and read the values.
Confirm the stop is excluded.
Use it to build reversed index positions.
learn.realWorld: Rendering a stack from top to bottom, or walking a time series backwards, is a negative-step range.
mistakes: Using a negative step with start < stop and getting an empty array.
Expecting 0 in the output.

learn.title: linspace controls the step you get
learn.body: `linspace(start, stop, n)` includes the endpoint and spaces `n` values evenly, which `arange` with floats cannot promise.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
learn.simple: Linspace me aap count dete ho, step khud nikalta hai: (stop − start) / (count − 1). Zyada points maange to step chhota ho jaayega.
learn.pro: linspace derives the step as the span divided by count − 1 so both endpoints are included. That is why increasing the count refines the grid without moving its ends.
steps: Create five points from 0 to 1.
Compute the step as range divided by (count − 1).
Change the count and observe the step change.
learn.realWorld: Plotting a smooth curve needs a density decision: more points, smaller step, same endpoints.
mistakes: Dividing by count instead of count − 1.
Assuming the step is an argument.

learn.title: arange versus linspace
learn.body: arange takes a step and can miss the stop value; linspace takes a count and always includes both ends. For floats, linspace is usually the safer choice.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
learn.simple: `arange` bolta hai "kitna-kitna badhao" — jaise 0 se shuru karke 0.25 ke steps. `linspace` bolta hai "kitne number chahiye" aur wo dono ends pakka include karta hai. Decimal steps me arange kabhi stop ko miss kar deta hai, isliye jab ginti zaroori ho to linspace safe hai.
learn.pro: arange is step-driven and excludes the stop, with float steps accumulating representation error; linspace is count-driven and includes both endpoints by construction. When a specification says "n points between a and b", linspace encodes that requirement directly and avoids off-by-one surprises.
learn.syntax: arange(start, stop, step) vs linspace(start, stop, count)
steps: Build the same range both ways and compare lengths.
Change the step and see arange's length change.
Change the count and see linspace's step change.
learn.visual:
arange(0,1,0.25) → 4 values, step fixed
linspace(0,1,5)  → 5 values, step derived
learn.realWorld: Grids for plotting and for numerical integration are linspace; index arithmetic is arange.
mistakes: Choosing arange for a required number of samples.
Choosing linspace when an exact step is the requirement.
revision: Pick by which quantity is fixed: step or count.

learn.title: Identity and eye
learn.body: eye builds an identity of any rectangular shape, while identity requires a square one. Both put ones on the main diagonal.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(3, dtype=int))
print(np.identity(2, dtype=int))
learn.simple: Identity matrix ek jaadu wala number hai: kisi bhi matrix ko usse multiply karo, matrix wahi rehta hai. `np.identity(2)` sirf square (2×2) banata hai, jabki `np.eye(3, 4)` lambi-chaudi shape bhi bana sakta hai — diagonal par 1, baaki jagah 0.
learn.pro: identity requires a square matrix; eye accepts independent row and column counts and places ones on the main diagonal of a rectangular shape. Both default to float64, so pass dtype=int when the matrix participates in integer arithmetic. For a rectangular shape only the main diagonal receives ones; every other cell is zero by construction.
steps: Create a 3×3 eye and compare with identity(3).
Create a rectangular eye(3, 4) that identity cannot build.
Pass dtype=int where integers matter.
learn.realWorld: Rectangular identity blocks appear when padding a design matrix or building a selection mask.
mistakes: Calling identity with two arguments.
Assuming eye's default dtype is int.
revision: identity is the square special case.

learn.title: diag builds a matrix from a vector
learn.body: `np.diag` turns a vector into a matrix with those values on the diagonal, and given a matrix it extracts that diagonal back out.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.diag([1, 2, 3]).tolist())
print(np.diag(np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.diag` ek vector ko aisa matrix bana deta hai jisme woh numbers tirchhi line par baithe hon, baaki jagah zero. Matrix do to woh tirchhi line wapas nikaal deta hai.
learn.pro: `np.diag` is two functions in one: given a vector it embeds the values on the main diagonal of a square matrix, and given a matrix it extracts that diagonal as a vector. The direction is decided by the input's number of dimensions, not by a flag, so an accidental 1-D input changes the meaning.
steps: Pass a vector to `np.diag` and print the square matrix.
Pass a matrix and print the extracted diagonal.
Compare the two shapes.
learn.realWorld: Covariance matrices and scaling operators are built from a diagonal vector.
mistakes: Forgetting that a 1-D input produces a matrix, not a diagonal.
revision: The input rank decides the direction.
Values off the diagonal are zero.

learn.title: tril and triu keep one triangle
learn.body: `tril` zeroes everything above the diagonal and `triu` zeroes everything below it. Both accept an offset to move the boundary.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 3), dtype=int)
print(np.tril(a).tolist())
print(np.triu(a, 1).sum())
learn.simple: `tril` diagonal ke neeche wala hissa rakhta hai aur upar sab zero kar deta hai; `triu` ulta karta hai. Dono me offset se boundary ko aage-peeche kar sakte ho.
learn.pro: `tril` and `triu` zero everything on one side of a diagonal selected by `k`, which is how triangular systems and masked attention patterns are built. They return a new array by default, so the original matrix is untouched unless you assign the result back.
steps: Create a matrix of ones.
Apply `tril` and print it.
Apply `triu` with an offset and compare.
learn.realWorld: A correlation matrix is often read as its lower triangle to avoid duplicate pairs.
mistakes: Assuming the operation edits the original matrix.
revision: Both return a new array by default.

learn.title: repeat repeats each element
learn.body: `np.repeat` duplicates individual values in place, so `[1, 2]` repeated twice becomes `[1, 1, 2, 2]`. It is different from tiling the whole sequence.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.repeat([1, 2], 2).tolist())
print(np.repeat([1, 2], [3, 1]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.repeat` har number ko usi jagah baar-baar likh deta hai: `[1, 2]` do baar karne par `[1, 1, 2, 2]`. Yeh poori list ko copy karne se alag hai.
learn.pro: `np.repeat` duplicates each element in place, and accepts a per-element count so different values can repeat different numbers of times. The output length is the sum of those counts, which is why it is the tool for expanding labels to match a longer feature array rather than for tiling a whole block.
steps: Repeat a short vector a fixed number of times.
Print the result and its length.
Repeat with per-element counts.
learn.realWorld: Expanding a per-group label to match the rows of each group is a repeat operation.
mistakes: Confusing repeat with tile and getting the wrong grouping.
revision: Output length is the sum of counts.

learn.title: tile repeats the whole block
learn.body: `np.tile` copies the entire sequence as a unit, so a pair tiled twice becomes the pair twice. The output length is the input length times the repeat count.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.tile([1, 2], 2).tolist())
print(np.tile([[1], [2]], (1, 2)).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.tile` poori list ko ek block maankar usko dohrata hai: `[1, 2]` do baar karne par `[1, 2, 1, 2]`. Output ki lambai input ki lambai guna repeat hoti hai.
learn.pro: `np.tile` repeats the entire array as a unit along each axis, so the output length is the input length multiplied by the repeat count. That block semantics is what makes it suitable for building periodic patterns, while `repeat` is the right call when each value itself must be duplicated.
steps: Tile a short vector twice.
Print the result and check the order.
Tile a column block along the second axis.
learn.visual:
[1 2] tiled 2 → [1 2 1 2]
block repeated as a unit
learn.realWorld: Periodic patterns and repeated feature blocks are built with tile.
mistakes: Using tile when each value itself should repeat.
revision: Output length multiplies by the repeat count.

learn.title: logspace spaces powers of ten
learn.body: `np.logspace(start, stop, n)` returns values evenly spaced on a log scale, which is how learning rates and frequencies are sampled.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.logspace(0, 2, 3).tolist())
print(np.logspace(0, 1, 3, base=2).round(3).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.logspace` numbers ko log scale par barabar gap me deta hai — jaise 1, 10, 100. Learning rate ya frequency aise ranges me hi ghoomte hain.
learn.pro: `np.logspace(start, stop, n)` returns values evenly spaced in the exponent, so consecutive entries share a constant ratio rather than a constant difference. That is why it is used for learning-rate sweeps and frequency grids, where a linear `linspace` would spend most samples in the large end.
steps: Ask for three values from 10⁰ to 10².
Print them and check the ratio.
Change the base and compare.
learn.realWorld: Learning-rate sweeps and frequency grids are sampled on a log scale.
mistakes: Expecting equal differences between consecutive values.
revision: Spacing is constant in the exponent.
The ratio between neighbours is fixed.

learn.title: fromfunction builds from indices
learn.body: `np.fromfunction` calls a function once per index tuple, so a grid can be written as an expression of its row and column numbers.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
grid = np.fromfunction(lambda i, j: i * 10 + j, (2, 3))
print(grid.tolist())
learn.simple: `np.fromfunction` har cell ke row aur column number par tumhara function chalata hai, isliye grid ko uske coordinates ka formula likh kar bana sakte ho — loop likhne ki zarurat nahi.
learn.pro: `np.fromfunction` calls the supplied function once per index tuple over the requested shape, so a grid can be expressed directly as a function of its coordinates. The callable receives index arrays, not scalars, which is why the function must be written with vectorised arithmetic to benefit.
steps: Define a function of row and column index.
Pass it with the desired shape.
Print the grid and verify one cell by hand.
learn.realWorld: Coordinate grids for plots and physics simulations come from index formulas.
mistakes: Writing a scalar-only function that cannot take index arrays.

interview.q: When is `linspace` a better choice than `arange`?
interview.answer: When the number of points matters and the endpoints must be exact. `linspace` computes each point from the count, avoiding the floating step error that can add or drop the last element of `arange`.

interview.q: What is the difference between `zeros` and `empty`?
interview.answer: `zeros` writes every element as 0; `empty` only allocates, so the values are whatever was in memory. Use `empty` only when you will overwrite all of it.

interview.q: Why does `np.eye(3, 4)` exist when `np.identity(3)` does?
interview.answer: `eye` allows a rectangular shape and an offset diagonal via `k`; `identity` is only the square case.

interview.q: Why does `np.full` take a shape but `np.full_like` does not?
interview.answer: `full_like` copies the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is why it takes that array instead of a shape.

interview.q: What does `np.arange(5).reshape(1, -1)` produce?
interview.answer: A single row with five columns: the `1` fixes the row count and `-1` infers the columns.

interview.q: Why is `np.zeros` slower than `np.empty`?
interview.answer: `zeros` writes every element; `empty` only allocates, leaving whatever bytes were there.

interview.q: What does `np.full_like(a, 7)` reuse from `a`?
interview.answer: Its shape and dtype, so only the fill value is new.

interview.q: How do you build a diagonal matrix from a vector?
interview.answer: `np.diag(v)` places the values on the main diagonal of a square matrix.

interview.q: Why does `np.arange(5.0)` produce floats?
interview.answer: The start value is a float, so the inferred dtype is float64 rather than an integer type.

interview.q: A test fixture needs 50 points from 0 to 10 inclusive. Why is np.linspace(0, 10, 50) safer than np.arange(0, 10, 0.2)?
interview.answer: linspace takes a count and always includes both ends; arange takes a step, can include the stop unexpectedly with float steps, and can produce 50 or 51 points depending on rounding. Choose by count when the count is the requirement.

followUps.q: When is `arange` the better call than `linspace`?
followUps.answer: When the step is the requirement — integer ranges and fixed increments where the count is incidental. `linspace` wins when the count is what the test asserts.

followUps.q: How do you confirm the count before relying on it?
followUps.answer: Check `.size` (and the first/last values) on a tiny equivalent range first; float steps are exactly where off-by-one surprises appear.

interview.q: An identity matrix is needed for a 3×4 system, but np.identity(3, 4) raises. What is the right call?
interview.answer: identity only builds square matrices. Use np.eye(3, 4) (rows, columns), which puts ones on the main diagonal of a rectangular shape.

followUps.q: What does the second argument of `np.eye` change?
followUps.answer: The number of columns: `np.eye(3, 4)` is three rows by four columns, with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

followUps.q: How would you build the same rectangular identity without `eye`?
followUps.answer: `a = np.zeros((3, 4)); np.fill_diagonal(a, 1)` — useful when the diagonal value is not 1.

defense.q: Defend using `arange` for indices and `linspace` for plotted ranges.
defense.answer: Integer positions want an exact step and an exclusive stop, which is what `arange` gives. A plotted range wants a fixed count with both ends included, which `linspace` guarantees.

defense.q: Why can `np.arange(0, 1, 0.1)` return eleven values instead of ten?
defense.answer: The step is not exactly representable in binary, so repeated addition lands just below or above 1.0. A `linspace(0, 1, 10)` avoids the ambiguity.

defense.q: Defend choosing the dtype at creation instead of fixing it later.
defense.answer: The dtype decides memory and the arithmetic that follows; converting later copies the whole array and can change results. Declaring it once keeps the intent visible.

defense.q: Defend `linspace` for a fixed number of dashboard points.
defense.answer: The chart needs exactly N points across a closed range, and `linspace` guarantees the count and both endpoints without floating-step drift.

defense.q: Why does `np.eye(3)` print floats?
defense.answer: The default dtype is float64, because an identity is usually used in floating-point algebra. Pass `dtype=int` for an integer one.

defense.q: Defend building an index array once and reusing it.
defense.answer: Positions rarely change while data does, so recomputing them wastes work and risks drift. One array documents the layout the rest of the code assumes.

defense.q: Defend `zeros_like` over an explicit shape when copying a layout.
defense.answer: It keeps shape and dtype in one expression, so they cannot drift apart when the source changes.

defense.q: Explain why `np.empty` is not a shortcut for zeros.
defense.answer: It leaves whatever bytes were in memory, so values are arbitrary until written.

defense.q: Defend computing an index grid once and reusing it.
defense.answer: The positions do not depend on the data, and recomputing them only adds work and a chance to drift.

modules.title: Data Types and Type Conversion
modules.goal: Choose an explicit dtype, convert safely with astype and understand overflow, precision and memory cost.

topics.title: Converting with astype
topics.body: astype returns a NEW array with the requested dtype and truncates floats toward zero, so 1.7 becomes 1; the original array is untouched.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.7, 2.9])
print(a.astype(int))

topics.title: Overflow is silent
topics.body: Integer dtypes wrap around on overflow instead of raising, so uint8 arithmetic can turn a large result into a small one — use a wider dtype when the range is not guaranteed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8)
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Smaller dtype, smaller memory
topics.body: float32 uses four bytes per element against eight for float64; choosing it deliberately cuts memory and bandwidth in half, at the cost of precision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)
print(a.dtype, a.nbytes)

topics.title: astype truncates toward zero
topics.body: Casting float to int does not round: it drops the fractional part, so 1.9 becomes 1 and -1.9 becomes -1.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1.9, -1.9]).astype(int))

topics.title: Text becomes a number with astype
topics.body: Numeric strings cast cleanly to int or float, which is exactly why one bad token in a loaded column raises instead of silently becoming zero.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["1", "2"]).astype(float))

topics.title: Division always yields floats
topics.body: True division produces float64 even when both operands are integers, so `int / int` never silently loses the remainder.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2]) / 2).dtype)

topics.title: Numbers become booleans by truthiness
topics.body: Casting to bool keeps only whether a value is non-zero, so 0 becomes False and every other number becomes True.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([0, 1, 2]).astype(bool))

topics.title: Count with a boolean array
topics.body: Booleans add as 1 and 0, so sum() on a mask counts the matches without any branching code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False, True])
print(m.sum())

topics.title: dtype reports the element type
topics.body: The dtype belongs to the whole array, not to each element. Mixing an int and a float array promotes to float.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0]).dtype)

topics.title: A float array prints a decimal point
topics.body: The printed form already tells you the dtype: `[1. 2.]` is float, `[1 2]` is int. Reading the output is faster than checking.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2], dtype=float))

topics.title: Each dtype has a size in bytes
topics.body: `itemsize` is bytes per element. Ten million `int64` values need 80 MB before any copy, which is why dtype choice is a memory decision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dtype('int64').itemsize, np.dtype('int32').itemsize)

topics.title: A comparison produces booleans
topics.body: Masks are a dtype, not a special object. `bool` arrays are one byte per element and are the currency of filtering.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([1, 2, 3]) > 1).dtype)

topics.title: Casting a float to an integer truncates
topics.body: astype does not round; it drops the fractional part toward zero. Convert after rounding when the value should not lose precision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.9, -1.9, 2.5])
print(a.astype(np.int64))
print(np.round(a).astype(np.int64))

topics.title: Type promotion with result_type
topics.body: When two dtypes meet in an operation NumPy promotes to one that can hold both. result_type tells you which dtype that will be before you compute anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.result_type(np.int32, np.float32))
print((np.array([1], dtype=np.int8) + 0.5).dtype)

topics.title: Casting to a wider type is lossless
topics.body: Moving from a smaller integer to a wider one preserves every value, which is why int32 → int64 is safe and the reverse is not.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.int8)
print(a.astype(np.int64).dtype, int(a.astype(np.int64).sum()))

topics.title: Booleans cast back to integers
topics.body: Casting a bool array to int gives exactly 1 and 0, which is why boolean counts and arithmetic masks compose.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False, True])
print(m.astype(int).tolist(), int(m.astype(int).sum()))

topics.title: float32 keeps fewer digits
topics.body: float32 stores about seven significant digits against float64's fifteen. Printing a float32 array shows the shorter precision directly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.234567890123], dtype=np.float32)
print(a, a.dtype)

topics.title: int8 has a small range
topics.body: An int8 holds only -128 to 127, so a counter that grows past that wraps. Checking `np.iinfo` before choosing a narrow type is the cheap safeguard.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
info = np.iinfo(np.int8)
print(info.min, info.max)
print((np.array([127], dtype=np.int8) + 1)[0])

topics.title: astype accepts a dtype string
topics.body: The dtype argument can be an object or a short string like `'f4'` or `'int32'`, which keeps conversions readable in configuration-driven code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3).astype('f4').dtype)
print(np.arange(3).astype('int16').dtype)

topics.title: promote_types compares two dtypes
topics.body: `np.promote_types` returns the smallest dtype that can represent both inputs, which is the question to ask before mixing arrays in an expression.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.promote_types('int8', 'int16'))
print(np.promote_types('float32', 'int64'))

interviewBank.q: Why does adding `0.0` to an integer array change more than the values?
interviewBank.answer: It promotes the dtype to float64, doubling memory and changing later arithmetic. Integer division and overflow are no longer possible after that promotion.

interviewBank.q: How do you choose between `float32` and `float64`?
interviewBank.answer: `float64` for accumulation and anything needing precision; `float32` when memory and bandwidth dominate and about seven significant digits are enough, as in many model inputs.

interviewBank.q: What is the risk of `astype(int)` on float data?
interviewBank.answer: It truncates toward zero rather than rounding, so 1.9 becomes 1, and it silently discards fractional data. For rounding, use `np.round` first and say so.

interviewBank.q: What do you gain and lose with `dtype="int8"`?
interviewBank.answer: Four times less memory than int64, at the cost of a range of only -128 to 127, so overflow becomes possible.

interviewBank.q: What happens to a float array cast to `int32`?
interviewBank.answer: Each value is truncated toward zero, losing the fractional part without warning.

interviewBank.q: Why is `0.1 + 0.2` not exactly `0.3` in float64?
interviewBank.answer: Neither decimal is representable exactly in binary, so the stored approximations add to a value one bit away from the nearest 0.3.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.result_type` decide?
interviewBank.answer: The dtype that a set of operands would promote to in an operation.

interviewBank.q: How do you inspect the range of an integer dtype?
interviewBank.answer: `np.iinfo(dtype)` gives its minimum and maximum; `np.finfo` does the same for floats.

interviewBank.q: Why is `float16` risky for accumulation?
interviewBank.answer: It has roughly three decimal digits, so repeated additions lose precision quickly.

interviewBank.q: A price column is stored as float64 and cast to int to save memory; customers see 99 instead of 99.99. What went wrong?
interviewBank.answer: astype(int) truncates toward zero, it does not round. Either round first (`np.round(price).astype(int)`) or keep cents as integers at the source; casting decimals to integers always loses the fraction.

followUps.q: Which rounding rule does `np.round` use at exactly .5?
followUps.answer: Round-half-to-even (banker's rounding), so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4. Code that assumes "always up" is wrong at the boundary.

followUps.q: Why are integer cents often preferred for money?
followUps.answer: Integer arithmetic is exact within range, so sums do not drift; convert to a display string only at the edge.

interviewBank.q: An int32 array of large sensor counters overflows silently negative. How would you have caught it before shipping?
interviewBank.answer: Check np.result_type and the dtype's maximum (np.iinfo(np.int32).max) against the expected range, or promote to int64. NumPy does not raise on overflow for integer arithmetic, so the check has to be explicit.

followUps.q: How do you detect an overflow after it happened?
followUps.answer: Compare the result against `np.iinfo(dtype).min/max`, or watch for a sign flip; a negative counter or wrapped value is the fingerprint of overflow.

followUps.q: Why does NumPy not raise the way Python ints do?
followUps.answer: NumPy uses fixed-width machine integers for speed, so overflow wraps by definition; detecting it costs a check on every operation.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing coordinates as `float32`.
defenseBank.answer: Screen and sensor coordinates rarely need more than seven digits, and halving the bytes halves bandwidth in rendering and model input. The error is far below one pixel.

defenseBank.q: Explain integer overflow, and why `uint8` arithmetic wraps instead of raising.
defenseBank.answer: Fixed-width integers have a fixed range, so arithmetic is modular: `uint8(200) + uint8(100)` wraps to 44. NumPy keeps the C behaviour rather than paying a check per element.

defenseBank.q: A model expects `float32` but your pipeline produces `float64`. Defend where you convert.
defenseBank.answer: Convert once, at the boundary where the model is called, after all precise arithmetic is finished. Converting early throws away precision the pipeline still needs and gains nothing.

defenseBank.q: Defend float64 until a calculation reaches a money boundary.
defenseBank.answer: Intermediate work needs precision, and rounding should happen once, deliberately, at the boundary. Rounded intermediate values compound error.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `int + float` promoting to float64 surprises people.
defenseBank.answer: The dtype changes silently, so later integer division or exact equality no longer behaves as before. The promotion is correct, but it is not obvious.

defenseBank.q: Defend stating a dtype contract in a data loader.
defenseBank.answer: Every downstream step inherits the dtype, so declaring it once prevents implicit promotions and documents the memory budget.

defenseBank.q: Defend writing `dtype=np.float32` explicitly in a loader.
defenseBank.answer: The default float64 doubles memory and silently changes what downstream code receives.

defenseBank.q: Explain why casting a large float to `int8` can wrap.
defenseBank.answer: The value is forced into a fixed-width integer range, which is modular rather than saturating.

defenseBank.q: Defend checking `np.can_cast` instead of trusting `astype`.
defenseBank.answer: `astype` always converts, while `can_cast` states whether information would be lost.
