modules.title: Slicing and Array Views
modules.goal: Slice arrays with start/stop/step, slice rows and columns, and know when a slice shares memory.

topics.title: Slice with a step
topics.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns
topics.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

topics.title: A slice is a view
topics.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

topics.title: Reverse a row with a negative step
topics.body: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[::-1])

topics.title: Slice assignment writes through
topics.body: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Step in both dimensions
topics.body: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

topics.title: Copy breaks the view link
topics.body: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

topics.title: Slices clamp instead of failing
topics.body: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

topics.title: The end of a slice is exclusive
topics.body: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

topics.title: Omit a bound to keep it open
topics.body: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

topics.title: A step of two skips elements
topics.body: The third slot of a slice is the step. It can be larger than one or negative, and it never changes the source array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(10)[::2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns at once
topics.body: Each axis gets its own slice separated by a comma. The result is a rectangular block, never a ragged one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[1:, :2])

topics.title: Writing through a slice edits the original
topics.body: Slicing returns a view of the same buffer, so writing through the slice changes the original. Use copy when the two must be independent.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99
print(a, b)

topics.title: Reverse with a negative step
topics.body: A step of -1 walks the axis backwards and keeps the shape otherwise unchanged. The same syntax works per axis on a 2-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::-1])
print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])[::-1, ::-1])

topics.title: Slice with a negative start
topics.body: A negative start counts from the end and the stop still excludes its position, so `a[-3:-1]` keeps two values ending before the last one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[-3:-1].tolist())
print(a[-2:].tolist())

topics.title: Slice a three-dimensional array
topics.body: Every axis can take its own slice, so a 3-D array is narrowed one axis at a time without loops.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print(a[:, 1, :].shape)
print(a[0, :, 1].tolist())

topics.title: Assign a scalar to a slice
topics.body: A scalar on the right of a slice assignment fills every selected cell at once, which is how a block is cleared or reset.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
a[1:4] = 0
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Assign an array to a slice
topics.body: An array on the right must match the slice's shape. The values are copied position by position into the same buffer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros(4, dtype=int)
a[1:3] = np.array([7, 8])
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Slice with an omitted stop
topics.body: Leaving the stop empty means "to the end", so one number plus a colon is enough for a tail. Omitting both bounds copies the whole axis as a view.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[3:].tolist())
print(a[:].tolist())

topics.title: Slice every other column
topics.body: A step on the column axis samples alternate features in one expression, and the row axis stays untouched.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a[:, ::2].tolist())

lab.title: Slice a matrix
lab.brief: From a 4x4 matrix, print the top-left 2x2 block and the last column.

interviewBank.q: When does a slice return a view rather than a copy?
interviewBank.answer: Always for basic slicing: it only changes offset, shape and strides on the existing buffer. Fancy indexing and boolean masks are the operations that copy.

interviewBank.q: Why does assigning to a slice change the original array?
interviewBank.answer: The slice shares the buffer, so the assignment writes through it. Use `.copy()` when the caller must keep the original intact.

interviewBank.q: What does a negative step such as `arr[::-1]` actually do?
interviewBank.answer: It reverses the traversal by negating the stride; no data moves, so the result is a view that reads backwards.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `arr[::2]` and `arr[1::2]`?
interviewBank.answer: The first takes even positions starting at 0; the second starts at 1 and takes every second value after it.

interviewBank.q: How do you reverse only the rows of a 2-D array?
interviewBank.answer: Use `arr[::-1]`, which flips axis 0 and leaves the columns in order.

interviewBank.q: Why does `arr[2:2]` return an empty array instead of raising?
interviewBank.answer: A slice with equal bounds is a legal empty selection, not an error, which keeps loop code simple.

interviewBank.q: What does a slice with step -1 return?
interviewBank.answer: A reversed view over the same buffer, with no data moved.

interviewBank.q: How do you take every second row of a matrix?
interviewBank.answer: `arr[::2]`, which slices axis 0 and keeps the columns.

interviewBank.q: Why is `arr[:]` not a copy?
interviewBank.answer: It is a full slice of the same buffer, so writes through it reach the original.

interviewBank.q: A rolling window is extracted with `series[i:i+window]` and stored in a list; later someone edits one window and the whole series changes. Why?
interviewBank.answer: Each slice is a view of the same buffer, so editing the window edits the series. Copy the window (`series[i:i+window].copy()`) when it will be stored and modified independently.

followUps.q: What is the cheapest fix if callers expect independent windows?
followUps.answer: Copy at extraction (`series[i:i+window].copy()`); it costs one buffer per window but removes hidden coupling.

followUps.q: How do you test that a helper returns a copy?
followUps.answer: Mutate the returned array and assert the input is unchanged, or assert `np.shares_memory(result, source)` is False.

interviewBank.q: Reversing a 200 MB price series with `[::-1]` takes almost no time. What did NumPy actually do?
interviewBank.answer: It returned a view with negative strides — no data was moved. Any operation that needs contiguous order (such as some libraries' C-API calls) will copy later, which is where the cost appears.

followUps.q: Which later operations force a real copy after a reverse?
followUps.answer: Anything needing contiguous layout: `np.ascontiguousarray`, C-API consumers, and some library calls. The copy happens there, not at the slice.

followUps.q: How do you measure whether the copy happened?
followUps.answer: Check `.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS']` and `np.shares_memory`, or watch resident memory before and after the operation rather than timing the slice alone.

defenseBank.q: Defend calling `.copy()` when trimming a training set.
defenseBank.answer: A slice keeps the whole original buffer alive, so a small training split can pin a large dataset in memory. The copy lets the original be freed.

defenseBank.q: Explain how `arr[1:3] = 0` can surprise a caller who still holds a slice of `arr`.
defenseBank.answer: Both names point at the same buffer, so the write is visible through the slice too. That aliasing is the source of many "the data changed by itself" reports.

defenseBank.q: A slice with step 2 has non-contiguous strides. Defend that as a feature, not a bug.
defenseBank.answer: Strides describe how to walk the buffer, so a step of 2 is just a doubled stride. Nothing is copied, and any ufunc reads the elements correctly.

defenseBank.q: Defend clamping slice bounds in a parser.
defenseBank.answer: Input lengths vary, and Python slicing already clamps, so explicit `min(n, len(a))` documents the intent without changing behaviour.

defenseBank.q: Explain why writing to `arr[:, 0]` changes every reference to that array.
defenseBank.answer: The column is a view on the shared buffer, so assignment writes real memory rather than a copy. Any other name for that array sees it.

defenseBank.q: Defend a negative-step slice over `np.flip` when trimming.
defenseBank.answer: It expresses the reversal without a function call and returns a view, so it is cheaper when no copy is needed.

defenseBank.q: Defend copying a slice before handing it to another function.
defenseBank.answer: The callee may mutate it, and a view would change the caller's data as a side effect.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a slice can keep a large source array alive.
defenseBank.answer: The view holds a reference to the buffer, so the whole allocation stays in memory.

defenseBank.q: Defend slicing over fancy indexing for contiguous blocks.
defenseBank.answer: A slice needs no gather and returns a view, while fancy indexing always copies.

learn.title: Slice with a step
learn.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

learn.title: Slice rows and columns
learn.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

learn.title: A slice is a view
learn.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

learn.title: Reverse a row with a negative step
learn.body: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[::-1])

learn.title: Slice assignment writes through
learn.body: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

learn.title: Step in both dimensions
learn.body: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

learn.title: Copy breaks the view link
learn.body: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

learn.title: Slices clamp instead of failing
learn.body: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

learn.title: The end of a slice is exclusive
learn.body: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

learn.title: Omit a bound to keep it open
learn.body: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

learn.title: A step of two skips elements
learn.body: The third slot of a slice is the step. It can be larger than one or negative, and it never changes the source array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(10)[::2])

learn.title: Slice rows and columns at once
learn.body: Each axis gets its own slice separated by a comma. The result is a rectangular block, never a ragged one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[1:, :2])

learn.title: Writing through a slice edits the original
learn.body: Slicing returns a view of the same buffer, so writing through the slice changes the original. Use copy when the two must be independent.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99
print(a, b)
learn.simple: Slice koi nayi copy nahi hoti — wo usi dabbe ki ek khidki hai. Agar tum khidki se andar haath daal kar number badloge, to asli array bhi badal jayega. Agar tumhe alag copy chahiye to `.copy()` likho.
learn.pro: A basic slice returns a view: same buffer, different offset and strides, so an assignment through the view mutates the parent. Call .copy() when the slice must outlive or diverge from the original, and prove the distinction with np.shares_memory.

learn.title: Reverse with a negative step
learn.body: A step of -1 walks the axis backwards and keeps the shape otherwise unchanged. The same syntax works per axis on a 2-D array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::-1])
print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])[::-1, ::-1])
learn.simple: Step `-1` ka matlab hai peeche ki taraf chalo — jaise seedhi par ulta utarna. `a[::-1]` poora array ulta kar deta hai, aur 2D me `[::-1, ::-1]` dono directions ulta kar deta hai. Ye naya data nahi banata, sirf padhne ka rukh badalta hai.
learn.pro: A negative step reverses the traversal of an axis by negating that axis's stride; the buffer is untouched, so the result is a view. Combining negative steps across axes flips rows and columns in one expression, and any later contiguity requirement will force a copy.

learn.title: Slice with a negative start
learn.body: A negative start counts from the end and the stop still excludes its position, so `a[-3:-1]` keeps two values ending before the last one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[-3:-1].tolist())
print(a[-2:].tolist())
learn.simple: Negative start end se ginti shuru karta hai, aur stop wali jagah phir bhi shaamil nahi hoti. Isliye `a[-3:-1]` do values deta hai, aakhri se pehle tak.
learn.pro: A negative start is resolved against the axis length before the slice is taken, and the stop remains exclusive. `a[-3:-1]` therefore keeps two values ending just before the last, which is the safe way to drop only a trailing element.
steps: Create a vector from 0 to 5.
Slice with a negative start and stop.
Print the tail with an open stop.
learn.realWorld: Keeping the last two readings of a sensor stream uses a negative slice.
mistakes: Expecting the stop index to be included.
revision: Negative bounds count from the end.

learn.title: Slice a three-dimensional array
learn.body: Every axis can take its own slice, so a 3-D array is narrowed one axis at a time without loops.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print(a[:, 1, :].shape)
print(a[0, :, 1].tolist())
learn.simple: 3-D array me har axis ki apni slice lag sakti hai, isliye ek hi line me volume ka ek tukda nikal aata hai — loop ki zarurat nahi.
learn.pro: Every axis of a three-dimensional array accepts its own slice, so one expression can narrow a volume to a sub-block. The resulting shape is the tuple of the chosen lengths, which makes the slice itself the documentation of what was selected.
steps: Build a (2, 3, 4) array.
Slice the middle axis and print the shape.
Slice a single depth and column, then compare.
learn.realWorld: Extracting one channel from an image batch is a middle-axis slice.
mistakes: Mixing the axis order and selecting the wrong channel.
revision: The remaining axes give the output shape.

learn.title: Assign a scalar to a slice
learn.body: A scalar on the right of a slice assignment fills every selected cell at once, which is how a block is cleared or reset.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
a[1:4] = 0
print(a.tolist())
learn.simple: Slice ke left side par ek number do to woh chuni hui saari jagahon me ek saath chala jaata hai. Poore block ko reset karne ka sabse seedha tarika yahi hai.
learn.pro: Assigning a scalar to a basic slice fills every selected cell in one operation, writing into the existing buffer rather than creating a new array. That in-place behaviour is why a slice assignment is visible through every view of the same memory.
steps: Create a vector.
Assign zero to a middle slice.
Print the array to confirm only that range changed.
learn.realWorld: Clearing a padded region of a batch is a slice assignment.
mistakes: Using a copy and expecting the source to change.
revision: A basic slice writes into the buffer.
Every view of that buffer sees the change.

learn.title: Assign an array to a slice
learn.body: An array on the right must match the slice's shape. The values are copied position by position into the same buffer.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros(4, dtype=int)
a[1:3] = np.array([7, 8])
print(a.tolist())
learn.simple: Slice me array daalne ke liye uski shape slice se match karni chahiye. Values ek-ek karke usi memory me copy hoti hain.
learn.pro: An array assigned to a basic slice must match the slice's shape, and its values are copied position by position into the destination buffer. Broadcasting expands only size-one dimensions; a genuinely different shape raises instead of silently truncating.

Assign a two-value array to a slice of length two.
Print the result and try a mismatched shape.

slice length 2 ← array length 2
mismatch raises ValueError
learn.realWorld: Filling a column range from a computed vector is a routine preprocessing step.
mistakes: Assigning a longer array to a shorter slice.
revision: Values are copied into the destination.

learn.title: Slice with an omitted stop
learn.body: Leaving the stop empty means "to the end", so one number plus a colon is enough for a tail. Omitting both bounds copies the whole axis as a view.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[3:].tolist())
print(a[:].tolist())
learn.simple: Stop khaali chhodne ka matlab hai 'aakhri tak'. Isliye `a[3:]` tail deta hai, aur `a[:]` poori axis ka view.
learn.pro: An omitted stop means the axis length, so `a[3:]` keeps the tail and `a[:]` selects the whole axis as a view. Because both bounds are optional, the slice stays a basic selection and never triggers advanced-index copying.
steps: Create a vector.
Print the tail from index 3.
Print a full slice and confirm it is a view.
learn.realWorld: Skipping a header row is `a[1:]`, the most common tail slice.
mistakes: Assuming an omitted stop copies the data.
revision: An omitted stop means the axis length.
A full slice is still a view.

learn.title: Slice every other column
learn.body: A step on the column axis samples alternate features in one expression, and the row axis stays untouched.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a[:, ::2].tolist())
learn.simple: Column axis par step lagane se alternate features ek hi expression me aa jaate hain, aur rows waise hi rehti hain. Yeh manual loop se kaafi saaf hai.
learn.pro: A step on the column axis samples alternate features while the row axis stays untouched, producing a strided view rather than a copy. That view is cheap, but its non-contiguous layout can make a later operation copy when a library requires contiguous memory.
steps: Build a matrix with four columns.
Slice alternate columns.
Print the shape to confirm two columns remain.
learn.realWorld: Dropping every second feature during a quick experiment uses a step slice.
mistakes: Putting the step on the row axis by mistake.
revision: A step belongs to one axis.
The result is a strided view.

interview.q: When does a slice return a view rather than a copy?
interview.answer: Always for basic slicing: it only changes offset, shape and strides on the existing buffer. Fancy indexing and boolean masks are the operations that copy.

interview.q: Why does assigning to a slice change the original array?
interview.answer: The slice shares the buffer, so the assignment writes through it. Use `.copy()` when the caller must keep the original intact.

interview.q: What does a negative step such as `arr[::-1]` actually do?
interview.answer: It reverses the traversal by negating the stride; no data moves, so the result is a view that reads backwards.

interview.q: What is the difference between `arr[::2]` and `arr[1::2]`?
interview.answer: The first takes even positions starting at 0; the second starts at 1 and takes every second value after it.

interview.q: How do you reverse only the rows of a 2-D array?
interview.answer: Use `arr[::-1]`, which flips axis 0 and leaves the columns in order.

interview.q: Why does `arr[2:2]` return an empty array instead of raising?
interview.answer: A slice with equal bounds is a legal empty selection, not an error, which keeps loop code simple.

interview.q: What does a slice with step -1 return?
interview.answer: A reversed view over the same buffer, with no data moved.

interview.q: How do you take every second row of a matrix?
interview.answer: `arr[::2]`, which slices axis 0 and keeps the columns.

interview.q: Why is `arr[:]` not a copy?
interview.answer: It is a full slice of the same buffer, so writes through it reach the original.

interview.q: A rolling window is extracted with `series[i:i+window]` and stored in a list; later someone edits one window and the whole series changes. Why?
interview.answer: Each slice is a view of the same buffer, so editing the window edits the series. Copy the window (`series[i:i+window].copy()`) when it will be stored and modified independently.

followUps.q: What is the cheapest fix if callers expect independent windows?
followUps.answer: Copy at extraction (`series[i:i+window].copy()`); it costs one buffer per window but removes hidden coupling.

followUps.q: How do you test that a helper returns a copy?
followUps.answer: Mutate the returned array and assert the input is unchanged, or assert `np.shares_memory(result, source)` is False.

interview.q: Reversing a 200 MB price series with `[::-1]` takes almost no time. What did NumPy actually do?
interview.answer: It returned a view with negative strides — no data was moved. Any operation that needs contiguous order (such as some libraries' C-API calls) will copy later, which is where the cost appears.

followUps.q: Which later operations force a real copy after a reverse?
followUps.answer: Anything needing contiguous layout: `np.ascontiguousarray`, C-API consumers, and some library calls. The copy happens there, not at the slice.

followUps.q: How do you measure whether the copy happened?
followUps.answer: Check `.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS']` and `np.shares_memory`, or watch resident memory before and after the operation rather than timing the slice alone.

defense.q: Defend calling `.copy()` when trimming a training set.
defense.answer: A slice keeps the whole original buffer alive, so a small training split can pin a large dataset in memory. The copy lets the original be freed.

defense.q: Explain how `arr[1:3] = 0` can surprise a caller who still holds a slice of `arr`.
defense.answer: Both names point at the same buffer, so the write is visible through the slice too. That aliasing is the source of many "the data changed by itself" reports.

defense.q: A slice with step 2 has non-contiguous strides. Defend that as a feature, not a bug.
defense.answer: Strides describe how to walk the buffer, so a step of 2 is just a doubled stride. Nothing is copied, and any ufunc reads the elements correctly.

defense.q: Defend clamping slice bounds in a parser.
defense.answer: Input lengths vary, and Python slicing already clamps, so explicit `min(n, len(a))` documents the intent without changing behaviour.

defense.q: Explain why writing to `arr[:, 0]` changes every reference to that array.
defense.answer: The column is a view on the shared buffer, so assignment writes real memory rather than a copy. Any other name for that array sees it.

defense.q: Defend a negative-step slice over `np.flip` when trimming.
defense.answer: It expresses the reversal without a function call and returns a view, so it is cheaper when no copy is needed.

defense.q: Defend copying a slice before handing it to another function.
defense.answer: The callee may mutate it, and a view would change the caller's data as a side effect.

defense.q: Explain why a slice can keep a large source array alive.
defense.answer: The view holds a reference to the buffer, so the whole allocation stays in memory.

defense.q: Defend slicing over fancy indexing for contiguous blocks.
defense.answer: A slice needs no gather and returns a view, while fancy indexing always copies.

modules.title: Array Reshaping and Manipulation
modules.goal: Reshape, flatten, transpose, combine and split arrays so data fits the shape an operation needs.

topics.title: reshape
topics.body: reshape changes the shape without changing the data or its order; the element count must stay the same, so 6 values can become (2, 3) but never (4, 2).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)

topics.title: ravel and transpose
topics.body: ravel flattens to one dimension (often as a view) and .T swaps rows with columns; together they move a matrix between the two layouts most libraries expect.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.ravel(), a.T)

topics.title: concatenate and stack
topics.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis and stack creates a NEW axis, which is why two length-2 arrays stack into a (2, 2) matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.concatenate([a, a]), np.stack([a, a]).shape)

topics.title: reshape with -1 infers the size
topics.body: One dimension may be written as -1 and NumPy fills it from the element count, which is how you ask for rows of a fixed width without arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(-1, 2))

topics.title: newaxis makes a column
topics.body: Indexing with np.newaxis inserts an axis of length 1, turning a (3,) vector into a (3, 1) column that broadcasting can line up against rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3)[:, np.newaxis].shape)

topics.title: stack adds a new axis
topics.body: stack joins arrays of equal shape along a brand-new axis, so two (2,) arrays become a (2, 2) matrix instead of a (4,) flat one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.stack([np.zeros(2), np.ones(2)]).shape)

topics.title: split cuts an array into pieces
topics.body: split divides an array into equal parts and returns a list, which is handy for batches or train/test cuts.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.split(np.arange(4), 2))

topics.title: flatten always copies
topics.body: flatten returns a fresh 1-D array, so editing it never touches the source; ravel returns a view whenever the layout allows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
f = a.flatten()
f[0] = 9
print(a[0])

topics.title: ravel flattens without copying when it can
topics.body: A contiguous array can be flattened as a view. `base` proves whether the new array still points at the old memory.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.ravel().base is a)

topics.title: reshape turns a vector into a column
topics.body: `(4, 1)` and `(1, 4)` look similar but broadcast in opposite directions. The shape is the whole difference.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
print(a.reshape(4, 1))

topics.title: vstack stacks arrays into rows
topics.body: `vstack` adds a new first axis, so two `(2,)` arrays become one `(2, 2)` array. `hstack` joins along the existing axis instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.vstack([np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4])]))

topics.title: Transpose swaps the axes
topics.body: `.T` reverses the axis order and is a view, not a copy. For a matrix it swaps rows with columns.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.shape)

topics.title: reshape returns a view when it can
topics.body: reshape never copies if the existing strides allow the new shape; ravel returns a view where possible and a copy otherwise. Use flatten when a copy is required.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
b[0, 0] = 99
print(a, b.shape)

topics.title: Stack and concatenate
topics.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis, vstack adds rows and hstack adds columns. stack creates a new axis instead of joining one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(np.vstack([a, b]))
print(np.hstack([a, b]))
print(np.stack([a, b]).shape)

topics.title: reshape groups values in C order
topics.body: Reshaping walks the buffer left to right, then down, so a flat `0..5` becomes `[[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]`. The order is C by default.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(2, 3).tolist())
print(a.reshape(3, 2).tolist())

topics.title: ravel returns a flat view
topics.body: ravel flattens without copying when the layout allows it, so the result may share memory with the source. Check with shares_memory before mutating it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.ravel().tolist(), np.shares_memory(a, a.ravel()))

topics.title: flatten returns a copy
topics.body: flatten always allocates, so the result is independent of the source. That is the safe choice when a helper expects to modify its input.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4).reshape(2, 2)
f = a.flatten()
f[0] = 99
print(a.tolist(), f.tolist())

topics.title: concatenate along columns
topics.body: With `axis=1`, concatenate joins matching rows side by side, so the row count must agree and the column counts add.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
b = np.ones((2, 1), dtype=int)
print(np.concatenate([a, b], axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: split into equal parts
topics.body: `np.split` divides an array along an axis when the length divides evenly; otherwise use array_split, which allows unequal pieces.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
parts = np.split(np.arange(6), 3)
print([p.tolist() for p in parts])

topics.title: transpose a three-dimensional array
topics.body: `transpose` accepts an axis order, so a (2, 3, 4) block can become (4, 2, 3) without touching the values in memory.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.transpose(2, 0, 1).shape)

interviewBank.q: What does `reshape(-1, 3)` mean?
interviewBank.answer: Three columns are fixed and the row count is inferred from the total element count. It fails if the size is not divisible by three.

interviewBank.q: How do `ravel`, `flatten` and `reshape(-1)` differ?
interviewBank.answer: `ravel` returns a view when it can, `flatten` always copies, and `reshape(-1)` is a view when the memory layout allows it.

interviewBank.q: When do you use `stack` rather than `concatenate`?
interviewBank.answer: `stack` adds a new axis and requires equal shapes; `concatenate` joins along an existing axis of the same rank.

interviewBank.q: What does `reshape` require about the element count?
interviewBank.answer: The target shape must hold exactly the same number of elements, or NumPy raises instead of padding.

interviewBank.q: How do you add a batch axis to one sample?
interviewBank.answer: `sample[np.newaxis, ...]` or `expand_dims(sample, 0)`, giving shape `(1, ...)` that a batched model accepts.

interviewBank.q: Why does `ravel()` sometimes copy?
interviewBank.answer: When the memory layout cannot be traversed in the requested order with strides, it must materialise a contiguous copy.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.concatenate` require of its inputs?
interviewBank.answer: Matching ranks and matching shapes on every axis except the one being joined.

interviewBank.q: How do you turn a column into a row?
interviewBank.answer: `arr.reshape(1, -1)`, or `.T` when the data is genuinely a matrix.

interviewBank.q: Why does `flatten()` always copy?
interviewBank.answer: It guarantees a new contiguous array, independent of the source layout.

interviewBank.q: A model expects (samples, features) but the loader produced (features, samples). Which fix is safer: reshape, transpose or resize?
interviewBank.answer: Transpose (`.T`) or reshape with explicit dimensions; resize is not a NumPy ndarray method and reshape alone can scramble the value order. Verify with a known 2×3 array before trusting the shape.

followUps.q: How do you verify `reshape` did not scramble values?
followUps.answer: Compare `a.reshape(new).ravel()` with `a.ravel()`; if the value order differs, a copy with the wrong order was used somewhere.

followUps.q: Why can reshape reorder data after a transpose?
followUps.answer: The default `order='C'` re-packs a non-contiguous view into C order, so the logical order changes; pass the order you mean or copy deliberately.

interviewBank.q: Two arrays of shape (100, 3) are joined with np.vstack and the result is (200, 3). Was np.concatenate with axis=0 the same thing here?
interviewBank.answer: Yes — vstack is concatenate along axis 0 after promoting 1-D inputs to rows. The distinction matters for 1-D inputs, where vstack adds a row axis and concatenate does not.

followUps.q: What does `np.concatenate` do with two 1-D arrays on axis=0?
followUps.answer: It joins them end to end, without adding a row axis — the key difference from `vstack`.

followUps.q: Which tool would you use to join by a key instead of position?
followUps.answer: Not a NumPy join: sort both arrays and use `searchsorted`/boolean masks, or let pandas merge by key and convert back to arrays.

defenseBank.q: Defend C order for a freshly built feature matrix.
defenseBank.answer: Rows are samples and each row is contiguous, so slicing a sample or feeding a row-major consumer reads sequential memory. Fortran order is for column-major consumers.

defenseBank.q: How do you know whether a reshape copied?
defenseBank.answer: Check `result.base is not None` or `np.shares_memory(original, result)`. A reshape copies only when the requested order cannot be expressed with strides.

defenseBank.q: A model wants `(N, C, H, W)` and your data is `(N, H, W, C)`. Defend the transformation you choose.
defenseBank.answer: Move the channel axis with `transpose(0, 3, 1, 2)` rather than reshaping, because reshaping would interleave values instead of permuting axes, and follow it with `ascontiguousarray` if the model needs contiguous input.

defenseBank.q: Defend `reshape(-1)` at the end of a feature pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: It states that the flattened length is whatever the data implies, so a changed batch size does not break the call.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `concatenate` needs matching ranks.
defenseBank.answer: It joins along an existing axis, so every operand must have the same number of axes and match on the others. `stack` is the operation that adds an axis.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing images as `(N, H, W, C)`.
defenseBank.answer: Channels last keeps each pixel's channels adjacent, which matches how most image decoders write memory and what many frameworks accept.

defenseBank.q: Defend `reshape` over `flatten` in a hot path.
defenseBank.answer: Reshape returns a view when the layout allows it, so it avoids a full copy.

defenseBank.q: Explain why reshaping after a transpose may not be a view.
defenseBank.answer: The memory order no longer matches the requested traversal, so NumPy must materialise a copy.

defenseBank.q: Defend stacking with a named axis over transposing afterwards.
defenseBank.answer: The axis is stated where the array is created, which is easier to check than a later permutation.

learn.title: reshape
learn.body: reshape changes the shape without changing the data or its order; the element count must stay the same, so 6 values can become (2, 3) but never (4, 2).
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)

learn.title: ravel and transpose
learn.body: ravel flattens to one dimension (often as a view) and .T swaps rows with columns; together they move a matrix between the two layouts most libraries expect.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.ravel(), a.T)

learn.title: concatenate and stack
learn.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis and stack creates a NEW axis, which is why two length-2 arrays stack into a (2, 2) matrix.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.concatenate([a, a]), np.stack([a, a]).shape)

learn.title: reshape with -1 infers the size
learn.body: One dimension may be written as -1 and NumPy fills it from the element count, which is how you ask for rows of a fixed width without arithmetic.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(-1, 2))

learn.title: newaxis makes a column
learn.body: Indexing with np.newaxis inserts an axis of length 1, turning a (3,) vector into a (3, 1) column that broadcasting can line up against rows.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3)[:, np.newaxis].shape)

learn.title: stack adds a new axis
learn.body: stack joins arrays of equal shape along a brand-new axis, so two (2,) arrays become a (2, 2) matrix instead of a (4,) flat one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.stack([np.zeros(2), np.ones(2)]).shape)

learn.title: split cuts an array into pieces
learn.body: split divides an array into equal parts and returns a list, which is handy for batches or train/test cuts.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.split(np.arange(4), 2))

learn.title: flatten always copies
learn.body: flatten returns a fresh 1-D array, so editing it never touches the source; ravel returns a view whenever the layout allows.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
f = a.flatten()
f[0] = 9
print(a[0])

learn.title: ravel flattens without copying when it can
learn.body: A contiguous array can be flattened as a view. `base` proves whether the new array still points at the old memory.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.ravel().base is a)

learn.title: reshape turns a vector into a column
learn.body: `(4, 1)` and `(1, 4)` look similar but broadcast in opposite directions. The shape is the whole difference.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
print(a.reshape(4, 1))

learn.title: vstack stacks arrays into rows
learn.body: `vstack` adds a new first axis, so two `(2,)` arrays become one `(2, 2)` array. `hstack` joins along the existing axis instead.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.vstack([np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4])]))

learn.title: Transpose swaps the axes
learn.body: `.T` reverses the axis order and is a view, not a copy. For a matrix it swaps rows with columns.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.shape)

learn.title: reshape returns a view when it can
learn.body: reshape never copies if the existing strides allow the new shape; ravel returns a view where possible and a copy otherwise. Use flatten when a copy is required.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
b[0, 0] = 99
print(a, b.shape)
learn.simple: `reshape` se hum ek hi dabbe ke numbers ko naya shape de dete hain — jaise 6 chocolates ko 2 lines ki 3-3 me rakhna. Dabba wahi rehta hai, sirf dekhne ka tarika badalta hai. Isliye reshape ke baad number badlo to asli array me bhi badal jata hai.
learn.pro: reshape reinterprets the same buffer when the existing strides permit the new shape, returning a view rather than allocating. ravel prefers a view and falls back to a copy for non-contiguous layouts; flatten always copies, which is the safe choice when independence is required.

learn.title: Stack and concatenate
learn.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis, vstack adds rows and hstack adds columns. stack creates a new axis instead of joining one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(np.vstack([a, b]))
print(np.hstack([a, b]))
print(np.stack([a, b]).shape)
learn.simple: `concatenate` do arrays ko jodta hai — jaise do pencils ko end-to-end jodna. `vstack` unhe upar-neeche rakhta hai (nayi rows), `hstack` side-by-side (naye columns), aur `stack` ek naya dimension bana kar unhe ek doosre ke upar rakh deta hai.
learn.pro: concatenate joins along an existing axis, vstack/hstack are axis-0/axis-1 conveniences with 1-D promotion, and stack creates a new leading (or named) axis instead of joining one. Pick stack when the arrays are observations of the same variable and the extra dimension carries meaning.

learn.title: reshape groups values in C order
learn.body: Reshaping walks the buffer left to right, then down, so a flat `0..5` becomes `[[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]`. The order is C by default.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(2, 3).tolist())
print(a.reshape(3, 2).tolist())
learn.simple: Reshape values ko left-to-right, phir neeche wali line me bharta hai. Isliye flat `0..5` pehle `[[0,1,2],[3,4,5]]` banta hai, ulta nahi.
learn.pro: Reshape walks the buffer in C order by default, filling the last axis fastest, so a flat range becomes row-major groups. Passing `order='F'` switches that traversal, which is why the order argument changes the values even though the shape is identical.
steps: Create a flat range of six values.
Reshape to 2×3 and print it.
Reshape to 3×2 and compare the grouping.
learn.realWorld: A flat image buffer becomes a height-by-width array through a C-order reshape.
mistakes: Expecting column-major fill without `order='F'`.
revision: C order fills the last axis fastest.
The element count must stay the same.

learn.title: ravel returns a flat view
learn.body: ravel flattens without copying when the layout allows it, so the result may share memory with the source. Check with shares_memory before mutating it.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.ravel().tolist(), np.shares_memory(a, a.ravel()))
learn.simple: `ravel` array ko flat karta hai aur jab layout allow kare to naya memory nahi banata. Isliye likhne se pehle `shares_memory` se check karna zaroori hai.
learn.pro: `ravel` returns a flattened view whenever the layout permits it, so it may share the source buffer and writes can propagate back. When the strides cannot be flattened without copying, it silently returns a copy instead, which is why `shares_memory` is the reliable check.
steps: Build a contiguous matrix.
Flatten it with `ravel`.
Check sharing with `shares_memory`.
learn.realWorld: Passing a matrix to a flat API can avoid a copy when ravel returns a view.
mistakes: Mutating the ravel result and forgetting it may be a view.
revision: Ravel copies only when it must.

learn.title: flatten returns a copy
learn.body: flatten always allocates, so the result is independent of the source. That is the safe choice when a helper expects to modify its input.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4).reshape(2, 2)
f = a.flatten()
f[0] = 99
print(a.tolist(), f.tolist())
learn.simple: `flatten` hamesha naya array banata hai, isliye usme badlav original tak nahi pahunchta. Jab helper ko input badalna ho to yahi safe choice hai.
learn.pro: `flatten` always allocates a new contiguous buffer, so the result is independent of the source and mutations never propagate. That guarantee costs a full copy, which is the trade-off to accept when a consumer must be free to modify its input.
steps: Build a matrix.
Flatten it and mutate the result.
Print the source to prove it did not change.
learn.visual:
flatten → independent copy
source stays the same
learn.realWorld: A helper that mutates its input receives `flatten()` to keep the caller's data safe.
mistakes: Using flatten in a hot loop and paying for a copy each time.
revision: The result is independent of the source.

learn.title: concatenate along columns
learn.body: With `axis=1`, concatenate joins matching rows side by side, so the row count must agree and the column counts add.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
b = np.ones((2, 1), dtype=int)
print(np.concatenate([a, b], axis=1).tolist())
learn.simple: `axis=1` ke saath concatenate rows ko side-by-side jodta hai. Isliye rows ki ginti same honi chahiye aur columns ki ginti jud jaati hai.
learn.pro: With `axis=1`, `concatenate` joins arrays side by side, requiring equal row counts and adding the column counts. The axis argument names the axis along which the pieces are laid out, so a wrong axis raises a shape error rather than transposing the data.
steps: Create two blocks with the same row count.
Concatenate them along axis 1.
Print the resulting shape.
learn.realWorld: Adding an engineered feature column to a design matrix is a column concatenation.
mistakes: Joining blocks with different row counts.
revision: The named axis is the one that grows.

learn.title: split into equal parts
learn.body: `np.split` divides an array along an axis when the length divides evenly; otherwise use array_split, which allows unequal pieces.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
parts = np.split(np.arange(6), 3)
print([p.tolist() for p in parts])
learn.simple: `np.split` array ko barabar hisson me kaatta hai jab lambai puri tarah divide ho. Warna `array_split` use karo, jo thode unequal hisse bhi deta hai.
learn.pro: `np.split` divides along an axis only when the length is divisible by the part count, otherwise it raises. `array_split` relaxes that requirement by distributing the remainder, which is why it is the correct choice for arbitrary lengths.

learn.title: transpose a three-dimensional array
learn.body: `transpose` accepts an axis order, so a (2, 3, 4) block can become (4, 2, 3) without touching the values in memory.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.transpose(2, 0, 1).shape)
learn.simple: `transpose` me axis ka order dena hota hai, isliye `(2,3,4)` ko `(4,2,3)` bana sakte ho — values memory me hilte nahi, sirf padhne ka rasta badalta hai.
learn.pro: `transpose` accepts an explicit permutation of axes, so a `(2, 3, 4)` block can become `(4, 2, 3)` without moving values. It returns a view with reordered strides, which is why a later C-contiguous operation may pay for a copy.
steps: Create a (2, 3, 4) array.
Transpose with an explicit axis order.
Print the new shape and verify one value.
learn.realWorld: Frameworks differ on channel-first versus channel-last, and transpose bridges them.
mistakes: Assuming transpose reverses all axes in 3-D.
revision: The argument is the new axis order.

interview.q: What does `reshape(-1, 3)` mean?
interview.answer: Three columns are fixed and the row count is inferred from the total element count. It fails if the size is not divisible by three.

interview.q: How do `ravel`, `flatten` and `reshape(-1)` differ?
interview.answer: `ravel` returns a view when it can, `flatten` always copies, and `reshape(-1)` is a view when the memory layout allows it.

interview.q: When do you use `stack` rather than `concatenate`?
interview.answer: `stack` adds a new axis and requires equal shapes; `concatenate` joins along an existing axis of the same rank.

interview.q: What does `reshape` require about the element count?
interview.answer: The target shape must hold exactly the same number of elements, or NumPy raises instead of padding.

interview.q: How do you add a batch axis to one sample?
interview.answer: `sample[np.newaxis, ...]` or `expand_dims(sample, 0)`, giving shape `(1, ...)` that a batched model accepts.

interview.q: Why does `ravel()` sometimes copy?
interview.answer: When the memory layout cannot be traversed in the requested order with strides, it must materialise a contiguous copy.

interview.q: What does `np.concatenate` require of its inputs?
interview.answer: Matching ranks and matching shapes on every axis except the one being joined.

interview.q: How do you turn a column into a row?
interview.answer: `arr.reshape(1, -1)`, or `.T` when the data is genuinely a matrix.

interview.q: Why does `flatten()` always copy?
interview.answer: It guarantees a new contiguous array, independent of the source layout.

interview.q: A model expects (samples, features) but the loader produced (features, samples). Which fix is safer: reshape, transpose or resize?
interview.answer: Transpose (`.T`) or reshape with explicit dimensions; resize is not a NumPy ndarray method and reshape alone can scramble the value order. Verify with a known 2×3 array before trusting the shape.

followUps.q: How do you verify `reshape` did not scramble values?
followUps.answer: Compare `a.reshape(new).ravel()` with `a.ravel()`; if the value order differs, a copy with the wrong order was used somewhere.

followUps.q: Why can reshape reorder data after a transpose?
followUps.answer: The default `order='C'` re-packs a non-contiguous view into C order, so the logical order changes; pass the order you mean or copy deliberately.

interview.q: Two arrays of shape (100, 3) are joined with np.vstack and the result is (200, 3). Was np.concatenate with axis=0 the same thing here?
interview.answer: Yes — vstack is concatenate along axis 0 after promoting 1-D inputs to rows. The distinction matters for 1-D inputs, where vstack adds a row axis and concatenate does not.

followUps.q: What does `np.concatenate` do with two 1-D arrays on axis=0?
followUps.answer: It joins them end to end, without adding a row axis — the key difference from `vstack`.

followUps.q: Which tool would you use to join by a key instead of position?
followUps.answer: Not a NumPy join: sort both arrays and use `searchsorted`/boolean masks, or let pandas merge by key and convert back to arrays.

defense.q: Defend C order for a freshly built feature matrix.
defense.answer: Rows are samples and each row is contiguous, so slicing a sample or feeding a row-major consumer reads sequential memory. Fortran order is for column-major consumers.

defense.q: How do you know whether a reshape copied?
defense.answer: Check `result.base is not None` or `np.shares_memory(original, result)`. A reshape copies only when the requested order cannot be expressed with strides.

defense.q: A model wants `(N, C, H, W)` and your data is `(N, H, W, C)`. Defend the transformation you choose.
defense.answer: Move the channel axis with `transpose(0, 3, 1, 2)` rather than reshaping, because reshaping would interleave values instead of permuting axes, and follow it with `ascontiguousarray` if the model needs contiguous input.

defense.q: Defend `reshape(-1)` at the end of a feature pipeline.
defense.answer: It states that the flattened length is whatever the data implies, so a changed batch size does not break the call.

defense.q: Explain why `concatenate` needs matching ranks.
defense.answer: It joins along an existing axis, so every operand must have the same number of axes and match on the others. `stack` is the operation that adds an axis.

defense.q: Defend storing images as `(N, H, W, C)`.
defense.answer: Channels last keeps each pixel's channels adjacent, which matches how most image decoders write memory and what many frameworks accept.

defense.q: Defend `reshape` over `flatten` in a hot path.
defense.answer: Reshape returns a view when the layout allows it, so it avoids a full copy.

defense.q: Explain why reshaping after a transpose may not be a view.
defense.answer: The memory order no longer matches the requested traversal, so NumPy must materialise a copy.

defense.q: Defend stacking with a named axis over transposing afterwards.
defense.answer: The axis is stated where the array is created, which is easier to check than a later permutation.

modules.title: Array Operations and Universal Functions
modules.goal: Use arithmetic, math and comparison ufuncs elementwise, and read a ufunc type error correctly.

topics.title: Arithmetic is elementwise
topics.body: Operators on arrays are universal functions applied element by element; `a + 1` adds to every element and `a ** 2` squares each one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 1, a ** 2)

topics.title: Math ufuncs
topics.body: sqrt, exp and log are the same elementwise functions for arrays and scalars, so one call replaces a comprehension.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt(9), np.exp(0), np.log(1))

topics.title: Comparisons produce masks
topics.body: A comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape, and indexing the array with that mask keeps only the True positions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(a > 2, a[a > 2])

topics.title: sqrt of perfect squares is exact
topics.body: Universal functions run compiled loops over the whole array, so np.sqrt returns a float array of the same shape in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt([4, 9, 25]))

topics.title: reduce sums, accumulate keeps running totals
topics.body: Every binary ufunc offers reduce (fold the whole array to one value) and accumulate (return every intermediate total).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.add.reduce([1, 2, 3]), np.add.accumulate([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: clip limits every element
topics.body: clip pins values into a range without a single if, which is how pixel and probability pipelines stay inside their legal bounds.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.clip([0, 5, 10], 1, 8))

topics.title: round, floor and ceil differ
topics.body: round goes to the nearest even integer at .5, floor always drops down and ceil always climbs, so pick the one your data means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round([1.5, 2.4]), np.floor([1.5, 2.4]), np.ceil([1.5, 2.4]))

topics.title: sign tells you direction
topics.body: np.sign maps negatives to -1, zero to 0 and positives to 1, giving a direction array you can multiply into other data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sign([-3, 0, 5]))

topics.title: Exponentiation uses the ** operator
topics.body: `**` is elementwise on arrays. `np.power` is the same operation written as a function when you need it as a callback.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 3]) ** 2)

topics.title: abs works on whole arrays
topics.body: NumPy's functions accept arrays, lists and scalars through the same call. That consistency is what makes them composable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.abs(np.array([-3, 4])))

topics.title: cumsum keeps every running total
topics.body: `cumsum` returns an array of the same length, while `sum` collapses it to one number. Use the cumulative form for running balances and charts.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.cumsum(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

topics.title: log and exp invert each other
topics.body: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1.0, 10.0])
print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))

topics.title: reduce and accumulate
topics.body: add.reduce collapses an axis to one value, while add.accumulate keeps every running total. They are ufunc methods, so they work with any binary ufunc.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.add.reduce(a))
print(np.add.accumulate(a))

topics.title: Never compare floats with ==
topics.body: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so two computations that should agree can differ in the last bits. isclose compares within a tolerance instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

topics.title: maximum picks elementwise winners
topics.body: `np.maximum(a, b)` returns the larger value at each position, which is a clamp against another array rather than against constants.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.maximum([1, 5, 2], [3, 2, 9]).tolist())

topics.title: minimum pairs the same way
topics.body: `np.minimum` is the elementwise counterpart, useful for capping values by a per-row limit array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.minimum([1, 5, 2], [3, 2, 9]).tolist())

topics.title: divide warns on zero
topics.body: True division by zero returns inf or nan and raises a runtime warning instead of stopping the program. Check the mask first when zeros are possible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
    print((np.array([1.0, 0.0]) / 0).tolist())

topics.title: power raises elementwise
topics.body: `np.power(a, b)` applies the exponent position by position, so each cell can have its own power while one call does the work.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.power([2, 3, 4], [2, 2, 1]).tolist())

topics.title: hypot is a stable length
topics.body: `np.hypot(x, y)` computes the hypotenuse without intermediate overflow, which the direct `sqrt(x**2 + y**2)` can hit on large values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.hypot([3, 5], [4, 12]).tolist())

topics.title: ufuncs accept out=
topics.body: A ufunc can write into a preallocated output, so a hot loop reuses one buffer instead of allocating a new array per step.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4.0)
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.sqrt(a, out=out)
print(out.tolist())

lab.title: Vectorised calculator
lab.brief: Compute square root, square and absolute value of one array in three lines.

interviewBank.q: What is a ufunc?
interviewBank.answer: A compiled elementwise operation with its own loop selection, broadcasting and dtype resolution, plus methods such as `reduce`, `accumulate` and `outer`.

interviewBank.q: Why is `np.sqrt` on an array faster than `math.sqrt` in a loop?
interviewBank.answer: The ufunc dispatches once and loops in C over a typed buffer, while the Python loop pays call, type and attribute overhead per element.

interviewBank.q: What does passing `out=` buy you?
interviewBank.answer: The result is written into an existing array, so no allocation happens and repeated calls reuse memory, which matters in hot loops over large arrays.

interviewBank.q: Is `np.add(a, b)` different from `a + b`?
interviewBank.answer: No: `+` calls the same ufunc. The explicit form matters when you need ufunc methods or an `out` buffer.

interviewBank.q: How do you apply a ufunc per row instead of globally?
interviewBank.answer: Apply it elementwise as usual, then reduce with the ufunc's method, for example `np.add.reduce(arr, axis=1)`.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.divide` return `inf` on a zero denominator instead of raising?
interviewBank.answer: A ufunc processes a whole buffer and cannot abort on one element, so it follows IEEE semantics and warns.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.add.reduce` do?
interviewBank.answer: It applies the ufunc pairwise along an axis, producing that reduction.

interviewBank.q: How do you compute a running product?
interviewBank.answer: `np.multiply.accumulate(arr)`.

interviewBank.q: Why does `np.exp` overflow instead of raising?
interviewBank.answer: The ufunc follows float semantics and returns `inf` with a warning.

interviewBank.q: A revenue calculation is off by 0.01 in the last row. Is the formula wrong?
interviewBank.answer: Almost certainly not — binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so equality checks and repeated additions drift. Compare with np.isclose and round only for display, not for intermediate maths.

followUps.q: Which tolerance would you choose for money in `np.isclose`?
followUps.answer: For a float display path, `atol` around 1e-9 with the same units; for accounting, store integer cents so the tolerance question disappears.

followUps.q: Why can repeated addition drift more than `np.sum`?
followUps.answer: `np.sum` uses pairwise summation, keeping partial sums similar in magnitude; a naïve loop adds a small number to a large one repeatedly and loses low bits.

interviewBank.q: A running total is needed per row. Which is cheaper: a Python loop with a counter or np.add.accumulate?
interviewBank.answer: accumulate runs one compiled pass and allocates one output array; the loop pays interpreter overhead per element. For very long arrays the difference is orders of magnitude.

followUps.q: What does `accumulate` return compared with `reduce`?
followUps.answer: `accumulate` returns the whole running array, while `reduce` collapses it to the final scalar.

followUps.q: How would you measure the speedup honestly?
followUps.answer: Time both implementations on the same input with `timeit`, several repeats, and report the median — not one lucky run.

defenseBank.q: Defend clipping model predictions into `[0, 1]`.
defenseBank.answer: A metric or downstream consumer may assume a probability range, and clipping states that contract explicitly instead of letting outliers through.

defenseBank.q: Why does `np.sqrt(-1)` return `nan` instead of raising?
defenseBank.answer: The ufunc runs over a whole buffer and cannot stop on one element; it reports the domain error as `nan` and warns via `np.errstate`. Check with `np.isnan` when it matters.

defenseBank.q: A reviewer asks for a Python loop because it is easier to read. Defend a ufunc for 10 million rows.
defenseBank.answer: Ten million Python iterations cost seconds of interpreter overhead and allocate per element, while the ufunc loops in C. Readability is served by naming the vectorised step.

defenseBank.q: Defend wrapping a risky division in `np.errstate`.
defenseBank.answer: It states that division by zero is expected here, so the warning is suppressed deliberately rather than flooding logs. The handling stays local.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `np.abs` on a boolean array is meaningless.
defenseBank.answer: A boolean has no magnitude beyond true or false, so the operation either errors or silently converts. Use the values you actually mean.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.clip` over an `if` per element.
defenseBank.answer: One vectorised call replaces a Python loop and handles both bounds consistently, including for non-finite inputs.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.errstate(over="raise")` in a numerical pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: It turns a silent infinity into a failure you can locate.

defenseBank.q: Explain why applying a ufunc to a Python list returns an array.
defenseBank.answer: The ufunc converts the input to an array before it runs.

defenseBank.q: Defend using `out=` for a repeated large computation.
defenseBank.answer: It avoids allocating a result buffer on every call and keeps peak memory predictable.

learn.title: Arithmetic is elementwise
learn.body: Operators on arrays are universal functions applied element by element; `a + 1` adds to every element and `a ** 2` squares each one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 1, a ** 2)

learn.title: Math ufuncs
learn.body: sqrt, exp and log are the same elementwise functions for arrays and scalars, so one call replaces a comprehension.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt(9), np.exp(0), np.log(1))

learn.title: Comparisons produce masks
learn.body: A comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape, and indexing the array with that mask keeps only the True positions.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(a > 2, a[a > 2])

learn.title: sqrt of perfect squares is exact
learn.body: Universal functions run compiled loops over the whole array, so np.sqrt returns a float array of the same shape in one call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt([4, 9, 25]))

learn.title: reduce sums, accumulate keeps running totals
learn.body: Every binary ufunc offers reduce (fold the whole array to one value) and accumulate (return every intermediate total).
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.add.reduce([1, 2, 3]), np.add.accumulate([1, 2, 3]))

learn.title: clip limits every element
learn.body: clip pins values into a range without a single if, which is how pixel and probability pipelines stay inside their legal bounds.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.clip([0, 5, 10], 1, 8))

learn.title: round, floor and ceil differ
learn.body: round goes to the nearest even integer at .5, floor always drops down and ceil always climbs, so pick the one your data means.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round([1.5, 2.4]), np.floor([1.5, 2.4]), np.ceil([1.5, 2.4]))

learn.title: sign tells you direction
learn.body: np.sign maps negatives to -1, zero to 0 and positives to 1, giving a direction array you can multiply into other data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sign([-3, 0, 5]))

learn.title: Exponentiation uses the ** operator
learn.body: `**` is elementwise on arrays. `np.power` is the same operation written as a function when you need it as a callback.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 3]) ** 2)

learn.title: abs works on whole arrays
learn.body: NumPy's functions accept arrays, lists and scalars through the same call. That consistency is what makes them composable.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.abs(np.array([-3, 4])))

learn.title: cumsum keeps every running total
learn.body: `cumsum` returns an array of the same length, while `sum` collapses it to one number. Use the cumulative form for running balances and charts.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.cumsum(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

learn.title: log and exp invert each other
learn.body: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1.0, 10.0])
print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))

learn.title: reduce and accumulate
learn.body: add.reduce collapses an axis to one value, while add.accumulate keeps every running total. They are ufunc methods, so they work with any binary ufunc.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.add.reduce(a))
print(np.add.accumulate(a))
learn.simple: `reduce` saare numbers ko jod kar ek jawab deta hai, jaise poore mahine ka total. `accumulate` har step ka running total deta hai, jaise din-din ka hisaab — [1, 3, 6, 10]. Dono kisi bhi jodne wale function ke saath chalte hain.
learn.pro: reduce collapses an axis to a scalar and accumulate returns the full prefix sequence; both are ufunc methods, so the same call works with add, multiply or maximum. accumulate allocates an output the size of the input, which is the memory cost of keeping every running value.

learn.title: Never compare floats with ==
learn.body: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so two computations that should agree can differ in the last bits. isclose compares within a tolerance instead.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
learn.simple: Computer 0.1 aur 0.2 ko bilkul theek se store nahi kar sakta, isliye unka jod 0.3 se thoda alag aata hai. `==` turant "barabar nahi" bol dega. Iske liye `np.isclose` use karo, jo thodi si galti ko ignore karta hai.
learn.pro: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so computed values differ in the last bits even when the algebra says they are equal. Compare with np.isclose (or allclose for arrays) using a tolerance appropriate to the magnitudes involved; reserve == for exact integers and booleans.

learn.title: maximum picks elementwise winners
learn.body: `np.maximum(a, b)` returns the larger value at each position, which is a clamp against another array rather than against constants.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.maximum([1, 5, 2], [3, 2, 9]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.maximum` do arrays me har jagah bada number chunta hai. Yeh constant se clamp karne se alag hai — yahan limit khud ek array ho sakti hai.
learn.pro: `np.maximum(a, b)` compares position by position and returns the larger value at each coordinate, broadcasting the operands first. That makes it a per-element clamp against another array, unlike `clip` which applies fixed bounds.
steps: Create two vectors of equal length.
Apply `maximum` and print the winners.
Compare with a fixed clamp using `clip`.
learn.realWorld: A per-row floor stored as an array is applied with maximum.
mistakes: Using Python's `max` on whole arrays instead of elementwise.

learn.title: minimum pairs the same way
learn.body: `np.minimum` is the elementwise counterpart, useful for capping values by a per-row limit array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.minimum([1, 5, 2], [3, 2, 9]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.minimum` bilkul ulta hai: har jagah chhota number rakhta hai. Isliye per-row limit array se values cap kar sakte ho.
learn.pro: `np.minimum` is the elementwise counterpart that keeps the smaller value, broadcasting both operands to a common shape. It is the natural way to cap values by a per-row or per-column limit array without writing a loop.
steps: Create two vectors.
Apply `minimum` and print the smaller values.
Use a limit array to cap a result.
learn.realWorld: Capping predicted probabilities by a per-class threshold uses minimum.
mistakes: Forgetting that broadcasting can change the result shape.
revision: It is the array counterpart of a cap.

learn.title: divide warns on zero
learn.body: True division by zero returns inf or nan and raises a runtime warning instead of stopping the program. Check the mask first when zeros are possible.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
    print((np.array([1.0, 0.0]) / 0).tolist())
learn.simple: Zero se divide karne par program rukta nahi — `inf` ya `nan` aata hai aur ek warning chhapti hai. Isliye pehle mask dekho, warna baad me values kharab milengi.
learn.pro: True division by zero follows IEEE rules, producing `inf` or `nan` and emitting a runtime warning instead of raising. The warning is easy to miss in output, so guarding the denominator with a mask or `np.errstate` is the deliberate choice.
steps: Divide a vector containing zero by zero.
Observe the warning and the inf/nan values.
Guard the denominator with a mask.
learn.realWorld: Ratios computed from counts hit zero denominators, so the guard is part of the metric.
mistakes: Ignoring the warning until NaNs reach a mean.
revision: Division by zero returns inf or nan.

learn.title: power raises elementwise
learn.body: `np.power(a, b)` applies the exponent position by position, so each cell can have its own power while one call does the work.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.power([2, 3, 4], [2, 2, 1]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.power` har cell ko uske saamne wali power tak uthata hai, isliye ek hi call me har number ka apna exponent chal sakta hai.
learn.pro: `np.power(a, b)` applies the exponent position by position, broadcasting both arrays first. That per-cell exponent is what makes it more general than `a ** 2`, and integer bases with negative integer exponents raise rather than returning a float.
steps: Create a base and an exponent array.
Apply `power` and print the result.
Compare with the `**` operator.
learn.realWorld: Polynomial features are powers of one column with a fixed exponent.
mistakes: Using a negative integer exponent on an integer base.
revision: Exponents are broadcast with the base.

learn.title: hypot is a stable length
learn.body: `np.hypot(x, y)` computes the hypotenuse without intermediate overflow, which the direct `sqrt(x**2 + y**2)` can hit on large values.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.hypot([3, 5], [4, 12]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.hypot` seedha hypotenuse nikalta hai bina beech me numbers ko bahut bada hone diye. Isliye bade values par bhi result sahi aata hai.
learn.pro: `np.hypot(x, y)` computes the hypotenuse with internal scaling, avoiding the overflow and underflow that `sqrt(x**2 + y**2)` can hit for large or tiny magnitudes. The result is the same length with better numerical behaviour.
steps: Compute a length with `hypot`.
Compare it with `sqrt(x**2 + y**2)`.
Try large values where the naive form overflows.
learn.realWorld: Distances between coordinates are computed with hypot to avoid overflow.
mistakes: Squaring large values before taking the root.
revision: The result equals the Euclidean length.

learn.title: ufuncs accept out=
learn.body: A ufunc can write into a preallocated output, so a hot loop reuses one buffer instead of allocating a new array per step.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4.0)
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.sqrt(a, out=out)
print(out.tolist())
learn.simple: Ufunc ko pehle se banaya hua output de sakte ho, isliye loop me har baar naya array nahi banta. Ek hi buffer baar-baar reuse hota hai.
learn.pro: A ufunc accepts an `out=` buffer, writing results in place and avoiding a fresh allocation per call. That matters in hot loops and for large arrays where allocation and garbage collection dominate the runtime; the output shape and dtype must match.
steps: Preallocate an output array.
Call `sqrt` with `out=` and print the buffer.
Confirm no new array was needed.
learn.visual:
sqrt(a, out=out)
out holds the result
learn.realWorld: Streaming pipelines reuse buffers to keep allocation out of the hot path.
mistakes: Passing an output with the wrong shape or dtype.

interview.q: What is a ufunc?
interview.answer: A compiled elementwise operation with its own loop selection, broadcasting and dtype resolution, plus methods such as `reduce`, `accumulate` and `outer`.

interview.q: Why is `np.sqrt` on an array faster than `math.sqrt` in a loop?
interview.answer: The ufunc dispatches once and loops in C over a typed buffer, while the Python loop pays call, type and attribute overhead per element.

interview.q: What does passing `out=` buy you?
interview.answer: The result is written into an existing array, so no allocation happens and repeated calls reuse memory, which matters in hot loops over large arrays.

interview.q: Is `np.add(a, b)` different from `a + b`?
interview.answer: No: `+` calls the same ufunc. The explicit form matters when you need ufunc methods or an `out` buffer.

interview.q: How do you apply a ufunc per row instead of globally?
interview.answer: Apply it elementwise as usual, then reduce with the ufunc's method, for example `np.add.reduce(arr, axis=1)`.

interview.q: Why does `np.divide` return `inf` on a zero denominator instead of raising?
interview.answer: A ufunc processes a whole buffer and cannot abort on one element, so it follows IEEE semantics and warns.

interview.q: What does `np.add.reduce` do?
interview.answer: It applies the ufunc pairwise along an axis, producing that reduction.

interview.q: How do you compute a running product?
interview.answer: `np.multiply.accumulate(arr)`.

interview.q: Why does `np.exp` overflow instead of raising?
interview.answer: The ufunc follows float semantics and returns `inf` with a warning.

interview.q: A revenue calculation is off by 0.01 in the last row. Is the formula wrong?
interview.answer: Almost certainly not — binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, so equality checks and repeated additions drift. Compare with np.isclose and round only for display, not for intermediate maths.

followUps.q: Which tolerance would you choose for money in `np.isclose`?
followUps.answer: For a float display path, `atol` around 1e-9 with the same units; for accounting, store integer cents so the tolerance question disappears.

followUps.q: Why can repeated addition drift more than `np.sum`?
followUps.answer: `np.sum` uses pairwise summation, keeping partial sums similar in magnitude; a naïve loop adds a small number to a large one repeatedly and loses low bits.

interview.q: A running total is needed per row. Which is cheaper: a Python loop with a counter or np.add.accumulate?
interview.answer: accumulate runs one compiled pass and allocates one output array; the loop pays interpreter overhead per element. For very long arrays the difference is orders of magnitude.

followUps.q: What does `accumulate` return compared with `reduce`?
followUps.answer: `accumulate` returns the whole running array, while `reduce` collapses it to the final scalar.

followUps.q: How would you measure the speedup honestly?
followUps.answer: Time both implementations on the same input with `timeit`, several repeats, and report the median — not one lucky run.

defense.q: Defend clipping model predictions into `[0, 1]`.
defense.answer: A metric or downstream consumer may assume a probability range, and clipping states that contract explicitly instead of letting outliers through.

defense.q: Why does `np.sqrt(-1)` return `nan` instead of raising?
defense.answer: The ufunc runs over a whole buffer and cannot stop on one element; it reports the domain error as `nan` and warns via `np.errstate`. Check with `np.isnan` when it matters.

defense.q: A reviewer asks for a Python loop because it is easier to read. Defend a ufunc for 10 million rows.
defense.answer: Ten million Python iterations cost seconds of interpreter overhead and allocate per element, while the ufunc loops in C. Readability is served by naming the vectorised step.

defense.q: Defend wrapping a risky division in `np.errstate`.
defense.answer: It states that division by zero is expected here, so the warning is suppressed deliberately rather than flooding logs. The handling stays local.

defense.q: Explain why `np.abs` on a boolean array is meaningless.
defense.answer: A boolean has no magnitude beyond true or false, so the operation either errors or silently converts. Use the values you actually mean.

defense.q: Defend `np.clip` over an `if` per element.
defense.answer: One vectorised call replaces a Python loop and handles both bounds consistently, including for non-finite inputs.

defense.q: Defend `np.errstate(over="raise")` in a numerical pipeline.
defense.answer: It turns a silent infinity into a failure you can locate.

defense.q: Explain why applying a ufunc to a Python list returns an array.
defense.answer: The ufunc converts the input to an array before it runs.

defense.q: Defend using `out=` for a repeated large computation.
defense.answer: It avoids allocating a result buffer on every call and keeps peak memory predictable.
