modules.title: Broadcasting
modules.goal: Apply the broadcasting rules to scalars, rows and columns, and fix incompatible-shape errors.

topics.title: Scalar broadcasting
topics.body: A scalar is stretched across every element without being copied, which is why `a + 10` is both simple and memory-cheap.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Row and column broadcasting
topics.body: Shapes are compared from the right: (2, 3) with (3,) lines up the 3s, so each column is scaled by its own weight.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
w = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a * w)

topics.title: Incompatible shapes fail loudly
topics.body: If two sizes disagree and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError instead of guessing; that error is the rule working, not a bug.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 2))
try:
    a + b
except ValueError:
    print('broadcast error')

topics.title: A vector broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A (3,) vector added to a (2, 3) matrix is treated as one row repeated per matrix row, so the column count has to match.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: A column broadcasts down
topics.body: A (2, 1) column is stretched across every column, which is how one value per row is applied to a whole matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([[10], [20]]))

topics.title: Outer product uses two new axes
topics.body: Adding an axis to each operand makes broadcasting compute every pair, which is the outer product without writing a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(a[:, None] * b[None, :])

topics.title: Comparison broadcasts too
topics.body: Broadcasting is not limited to arithmetic: comparing a matrix with its per-column mean stretches the mean across rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [6, 5, 4]])
print(a > a.mean(axis=0))

topics.title: reshape prepares a strip for broadcasting
topics.body: Turning a vector into a (3, 1) column and adding a (1, 2) row yields a (3, 2) grid, which is the shape rule worth memorising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.arange(3)
print((v.reshape(3, 1) + np.zeros((1, 2))).shape)

topics.title: A row array broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A `(3,)` array lines up with the last axis of a `(2, 3)` array. That is the rule that makes row-wise maths a single line.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a + np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)

topics.title: A scalar is the smallest broadcast
topics.body: Scalars stretch to every position without copying. The result is a new array of the original shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

topics.title: Broadcast a column against a row
topics.body: A `(2, 1)` column and a `(2,)` row produce a `(2, 2)` grid — every combination, with no explicit loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([[1], [2]]) * np.array([10, 20])).tolist())

topics.title: A size of one stretches automatically
topics.body: An axis of length 1 is repeated to match the other operand. That is why `(3, 1) + ones(4)` becomes `(3, 4)`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.zeros((3, 1)) + np.ones(4)).shape)

topics.title: A column broadcasts against a row
topics.body: Shape (3, 1) against (1, 4) stretches both to (3, 4): each row value meets each column value. That single rule is how standardising every column is written without a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
col = np.array([[10], [20], [30]])
row = np.array([[1, 2, 3, 4]])
print(col + row)

topics.title: expand_dims adds the axis explicitly
topics.body: expand_dims is the function form of newaxis: it inserts a length-one axis at the position you name, which makes the intended broadcast shape obvious in code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.shape, np.expand_dims(a, 0).shape, np.expand_dims(a, 1).shape)

topics.title: broadcast_to makes the shape explicit
topics.body: `np.broadcast_to` returns a read-only view of the stretched shape without copying, which is how you inspect what a broadcast will look like.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.broadcast_to(v, (2, 3)).tolist())

topics.title: Trailing dimensions must match
topics.body: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, so a length-3 axis can only meet another length-3 axis or a length-1 axis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a * np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)
print((a * np.array([[1], [2]])).shape)

topics.title: keepdims prepares a column for broadcast
topics.body: Keeping the reduced axis as length 1 gives a shape that divides back into the original, so normalising rows needs no reshape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1.0, 3.0], [2.0, 6.0]])
totals = a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print((a / totals).tolist())

topics.title: A matrix broadcasts with a scalar
topics.body: A scalar needs no shape at all and stretches to every cell, which is why scaling a whole matrix is one multiplication.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

topics.title: Outer difference via newaxis
topics.body: Turning one vector into a column and the other into a row produces every pairwise difference in one subtraction.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2])[:, None] - np.array([1, 2])).tolist())

topics.title: A broadcast error names the shapes
topics.body: The ValueError message reports the operands' shapes, so read it right to left to find the axis that cannot stretch.

debug.title: A (2,) vector against (2, 3)
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2,))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a + b)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 1))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a + b)

debug.title: Transposed shape by mistake

a = np.zeros((2, 3))
b = np.zeros((3, 2))
print(a * b)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3))
b = np.zeros((3, 2))
print(a * b.T)
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (3,2)

debug.title: A row vector where a column was needed
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
v = np.array([1, 2])
print(a + v)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
v = np.array([1, 2]).reshape(2, 1)
print(a + v)
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (2,)

debug.title: Three values against two
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3) + np.ones(2))
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,) (2,)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3) + np.ones(3))

debug.title: Rows and columns swapped
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones((2, 3)) + np.ones((3, 2)))
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (3,2)
debug.fix:

debug.title: Columns that cannot stretch
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones((2, 1)) + np.ones((3, 1)))
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,1) (3,1)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones((2, 1)) + np.ones((2, 1)))

debug.title: In-place add into a smaller array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 2))
a += np.ones((2, 3))
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,2) (2,3) (2,2)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
a += np.ones((2, 3))

debug.title: Adding a length-3 vector to a length-4
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3) + np.ones(4))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3) + np.ones(3))
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,) (4,)

debug.title: Shapes that refuse to broadcast
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.broadcast_shapes((2, 3), (4,)))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.broadcast_shapes((2, 1), (1, 3)))
debug.error: ValueError: shape mismatch: objects cannot be broadcast to a single shape.  Mismatch is between arg 0 with shape (2, 3) and arg 1 with shape (4,).

debug.title: In-place multiply that would grow the array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
arr = np.ones(3)
arr *= np.ones((2, 3))
print(arr)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
arr = np.ones(3)
arr *= np.ones(3)
print(arr)

lab.title: Broadcast a batch
lab.brief: Apply three per-feature weights to a (4, 3) batch and prove the output shape stays (4, 3).

interviewBank.q: State the broadcasting rules in one sentence.
interviewBank.answer: Align shapes from the right; each pair of axes must be equal or one of them must be 1, and missing leading axes are treated as 1.

interviewBank.q: Why does `(3, 1) + (1, 4)` produce a `(3, 4)` grid?
interviewBank.answer: The first operand varies down rows and the second across columns, so every combination is paired exactly once.

interviewBank.q: How do you subtract a per-column mean from a matrix?
interviewBank.answer: Compute `arr.mean(axis=0)`, which has shape `(n_features,)`, and subtract it; the trailing axis aligns with the columns.

interviewBank.q: What happens when a `(2, 3)` array is added to a `(3,)` array?
interviewBank.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis and is reused for both rows, producing `(2, 3)`.

interviewBank.q: Why can a scalar broadcast against any shape?
interviewBank.answer: It has no axes to conflict with, so it applies to every element.

interviewBank.q: How do you build an outer product with broadcasting?
interviewBank.answer: Make one operand a column and the other a row, `a[:, None] * b[None, :]`, and the result is the full grid.

interviewBank.q: How do you subtract a row vector from every row of a matrix?
interviewBank.answer: Compute the vector with shape `(n_features,)` and subtract it; it aligns with the columns.

interviewBank.q: What shape does `(4, 1, 3) + (2, 1)` produce?
interviewBank.answer: `(4, 2, 3)`, after the trailing axes align.

interviewBank.q: Why is broadcasting not a copy?
interviewBank.answer: The smaller array is read with zero strides rather than materialised across the larger shape.

interviewBank.q: A store table has shape (500, 1) of discounts and a product table (1, 12) of prices. What happens on addition, and how much memory does the result take?
interviewBank.answer: Both broadcast to (500, 12): every product price meets every store discount. The result is materialised, so it costs 500×12 values even though the inputs are tiny — a real memory risk at scale.

followUps.q: How do you avoid materialising the full (500, 12) product?
followUps.answer: Chunk one axis and reduce as you go (or use `np.einsum` over chunks) when only aggregates are needed; the full product is only worth it when every cell is used.

followUps.q: Does `broadcast_to` itself allocate the big result?
followUps.answer: No — it returns a read-only view with zero strides; the allocation happens on the first arithmetic that materialises values.

interviewBank.q: An operation fails with 'operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (3, 1)'. What is the actual mismatch?
interviewBank.answer: The trailing dimensions must match or be 1: (4,) is treated as (1, 4), which cannot pair with (3, 1) on the last axis (4 vs 1 is fine, but 1 vs 3 on the first axis gives 4 vs 3 ... ). Fix by reshaping to (4, 1) or (1, 3) so the intended axis pairs.

followUps.q: Which reshape resolves `(4,)` against `(3, 1)`?
followUps.answer: `(3, 1)` wants a length-3 axis matched against something of length 3; reshape the vector to `(1, 3)` for a row pairing or `(4, 1)` for a column pairing, depending on which axis you mean.

followUps.q: How do you read broadcast compatibility quickly?
followUps.answer: Align shapes from the right; each pair must be equal or one of them 1. Incompatible means neither rule holds.

defenseBank.q: Defend standardising columns with broadcasting instead of a loop over columns.
defenseBank.answer: One subtraction and one division do the whole matrix with no Python loop, and the shape of the statistic documents that it is per column.

defenseBank.q: Describe a bug caused by mixing `(3,)` and `(3, 1)`.
defenseBank.answer: The `(3,)` vector aligns with the last axis, so adding it to a `(3, 3)` matrix adds along columns, not rows. The code runs and returns a plausible but wrong answer.

defenseBank.q: Broadcasting a `(1000, 1) + (1, 1000)` allocates a million values. Defend when that is acceptable.
defenseBank.answer: It is fine when the result is genuinely needed at that size and fits in memory. If only a reduction is wanted, use `einsum` or `sum` with an axis to avoid materialising it.

defenseBank.q: Defend writing shapes in comments beside broadcast arithmetic.
defenseBank.answer: The same expression means different things for `(n,)` and `(n, 1)`, and a comment makes the intended axis explicit for the next reader.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a column times a row is not a dot product.
defenseBank.answer: Broadcasting multiplies every pair and keeps both axes, while a dot product contracts the shared axis into one number.

defenseBank.q: Defend reshaping explicitly before an operation that relies on broadcasting.
defenseBank.answer: An explicit shape states which axis is being aligned, so a later data change fails loudly instead of broadcasting in the wrong direction.

defenseBank.q: Defend explicit `reshape` over relying on broadcast alignment.
defenseBank.answer: The intended axis is stated, so a shape change fails loudly instead of broadcasting the wrong way.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `(3,) + (3, 1)` gives `(3, 3)`.
defenseBank.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis, so every pair is combined into a grid.

defenseBank.q: Defend computing a reduction instead of materialising a broadcast grid.
defenseBank.answer: The reduction is far smaller and avoids allocating the full grid.

learn.title: Scalar broadcasting
learn.body: A scalar is stretched across every element without being copied, which is why `a + 10` is both simple and memory-cheap.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

learn.title: Row and column broadcasting
learn.body: Shapes are compared from the right: (2, 3) with (3,) lines up the 3s, so each column is scaled by its own weight.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
w = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a * w)

learn.title: Incompatible shapes fail loudly
learn.body: If two sizes disagree and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError instead of guessing; that error is the rule working, not a bug.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 2))
try:
    a + b
except ValueError:
    print('broadcast error')

learn.title: A vector broadcasts across rows
learn.body: A (3,) vector added to a (2, 3) matrix is treated as one row repeated per matrix row, so the column count has to match.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([1, 2, 3]))

learn.title: A column broadcasts down
learn.body: A (2, 1) column is stretched across every column, which is how one value per row is applied to a whole matrix.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([[10], [20]]))

learn.title: Outer product uses two new axes
learn.body: Adding an axis to each operand makes broadcasting compute every pair, which is the outer product without writing a loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(a[:, None] * b[None, :])

learn.title: Comparison broadcasts too
learn.body: Broadcasting is not limited to arithmetic: comparing a matrix with its per-column mean stretches the mean across rows.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [6, 5, 4]])
print(a > a.mean(axis=0))

learn.title: reshape prepares a strip for broadcasting
learn.body: Turning a vector into a (3, 1) column and adding a (1, 2) row yields a (3, 2) grid, which is the shape rule worth memorising.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.arange(3)
print((v.reshape(3, 1) + np.zeros((1, 2))).shape)

learn.title: A row array broadcasts across rows
learn.body: A `(3,)` array lines up with the last axis of a `(2, 3)` array. That is the rule that makes row-wise maths a single line.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a + np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)

learn.title: A scalar is the smallest broadcast
learn.body: Scalars stretch to every position without copying. The result is a new array of the original shape.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

learn.title: Broadcast a column against a row
learn.body: A `(2, 1)` column and a `(2,)` row produce a `(2, 2)` grid — every combination, with no explicit loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([[1], [2]]) * np.array([10, 20])).tolist())

learn.title: A size of one stretches automatically
learn.body: An axis of length 1 is repeated to match the other operand. That is why `(3, 1) + ones(4)` becomes `(3, 4)`.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.zeros((3, 1)) + np.ones(4)).shape)

learn.title: A column broadcasts against a row
learn.body: Shape (3, 1) against (1, 4) stretches both to (3, 4): each row value meets each column value. That single rule is how standardising every column is written without a loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
col = np.array([[10], [20], [30]])
row = np.array([[1, 2, 3, 4]])
print(col + row)
learn.simple: Socho ek column me tumhare 3 dost aur ek row me 4 chocolates ke daam hain. NumPy dono ko khud-ba-khud phaila deta hai aur har dost ke liye har daam ka hisaab kar deta hai — bina kisi loop ke, 3×4 ka table ban jata hai.
learn.pro: A (3, 1) column and a (1, 4) row broadcast to (3, 4): each axis is stretched where its length is 1, producing every pairwise combination. The result is materialised, so a tiny pair of inputs can allocate a large output — the shape to check before running it at scale.

learn.title: expand_dims adds the axis explicitly
learn.body: expand_dims is the function form of newaxis: it inserts a length-one axis at the position you name, which makes the intended broadcast shape obvious in code.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.shape, np.expand_dims(a, 0).shape, np.expand_dims(a, 1).shape)
learn.simple: `expand_dims` ek line ko ek row ya ek column banane ka saaf tareeka hai. `axis=0` se (1, 3) banta hai aur `axis=1` se (3, 1) — jaise ek list ko ya to horizontal line me rakhna ya vertical.
learn.pro: expand_dims inserts a length-one axis at the named position and is the function form of np.newaxis. Naming the axis makes the intended broadcast explicit in review, and choosing 0 versus 1 decides whether the vector lines up with rows or columns.

learn.title: broadcast_to makes the shape explicit
learn.body: `np.broadcast_to` returns a read-only view of the stretched shape without copying, which is how you inspect what a broadcast will look like.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.broadcast_to(v, (2, 3)).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.broadcast_to` dikhata hai ki chhota array bada hone par kaisa dikhega, bina values copy kiye. Result read-only hota hai, isliye usme likhna mana hai.
learn.pro: `np.broadcast_to` returns a read-only view with the stretched shape and zero strides on the broadcast axes, so it shows the expansion without allocating. Because several output cells map to one input cell, writing through it is refused.
steps: Create a length-3 vector.
Broadcast it to a 2×3 shape.
Try to write into the result and observe the refusal.
learn.realWorld: Inspecting the effective shape of a broadcast prevents a wrong arithmetic assumption.
mistakes: Writing through a broadcast view.
revision: Zero strides mark the stretched axes.

learn.title: Trailing dimensions must match
learn.body: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, so a length-3 axis can only meet another length-3 axis or a length-1 axis.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a * np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)
print((a * np.array([[1], [2]])).shape)
learn.simple: Broadcasting shapes ko right side se milata hai, isliye `3` wali axis sirf `3` ya `1` se mil sakti hai. Beech ki koi bhi mismatch error deti hai.
learn.pro: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, matching each trailing dimension if the lengths are equal or one of them is 1. A mismatch is reported with both shapes, and the fix is almost always an explicit `reshape` or `newaxis` rather than a different arithmetic order.
steps: Create a (2, 3) matrix.
Multiply by a length-3 vector and print the shape.
Multiply by a (3, 2) matrix and read the error.
learn.realWorld: Feature scaling works because the parameter vector aligns with the last axis.
mistakes: Aligning shapes from the left instead of the right.
revision: Lengths must be equal or one.

learn.title: keepdims prepares a column for broadcast
learn.body: Keeping the reduced axis as length 1 gives a shape that divides back into the original, so normalising rows needs no reshape.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1.0, 3.0], [2.0, 6.0]])
totals = a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print((a / totals).tolist())
learn.simple: Reduce karte waqt axis ko length 1 ke roop me rakhne se woh shape wapas original me fit ho jaati hai. Isliye rows ko unke total se divide karna bina reshape ke ho jaata hai.
learn.pro: `keepdims=True` leaves the reduced axis as length 1 instead of deleting it, so the result broadcasts back against the original shape. That is why normalising rows by their totals needs no reshape when the reduction kept its axis.
steps: Create a matrix of values.
Sum each row with `keepdims=True`.
Divide the matrix by that column.
learn.realWorld: Normalising each sample by its own total is a keepdims division.
mistakes: Dropping the axis and getting a length mismatch.
revision: That shape broadcasts back against the input.

learn.title: A matrix broadcasts with a scalar
learn.body: A scalar needs no shape at all and stretches to every cell, which is why scaling a whole matrix is one multiplication.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())
learn.simple: Scalar ki koi shape nahi hoti, isliye woh har cell me chala jaata hai. Poori matrix ko ek number se multiply karna isi wajah se ek line ka kaam hai.
learn.pro: A scalar has no axes to align, so broadcasting stretches it across every cell without a copy. That is why scaling a matrix is one multiplication, and why the same expression works unchanged for any shape.
steps: Create a matrix.
Multiply it by a scalar.
Print the result and confirm every cell changed.
learn.realWorld: Converting units across a whole table is one scalar multiplication.
mistakes: Looping over cells when one operation is enough.
revision: A scalar has no axes to align.

learn.title: Outer difference via newaxis
learn.body: Turning one vector into a column and the other into a row produces every pairwise difference in one subtraction.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2])[:, None] - np.array([1, 2])).tolist())
learn.simple: Ek vector ko column aur doosre ko row bana do, phir ghatao — har jodi ka difference ek hi operation me mil jaata hai. `newaxis` yahi kaam karta hai.
learn.pro: Turning one vector into a column and the other into a row produces every pairwise difference in a single broadcast subtraction. The result is the full outer table, which is why `newaxis` placement decides whether you get differences or a length error.
steps: Create two vectors.
Turn the first into a column with `newaxis`.
Subtract the second and print the pairwise table.
learn.realWorld: A distance matrix between two sets of points starts as an outer difference.
mistakes: Leaving both vectors 1-D and producing a length mismatch.
revision: The result is the full outer table.

learn.title: A broadcast error names the shapes
learn.body: The ValueError message reports the operands' shapes, so read it right to left to find the axis that cannot stretch.
learn.simple: Jab shapes match nahi hoti to error dono shapes likh deta hai. Message ko right se padho — wahi axis milegi jo stretch nahi ho sakti.
learn.pro: The `ValueError` reports both operand shapes, so reading them right to left identifies the axis whose lengths disagree. Fixing that axis explicitly is safer than reshaping blindly, because a wrong reshape can make the expression run while computing a different table.
learn.syntax: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes …
steps: Add two deliberately incompatible matrices.
Read the shapes in the error message.
Fix the axis with a reshape or transpose.
learn.realWorld: Most shape bugs in a preprocessing pipeline surface as this one error.
mistakes: Reshaping blindly until the error disappears.
revision: Fix the axis that cannot stretch.

interview.q: State the broadcasting rules in one sentence.
interview.answer: Align shapes from the right; each pair of axes must be equal or one of them must be 1, and missing leading axes are treated as 1.

interview.q: Why does `(3, 1) + (1, 4)` produce a `(3, 4)` grid?
interview.answer: The first operand varies down rows and the second across columns, so every combination is paired exactly once.

interview.q: How do you subtract a per-column mean from a matrix?
interview.answer: Compute `arr.mean(axis=0)`, which has shape `(n_features,)`, and subtract it; the trailing axis aligns with the columns.

interview.q: What happens when a `(2, 3)` array is added to a `(3,)` array?
interview.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis and is reused for both rows, producing `(2, 3)`.

interview.q: Why can a scalar broadcast against any shape?
interview.answer: It has no axes to conflict with, so it applies to every element.

interview.q: How do you build an outer product with broadcasting?
interview.answer: Make one operand a column and the other a row, `a[:, None] * b[None, :]`, and the result is the full grid.

interview.q: How do you subtract a row vector from every row of a matrix?
interview.answer: Compute the vector with shape `(n_features,)` and subtract it; it aligns with the columns.

interview.q: What shape does `(4, 1, 3) + (2, 1)` produce?
interview.answer: `(4, 2, 3)`, after the trailing axes align.

interview.q: Why is broadcasting not a copy?
interview.answer: The smaller array is read with zero strides rather than materialised across the larger shape.

interview.q: A store table has shape (500, 1) of discounts and a product table (1, 12) of prices. What happens on addition, and how much memory does the result take?
interview.answer: Both broadcast to (500, 12): every product price meets every store discount. The result is materialised, so it costs 500×12 values even though the inputs are tiny — a real memory risk at scale.

followUps.q: How do you avoid materialising the full (500, 12) product?
followUps.answer: Chunk one axis and reduce as you go (or use `np.einsum` over chunks) when only aggregates are needed; the full product is only worth it when every cell is used.

followUps.q: Does `broadcast_to` itself allocate the big result?
followUps.answer: No — it returns a read-only view with zero strides; the allocation happens on the first arithmetic that materialises values.

interview.q: An operation fails with 'operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4,) (3, 1)'. What is the actual mismatch?
interview.answer: The trailing dimensions must match or be 1: (4,) is treated as (1, 4), which cannot pair with (3, 1) on the last axis (4 vs 1 is fine, but 1 vs 3 on the first axis gives 4 vs 3 ... ). Fix by reshaping to (4, 1) or (1, 3) so the intended axis pairs.

followUps.q: Which reshape resolves `(4,)` against `(3, 1)`?
followUps.answer: `(3, 1)` wants a length-3 axis matched against something of length 3; reshape the vector to `(1, 3)` for a row pairing or `(4, 1)` for a column pairing, depending on which axis you mean.

followUps.q: How do you read broadcast compatibility quickly?
followUps.answer: Align shapes from the right; each pair must be equal or one of them 1. Incompatible means neither rule holds.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Scalar broadcasting
practice.task: A scalar is stretched across every element without being copied, which is why `a + 10` is both simple and memory-cheap.

print(a + 10)

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Row and column broadcasting

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Incompatible shapes fail loudly
practice.task: If two sizes disagree and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError instead of guessing; that error is the rule working, not a bug.
practice.solution:

    a + b

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Outer product uses two new axes

defense.q: Defend standardising columns with broadcasting instead of a loop over columns.
defense.answer: One subtraction and one division do the whole matrix with no Python loop, and the shape of the statistic documents that it is per column.

defense.q: Describe a bug caused by mixing `(3,)` and `(3, 1)`.
defense.answer: The `(3,)` vector aligns with the last axis, so adding it to a `(3, 3)` matrix adds along columns, not rows. The code runs and returns a plausible but wrong answer.

defense.q: Broadcasting a `(1000, 1) + (1, 1000)` allocates a million values. Defend when that is acceptable.
defense.answer: It is fine when the result is genuinely needed at that size and fits in memory. If only a reduction is wanted, use `einsum` or `sum` with an axis to avoid materialising it.

defense.q: Defend writing shapes in comments beside broadcast arithmetic.
defense.answer: The same expression means different things for `(n,)` and `(n, 1)`, and a comment makes the intended axis explicit for the next reader.

defense.q: Explain why a column times a row is not a dot product.
defense.answer: Broadcasting multiplies every pair and keeps both axes, while a dot product contracts the shared axis into one number.

defense.q: Defend reshaping explicitly before an operation that relies on broadcasting.
defense.answer: An explicit shape states which axis is being aligned, so a later data change fails loudly instead of broadcasting in the wrong direction.

defense.q: Defend explicit `reshape` over relying on broadcast alignment.
defense.answer: The intended axis is stated, so a shape change fails loudly instead of broadcasting the wrong way.

defense.q: Explain why `(3,) + (3, 1)` gives `(3, 3)`.
defense.answer: The vector aligns with the trailing axis, so every pair is combined into a grid.

defense.q: Defend computing a reduction instead of materialising a broadcast grid.
defense.answer: The reduction is far smaller and avoids allocating the full grid.

modules.title: Aggregation and Statistics
modules.goal: Summarise arrays with sum, mean, std, argmin and cumulative functions along a chosen axis.

topics.title: Mean along an axis
topics.body: Without an axis every element is reduced to one number; with axis=1 each ROW is reduced, so a (2, 2) array gives two means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(), a.mean(axis=1))

topics.title: Standard deviation and variance
topics.body: var is the mean squared deviation and std is its square root; both use ddof=0 by default, which is the population form.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(a.std(), a.var())

topics.title: Position and running totals
topics.body: argmin returns WHERE the smallest value is (not the value) and cumsum returns the running total at every position.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(a.argmin(), a.cumsum())

topics.title: median is not the mean
topics.body: One extreme value drags the mean but barely moves the median, so reporting both is how you notice a skewed column.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.median([1, 2, 100]), np.mean([1, 2, 100]))

topics.title: keepdims keeps a column
topics.body: keepdims=True leaves the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array without a reshape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True).shape)

topics.title: average can weight values
topics.body: np.average accepts weights, so a weighted mean is one call instead of a manual sum of products divided by a sum of weights.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.average([1, 2], weights=[1, 3]))

topics.title: any and all answer yes/no
topics.body: On a boolean array, any asks whether at least one element is True and all asks whether every element is, each returning a single bool.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False])
print(m.any(), m.all())

topics.title: prod multiplies the elements
topics.body: prod folds with multiplication instead of addition, which is how compound growth and factorial-style products are computed in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.prod(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])))

topics.title: mean of a matrix returns one number
topics.body: Without `axis`, a reduction flattens the array first. The result is a scalar, not a one-element array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).mean())

topics.title: axis=1 reduces each row
topics.body: The reduced axis disappears. Row sums are therefore one value per row, in a `(2,)` array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]).sum(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: std measures spread in the same units
topics.body: Variance is squared units; the standard deviation puts it back in the original scale, which is why reports use it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]).std())

topics.title: The maximum and where it lives
topics.body: `max` gives the value, `argmax` gives its position. Both accept an `axis` when you need one answer per row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([3, 9, 4])
print(a.max(), a.argmax())

topics.title: axis=0 sums columns, axis=1 sums rows
topics.body: The axis you name is the axis that disappears. Summing a (2, 3) array with axis=0 collapses the rows and leaves one value per column.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=0).shape)
print(a.sum(axis=1), a.sum(axis=1).shape)

topics.title: Percentiles answer rank questions
topics.body: percentile returns the value below which a percentage of the data falls, using linear interpolation by default. It is the number to quote for latency and marks, not the mean.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 15, 18, 22, 30, 41])
print(np.percentile(a, 50), np.percentile(a, [25, 75]))

topics.title: sum with keepdims keeps the axis
topics.body: `keepdims=True` leaves the reduced axis as length 1 instead of deleting it, which is exactly what later broadcasting needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.sum(axis=1).shape, a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True).shape)

topics.title: quantile uses fractions
topics.body: `np.quantile` is percentile on a 0–1 scale: the median is 0.5. Use it when the requested cut is naturally a fraction.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
print(np.quantile(a, 0.5), np.quantile(a, [0.25, 0.75]).tolist())

topics.title: argmax with an axis
topics.body: On a matrix, `argmax(axis=1)` gives the winning column for every row, so the output has one index per row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9, 2], [8, 3, 4]])
print(a.argmax(axis=1).tolist())
print(a.argmax(axis=0).tolist())

topics.title: cumulative sum along a row
topics.body: `cumsum(axis=1)` returns a running total within each row, keeping the matrix shape instead of flattening it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.cumsum(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: average accepts a weight per value
topics.body: `np.average` with `weights` computes a weighted mean and can return the weighted sum with `returned=True`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.average([1, 3], weights=[3, 1]))
print(np.average([1, 3], weights=[3, 1], returned=True)[1])

topics.title: ptp is max minus min
topics.body: `np.ptp` reports the range of the data in one call, which is the spread a box plot draws.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(int(np.ptp([4, 1, 9])))

lab.title: Statistics report
lab.brief: Produce a five-number summary (min, mean, median, std, max) for one array.

interviewBank.q: What does `axis=0` mean in `arr.mean(axis=0)`?
interviewBank.answer: The reduction collapses axis 0, the rows, leaving one value per column.

interviewBank.q: Population versus sample standard deviation: which does NumPy compute by default?
interviewBank.answer: Population, dividing by N. `ddof=1` divides by N-1 for the sample estimate.

interviewBank.q: What does `cumsum` return, and how does it differ from `sum`?
interviewBank.answer: A running total of the same shape as the input; `sum` collapses to one value per axis.

interviewBank.q: What does `keepdims=True` preserve, and why does it help?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array.

interviewBank.q: How do you normalise each row by its own mean in one expression?
interviewBank.answer: `arr - arr.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, which aligns the row means with the rows.

interviewBank.q: Why is `argmin` ambiguous on ties?
interviewBank.answer: It returns the first occurrence by position, so several equal minima report only one index.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.ptp` compute?
interviewBank.answer: The difference between the maximum and the minimum.

interviewBank.q: How do you get the index of the maximum per column?
interviewBank.answer: `arr.argmax(axis=0)`.

interviewBank.q: Why is the mean of an empty array NaN?
interviewBank.answer: There is no value to average, and NumPy reports that rather than inventing zero.

interviewBank.q: A dashboard reports the mean order value as 850, but the median is 120. Which number should be shown to explain 'typical' spending?
interviewBank.answer: The median — a few very large orders pull the mean up. Report both when the distribution is skewed, and say which is which.

followUps.q: Which percentile would you add next to the dashboard?
followUps.answer: p95 (or p99) for the tail: it shows the expensive orders the mean hides, and it needs no assumption about the distribution.

followUps.q: How do you compute a mean that ignores outliers?
followUps.answer: Define the rule first (for example drop values beyond the 1st–99th percentile), mask them, then use `np.mean` — and document the rule next to the number.

interviewBank.q: A (1000, 12) table of monthly sales needs the yearly total per product. Which axis, and what does the result shape look like?
interviewBank.answer: axis=1 collapses the months, giving one value per row (shape (1000,)); axis=0 would give one value per month.

followUps.q: How do you get both row and column totals in one pass?
followUps.answer: `total = table.sum()` plus `axis=1` and `axis=0` reductions, or use `keepdims` so the two can be broadcast against each other.

followUps.q: What does `keepdims` change for later broadcasting?
followUps.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so dividing a row by its total aligns automatically instead of failing on shape.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting `argmax` alongside `max` when classifying.
defenseBank.answer: `max` gives the score but not which class produced it, and the class index is what a prediction means. `argmax` returns exactly that.

defenseBank.q: Why is the mean of an empty array `nan`, and when should you guard it?
defenseBank.answer: There is no value to average, so NumPy returns `nan` rather than inventing zero. Guard with a size check when a report must not show a missing number.

defenseBank.q: A report needs per-column medians. Defend your axis choice and mention the cost.
defenseBank.answer: `np.median(arr, axis=0)` collapses rows and keeps one median per column. It sorts along each column, so it is O(n log n) per column, unlike a mean.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting mean together with standard deviation.
defenseBank.answer: A mean alone hides spread, and two datasets with the same mean can behave completely differently. The pair is the minimum honest summary.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a percentile is not a mean band.
defenseBank.answer: A percentile is a position in the sorted data and tolerates skew; mean plus standard deviation assumes a roughly symmetric spread.

defenseBank.q: Defend naming the axis that disappears when you choose `axis`.
defenseBank.answer: Axis errors are silent, and saying "rows collapse" out loud makes `axis=0` the obvious choice rather than a guess.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting a median when the data has outliers.
defenseBank.answer: The median is robust to extreme values, while the mean moves with them.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `std` with `ddof=0` and `ddof=1` differ.
defenseBank.answer: The denominator changes from N to N-1, which matters for small samples.

defenseBank.q: Defend a cumulative sum over recomputing partial sums in a loop.
defenseBank.answer: One compiled pass replaces repeated Python work and allocates a single result.

learn.title: axis=0 sums columns, axis=1 sums rows
learn.body: The axis you name is the axis that disappears. Summing a (2, 3) array with axis=0 collapses the rows and leaves one value per column.

learn.pro: The named axis is the one removed by the reduction: axis=0 collapses rows and leaves one value per column, axis=1 collapses columns and leaves one value per row. The shape of the result is the input shape with that axis deleted, which is exactly what keepdims reverses.

learn.title: Percentiles answer rank questions
learn.body: percentile returns the value below which a percentage of the data falls, using linear interpolation by default. It is the number to quote for latency and marks, not the mean.
learn.code:

print(np.percentile(a, 50), np.percentile(a, [25, 75]))
learn.simple: Percentile batata hai ki kitne log tumse neeche hain. Agar tumhari marks 90th percentile hain, to 90% students tumse kam marks laaye. Average se percentile behtar hai jab kuch bahut bade number sabko confuse kar rahe hon.
learn.pro: percentile returns the value below which a given fraction of observations fall, using linear interpolation between order statistics by default. It is robust to skew where the mean is not, which is why latency and score reports quote p50/p95 rather than the average alone.

learn.title: sum with keepdims keeps the axis
learn.body: `keepdims=True` leaves the reduced axis as length 1 instead of deleting it, which is exactly what later broadcasting needs.
learn.code:

print(a.sum(axis=1).shape, a.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True).shape)
learn.simple: `keepdims=True` reduced axis ko length 1 ka bana deta hai, hataata nahi. Isliye total ko wapas original array par broadcast karna aasan ho jaata hai.
learn.pro: `keepdims=True` retains the reduced axis as length 1, so the result's shape divides back into the input's shape. That property is what lets a normalisation step subtract or divide by the total without an extra `reshape`.
steps: Create a matrix.
Sum rows with and without keepdims.
Compare both shapes.
learn.realWorld: A row total kept as a column can be divided straight back into the matrix.
mistakes: Forgetting that the default reduction deletes the axis.

learn.title: quantile uses fractions
learn.body: `np.quantile` is percentile on a 0–1 scale: the median is 0.5. Use it when the requested cut is naturally a fraction.
learn.code:

print(np.quantile(a, 0.5), np.quantile(a, [0.25, 0.75]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.quantile` percentile ka 0 se 1 wala version hai: median 0.5 hota hai. Jab cut ko fraction me sochna natural ho to yahi use karo.
learn.pro: `np.quantile` expresses the cut as a fraction between 0 and 1, with 0.5 the median, while `percentile` uses 0 to 100. Both interpolate between order statistics, so the requested fraction decides the returned value rather than an exact data point.
steps: Create a small sorted array.
Ask for the median as 0.5.
Ask for the quartiles as a list.
learn.realWorld: Latency budgets are stated as p50 and p95 quantiles.
mistakes: Passing 50 instead of 0.5 to quantile.

learn.title: argmax with an axis
learn.body: On a matrix, `argmax(axis=1)` gives the winning column for every row, so the output has one index per row.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9, 2], [8, 3, 4]])
print(a.argmax(axis=1).tolist())
print(a.argmax(axis=0).tolist())
learn.simple: Matrix par `argmax(axis=1)` har row ka jeetne wala column deta hai. Isliye output me har row ke liye ek index aata hai, poora number nahi.
learn.pro: With `axis=1`, `argmax` returns the winning column index for every row, so the output has one entry per row. The axis argument names the axis that is collapsed, which is why it changes both the shape and the meaning of the result.
steps: Create a matrix with distinct rows.
Find the best column per row.
Find the best row per column and compare.
learn.visual:
axis=1 → one index per row
axis=0 → one index per column
learn.realWorld: Argmax turns per-class scores into a predicted class index.
mistakes: Expecting argmax to return the maximum value.
revision: The axis argument selects what is reduced.

learn.title: cumulative sum along a row
learn.body: `cumsum(axis=1)` returns a running total within each row, keeping the matrix shape instead of flattening it.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.cumsum(axis=1).tolist())
learn.simple: `cumsum(axis=1)` har row ke andar running total deta hai aur matrix ka shape waisa hi rehta hai. Isliye flattened list nahi milti.
learn.pro: `cumsum` with `axis=1` accumulates within each row and preserves the matrix shape, returning every intermediate total. That shape preservation is what makes it usable as a feature column alongside the original values.
steps: Create a matrix.
Cumulatively sum each row.
Print the result and check the last cell equals the row total.
learn.realWorld: Cumulative revenue or running totals are cumsum operations.
mistakes: Calling cumsum without an axis and flattening the matrix.
revision: The axis decides where it accumulates.

learn.title: average accepts a weight per value
learn.body: `np.average` with `weights` computes a weighted mean and can return the weighted sum with `returned=True`.
learn.code:

print(np.average([1, 3], weights=[3, 1], returned=True)[1])
learn.simple: `np.average` me har number ka apna weight de sakte ho, isliye zyada important value ka asar zyada padta hai. Weighted sum bhi saath me mil sakta hai.
learn.pro: `np.average` computes `sum(w * x) / sum(w)` when weights are supplied, so each value contributes in proportion to its weight. With `returned=True` it also returns the weight total, which keeps the denominator auditable.
steps: Create values and matching weights.
Compute the weighted average.
Return the weight total with `returned=True`.
learn.visual:
sum(w*x) / sum(w)
weights shift the centre
learn.realWorld: Survey results are weighted by population so each group contributes fairly.
mistakes: Passing weights of the wrong length.
revision: The denominator is the weight total.

learn.title: ptp is max minus min
learn.body: `np.ptp` reports the range of the data in one call, which is the spread a box plot draws.

learn.pro: `np.ptp` returns the difference between the maximum and minimum, which is the range a box plot draws. It works along an axis and ignores NaN only when you ask for the NaN-aware variant, so missing values need explicit handling.
steps: Create a vector with a known range.
Compute `ptp`.
Compare it with max minus min.
learn.realWorld: Quality control reports the spread of a batch as its range.
mistakes: Using ptp with NaN values and getting NaN.

interview.q: What does `axis=0` mean in `arr.mean(axis=0)`?
interview.answer: The reduction collapses axis 0, the rows, leaving one value per column.

interview.q: Population versus sample standard deviation: which does NumPy compute by default?
interview.answer: Population, dividing by N. `ddof=1` divides by N-1 for the sample estimate.

interview.q: What does `cumsum` return, and how does it differ from `sum`?
interview.answer: A running total of the same shape as the input; `sum` collapses to one value per axis.

interview.q: What does `keepdims=True` preserve, and why does it help?
interview.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array.

interview.q: How do you normalise each row by its own mean in one expression?
interview.answer: `arr - arr.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, which aligns the row means with the rows.

interview.q: Why is `argmin` ambiguous on ties?
interview.answer: It returns the first occurrence by position, so several equal minima report only one index.

interview.q: What does `np.ptp` compute?
interview.answer: The difference between the maximum and the minimum.

interview.q: How do you get the index of the maximum per column?
interview.answer: `arr.argmax(axis=0)`.

interview.q: Why is the mean of an empty array NaN?
interview.answer: There is no value to average, and NumPy reports that rather than inventing zero.

interview.q: A dashboard reports the mean order value as 850, but the median is 120. Which number should be shown to explain 'typical' spending?
interview.answer: The median — a few very large orders pull the mean up. Report both when the distribution is skewed, and say which is which.

followUps.q: Which percentile would you add next to the dashboard?
followUps.answer: p95 (or p99) for the tail: it shows the expensive orders the mean hides, and it needs no assumption about the distribution.

followUps.q: How do you compute a mean that ignores outliers?
followUps.answer: Define the rule first (for example drop values beyond the 1st–99th percentile), mask them, then use `np.mean` — and document the rule next to the number.

interview.q: A (1000, 12) table of monthly sales needs the yearly total per product. Which axis, and what does the result shape look like?
interview.answer: axis=1 collapses the months, giving one value per row (shape (1000,)); axis=0 would give one value per month.

followUps.q: How do you get both row and column totals in one pass?
followUps.answer: `total = table.sum()` plus `axis=1` and `axis=0` reductions, or use `keepdims` so the two can be broadcast against each other.

followUps.q: What does `keepdims` change for later broadcasting?
followUps.answer: It keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so dividing a row by its total aligns automatically instead of failing on shape.

defense.q: Defend reporting `argmax` alongside `max` when classifying.
defense.answer: `max` gives the score but not which class produced it, and the class index is what a prediction means. `argmax` returns exactly that.

defense.q: Why is the mean of an empty array `nan`, and when should you guard it?
defense.answer: There is no value to average, so NumPy returns `nan` rather than inventing zero. Guard with a size check when a report must not show a missing number.

defense.q: A report needs per-column medians. Defend your axis choice and mention the cost.
defense.answer: `np.median(arr, axis=0)` collapses rows and keeps one median per column. It sorts along each column, so it is O(n log n) per column, unlike a mean.

defense.q: Defend reporting mean together with standard deviation.
defense.answer: A mean alone hides spread, and two datasets with the same mean can behave completely differently. The pair is the minimum honest summary.

defense.q: Explain why a percentile is not a mean band.
defense.answer: A percentile is a position in the sorted data and tolerates skew; mean plus standard deviation assumes a roughly symmetric spread.

defense.q: Defend naming the axis that disappears when you choose `axis`.
defense.answer: Axis errors are silent, and saying "rows collapse" out loud makes `axis=0` the obvious choice rather than a guess.

defense.q: Defend reporting a median when the data has outliers.
defense.answer: The median is robust to extreme values, while the mean moves with them.

defense.q: Explain why `std` with `ddof=0` and `ddof=1` differ.
defense.answer: The denominator changes from N to N-1, which matters for small samples.

defense.q: Defend a cumulative sum over recomputing partial sums in a loop.
defense.answer: One compiled pass replaces repeated Python work and allocates a single result.

modules.title: Boolean Indexing and Filtering
modules.goal: Filter arrays with masks, replace values with where and test membership with isin.

topics.title: Filter with a mask
topics.body: A comparison builds a boolean array; indexing with it keeps the True positions and returns a new array of the passing values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([55, 72, 38])
print(a[a >= 60])

topics.title: np.where chooses without a loop
topics.body: where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is True and y where it is False, so a label column is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(np.where(a > 2, 'big', 'small'))

topics.title: Membership with isin
topics.body: isin answers "is each element in this list?" and returns a mask, which composes with other masks for multi-condition filters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.isin(a, [2, 4]))

topics.title: Combine masks with & and |
topics.body: Elementwise combination needs the bitwise operators inside parentheses; `and` and `or` would ask for one truth value and fail.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) & (a < 4)])

topics.title: Invert a mask with ~
topics.body: The tilde flips a boolean array, so `a[~(a > 1)]` keeps exactly the elements the mask rejected.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[~(a > 1)])

topics.title: Assign through a mask
topics.body: A boolean mask works on the left of an assignment, which replaces the selected elements in place instead of returning a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-1, 4, -5])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Count how many match
topics.body: Because True is 1, summing a mask gives the count directly — no filter and no len call needed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print((a % 2 == 0).sum())

topics.title: Filter rows by one column
topics.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, so `a[a[:, 1] > 5]` keeps every column of the rows that qualify.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [2, 3]])
print(a[a[:, 1] > 5])

topics.title: A mask keeps the shape of its array
topics.body: Comparing an array to a number never shortens it. Only indexing with the mask does that.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print((a % 2 == 0).shape)

topics.title: where chooses between two values
topics.body: `np.where(mask, a, b)` is a vectorised `if`. Neither branch is skipped, so both should be cheap expressions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.where(np.array([1, 5, 2]) > 3, 'big', 'small').tolist())

topics.title: Sum the mask to count matches
topics.body: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0, so `sum` on a mask is a count. Wrap it in `int` when you want a Python number.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(int((np.arange(10) > 5).sum()))

topics.title: Filter a matrix elementwise
topics.body: Indexing with a full-shape mask flattens the matches into a 1-D array. Row structure is not preserved.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[a % 2 == 0].tolist())

topics.title: where chooses between two arrays
topics.body: np.where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is true and y where it is false, which replaces an if/else loop over the elements.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
marks = np.array([35, 72, 48, 90])
print(np.where(marks >= 50, 'pass', 'fail'))

topics.title: Updating through a mask
topics.body: A boolean mask can be used on the left of an assignment, so only the selected cells change and the rest keep their values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-5, 3, -2, 8])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: nonzero returns the positions
topics.body: `np.nonzero` gives the indices of the True cells, so a mask can be turned back into coordinates for reporting.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([0, 3, 0, 4])
print(np.nonzero(a)[0].tolist())

topics.title: Count matches per column
topics.body: Summing a boolean mask along an axis counts matches in each column or row without a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [5, 5]])
print((a > 4).sum(axis=0).tolist())

topics.title: Select with an isin mask
topics.body: `np.isin` builds the membership mask, and the same mask filters the values, so a whitelist is one expression.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 4, 7])
print(a[np.isin(a, [4, 7])].tolist())

topics.title: Mask a matrix row-wise
topics.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, which is how records are filtered by a field.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [5, 5], [9, 1]])
print(a[a[:, 0] > 4].tolist())

topics.title: where with two arrays
topics.body: Both branches of `np.where` can be arrays, so a conditional replacement is expressed without an if inside a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 2])
print(np.where(a > 2, a * 10, a).tolist())

topics.title: Combine masks with and
topics.body: `&` combines two boolean arrays element by element and requires parentheses around each comparison because of operator precedence.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 8, 12])
print(a[(a > 2) & (a < 10)].tolist())

debug.fix:

debug.fix:

print(np.where(np.arange(3) > 0, np.arange(3), 0))

lab.title: Mask a sensor log
lab.brief: Flag readings outside 0–100, count them and replace them with the mean of the valid readings.

interviewBank.q: Why do you combine masks with `&` and `|` rather than `and` and `or`?
interviewBank.answer: The bitwise operators act elementwise on boolean arrays; `and` forces one truth value for the whole array and raises on a multi-element mask.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.where(mask, a, b)` return?
interviewBank.answer: An array that takes `a` where the mask is true and `b` elsewhere, with broadcasting applied to the branches.

interviewBank.q: How do you count how many elements satisfy a condition?
interviewBank.answer: `mask.sum()` or `np.count_nonzero(mask)`, both of which count true entries.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `arr > 5` and `arr[arr > 5]`?
interviewBank.answer: The first is the boolean mask; the second applies it and returns only the selected values.

interviewBank.q: How do you invert a boolean mask?
interviewBank.answer: Use `~mask`, the elementwise negation, which keeps the array shape.

interviewBank.q: Why do mask expressions need parentheses?
interviewBank.answer: `&` binds tighter than comparison, so `a > 1 & a < 3` compares against the result of the bitwise operation. Parenthesise each comparison.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.count_nonzero` count on a boolean mask?
interviewBank.answer: The number of true entries.

interviewBank.q: How do you replace negative values with zero?
interviewBank.answer: `np.where(arr < 0, 0, arr)`, or clipping at zero when only that bound matters.

interviewBank.q: Why does `arr > 1 and arr < 3` fail?
interviewBank.answer: `and` needs one truth value, and a multi-element array does not have one.

interviewBank.q: Customers with no purchases for 90 days must be flagged. Why is a boolean mask better than a loop that appends indices?
interviewBank.answer: The mask is one vectorised comparison over the whole column, and it can be reused for counting, filtering and assignment. A Python loop grows a list and pays per-row overhead.

followUps.q: How do you reuse one mask for counting and assignment?
followUps.answer: Build it once (`mask = arr > threshold`), then `mask.sum()` for the count and `arr[mask] = value` for the update — same mask, one comparison pass.

followUps.q: What does the mask cost in memory?
followUps.answer: One byte per element (bool), which is why a mask over a huge float64 array is usually affordable.

interviewBank.q: A codebase updates churn labels with `df[mask] = 1` then checks `df` and finds nothing changed. What kind of object was df likely to be?
interviewBank.answer: A NumPy array's boolean assignment does mutate in place, so if nothing changed the value was probably a copy (advanced indexing on a pandas object, or a slice that was copied earlier). Verify with `base is`/`np.shares_memory`.

followUps.q: How do you detect an accidental copy in a chain of operations?
followUps.answer: Check `np.shares_memory` after each step, especially after advanced indexing or a pandas round trip, and look at `.base`.

followUps.q: Which assignment form avoids the chained-index copy trap?
followUps.answer: Assign into the array itself (`arr[mask] = 1`), not into a chained result like `df[mask][col] = 1`.

defenseBank.q: Defend masking over an `if` loop when filtering a million rows.
defenseBank.answer: The mask is computed once as one vectorised comparison and applied as a single gather, instead of a million interpreter iterations and list appends.

defenseBank.q: Why must a mask match the length of the axis it filters?
defenseBank.answer: It selects positions of that axis, so a shorter or longer mask has no defined mapping and NumPy raises rather than guessing.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.isin` for membership tests instead of a Python `in` loop.
defenseBank.answer: `isin` sorts or hashes internally and answers for the whole array at once. A loop over `in` against a list is quadratic in the worst case.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.where` over assignment through a mask for three-way choices.
defenseBank.answer: `where` returns a complete new array from two branches, so no element is left in an intermediate state and the intent is one expression.

defenseBank.q: Explain why a mask of the wrong length raises.
defenseBank.answer: The mask maps one-to-one onto positions of an axis, so a different length has no defined alignment. Failing is better than guessing.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.isin` for filtering against a whitelist.
defenseBank.answer: It answers the whole array in one operation and stays fast for large lists, unlike a per-element Python membership loop.

defenseBank.q: Defend a mask expression over a Python filter loop.
defenseBank.answer: The comparison runs once over the buffer with no per-element call or list append.

defenseBank.q: Explain why an empty mask selects nothing rather than everything.
defenseBank.answer: It selects the positions it marks, and there are none.

defenseBank.q: Defend `np.where` over mutating the input inside a helper.
defenseBank.answer: It returns a new array, so the caller's data is untouched and the function stays predictable.

learn.title: Filter with a mask
learn.body: A comparison builds a boolean array; indexing with it keeps the True positions and returns a new array of the passing values.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([55, 72, 38])
print(a[a >= 60])

learn.title: np.where chooses without a loop
learn.body: where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is True and y where it is False, so a label column is one call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(np.where(a > 2, 'big', 'small'))

learn.title: Membership with isin
learn.body: isin answers "is each element in this list?" and returns a mask, which composes with other masks for multi-condition filters.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.isin(a, [2, 4]))

learn.title: Combine masks with & and |
learn.body: Elementwise combination needs the bitwise operators inside parentheses; `and` and `or` would ask for one truth value and fail.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) & (a < 4)])

learn.title: Invert a mask with ~
learn.body: The tilde flips a boolean array, so `a[~(a > 1)]` keeps exactly the elements the mask rejected.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[~(a > 1)])

learn.title: Assign through a mask
learn.body: A boolean mask works on the left of an assignment, which replaces the selected elements in place instead of returning a new array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-1, 4, -5])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

learn.title: Count how many match
learn.body: Because True is 1, summing a mask gives the count directly — no filter and no len call needed.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print((a % 2 == 0).sum())

learn.title: Filter rows by one column
learn.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, so `a[a[:, 1] > 5]` keeps every column of the rows that qualify.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [2, 3]])
print(a[a[:, 1] > 5])

learn.title: A mask keeps the shape of its array
learn.body: Comparing an array to a number never shortens it. Only indexing with the mask does that.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print((a % 2 == 0).shape)

learn.title: where chooses between two values
learn.body: `np.where(mask, a, b)` is a vectorised `if`. Neither branch is skipped, so both should be cheap expressions.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.where(np.array([1, 5, 2]) > 3, 'big', 'small').tolist())

learn.title: Sum the mask to count matches
learn.body: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0, so `sum` on a mask is a count. Wrap it in `int` when you want a Python number.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(int((np.arange(10) > 5).sum()))

learn.title: Filter a matrix elementwise
learn.body: Indexing with a full-shape mask flattens the matches into a 1-D array. Row structure is not preserved.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[a % 2 == 0].tolist())

learn.title: where chooses between two arrays
learn.body: np.where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is true and y where it is false, which replaces an if/else loop over the elements.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
marks = np.array([35, 72, 48, 90])
print(np.where(marks >= 50, 'pass', 'fail'))
learn.simple: `np.where` ek chhota judge hai: jahan condition sach ho wahan pehla option, jahan jhoot ho wahan doosra. Jaise pass/fail likhna — marks 50 se zyada to "pass", warna "fail", poore array par ek saath.
learn.pro: np.where(condition, x, y) is a vectorised select: it returns x where the condition is true and y elsewhere, broadcasting all three inputs. It replaces an elementwise if/else and always materialises an output array.

learn.title: Updating through a mask
learn.body: A boolean mask can be used on the left of an assignment, so only the selected cells change and the rest keep their values.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-5, 3, -2, 8])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)
learn.simple: Mask ek chashma hai jo sirf chuni hui jagah dikhata hai. `a[a < 0] = 0` ka matlab hai "jahan number negative hai wahan 0 rakh do" — baaki numbers ko chhue bina. Isse saara array ek saath saaf ho jata hai.
learn.pro: Assigning into a boolean mask mutates only the selected cells in place, leaving the rest untouched. The mask is computed once and reused; the same pattern serves counting (mask.sum()), filtering and conditional replacement.

learn.title: nonzero returns the positions
learn.body: `np.nonzero` gives the indices of the True cells, so a mask can be turned back into coordinates for reporting.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([0, 3, 0, 4])
print(np.nonzero(a)[0].tolist())
learn.simple: `np.nonzero` batata hai ki True wale cells kahan hain — row aur column ke numbers me. Isliye mask ko wapas coordinates me badal sakte ho.
learn.pro: `np.nonzero` returns one index array per dimension for the nonzero cells, so a mask can be turned back into coordinates for reporting or scatter plotting. For a 1-D array it returns a tuple with a single array, which is why the `[0]` is usually needed.
steps: Create a vector with zeros.
Call `nonzero` and print the index array.
Use the positions to select the values.
learn.realWorld: Finding the set bits or non-zero features of a sparse row uses nonzero.
mistakes: Treating the tuple as a single index array.
revision: Nonzero returns one array per dimension.

learn.title: Count matches per column
learn.body: Summing a boolean mask along an axis counts matches in each column or row without a loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [5, 5]])
print((a > 4).sum(axis=0).tolist())
learn.simple: Boolean mask ko column axis par jodne se har column ke matches ki ginti mil jaati hai, bina loop ke. Yeh per-feature quality check ke liye kaam aata hai.
learn.pro: Summing a boolean mask along an axis counts matches per column or row, because True casts to 1. The reduced axis is the one named in `axis`, so the output length matches the other dimension.
steps: Create a matrix.
Build a threshold mask.
Sum the mask down the rows to count per column.
learn.realWorld: Missing-value counts per feature are a boolean sum down the rows.
mistakes: Summing without an axis and losing the per-column meaning.
revision: The named axis is the one collapsed.

learn.title: Select with an isin mask
learn.body: `np.isin` builds the membership mask, and the same mask filters the values, so a whitelist is one expression.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 4, 7])
print(a[np.isin(a, [4, 7])].tolist())
learn.simple: `np.isin` batata hai kaunsi values allowed list me hain, aur wahi mask values chhaant leta hai. Whitelist filter ek hi line me ban jaata hai.
learn.pro: `np.isin` builds a boolean mask for membership in a set of values, which can then filter the array. It accepts `invert=True` for the complement, and the mask keeps the input shape so it composes with other conditions.
steps: Create a vector of categories.
Build the membership mask with `isin`.
Filter the values with that mask.
learn.realWorld: Keeping only known country codes in a dataset is an isin filter.
mistakes: Using `in` inside a loop instead of a vectorised mask.
revision: The mask preserves the input shape.

learn.title: Mask a matrix row-wise
learn.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, which is how records are filtered by a field.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [5, 5], [9, 1]])
print(a[a[:, 0] > 4].tolist())
learn.simple: Ek column se banaya mask poore rows chun sakta hai. Isliye kisi field ki value ke hisaab se records filter karna aasan hai.
learn.pro: A mask built from one column can select whole rows when applied to the first axis, which is how records are filtered by a field. The mask is 1-D, so it aligns with rows rather than with every cell.
steps: Create a matrix where the first column is a key.
Build a mask from that column.
Apply it to the matrix to keep whole rows.
learn.realWorld: Filtering records by one field keeps the other fields attached.
mistakes: Applying a column mask to every cell instead of whole rows.
revision: The mask length must equal the row count.

learn.title: where with two arrays
learn.body: Both branches of `np.where` can be arrays, so a conditional replacement is expressed without an if inside a loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 2])
print(np.where(a > 2, a * 10, a).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.where` ke dono branches array ho sakte hain, isliye conditional replacement bina if ke hota hai. Jahan condition True ho wahan pehla array aata hai.
learn.pro: Both branches of `np.where` can be arrays, so a conditional replacement is expressed as a whole-array operation. The branches broadcast against the condition, and the output dtype is the promotion of both branch dtypes.
steps: Create a condition and two value arrays.
Apply `where` and print the mix.
Swap the branches and compare.
learn.visual:
True → a, False → b
output shape is the broadcast shape
learn.realWorld: Replacing outliers with a capped value per cell is a where operation.
mistakes: Passing scalars when arrays were intended, then wondering about dtype.

learn.title: Combine masks with and
learn.body: `&` combines two boolean arrays element by element and requires parentheses around each comparison because of operator precedence.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 8, 12])
print(a[(a > 2) & (a < 10)].tolist())
learn.simple: Do conditions ko `&` se jodte hain, aur har condition ko bracket me rakhna padta hai. `and` yahan kaam nahi karta kyunki woh poore array par truthiness maangta hai.
learn.pro: `&` combines two boolean arrays elementwise, while Python's `and` would evaluate the truth value of an entire array and raise. Parentheses around each comparison are required because `&` binds tighter than the comparison operators.
steps: Create a vector.
Build two comparisons and combine them with `&`.
Filter with the combined mask.
learn.realWorld: A price range filter is two conditions combined elementwise.
mistakes: Using Python `and`, which raises on arrays.

interview.q: Why do you combine masks with `&` and `|` rather than `and` and `or`?
interview.answer: The bitwise operators act elementwise on boolean arrays; `and` forces one truth value for the whole array and raises on a multi-element mask.

interview.q: What does `np.where(mask, a, b)` return?
interview.answer: An array that takes `a` where the mask is true and `b` elsewhere, with broadcasting applied to the branches.

interview.q: How do you count how many elements satisfy a condition?
interview.answer: `mask.sum()` or `np.count_nonzero(mask)`, both of which count true entries.

interview.q: What is the difference between `arr > 5` and `arr[arr > 5]`?
interview.answer: The first is the boolean mask; the second applies it and returns only the selected values.

interview.q: How do you invert a boolean mask?
interview.answer: Use `~mask`, the elementwise negation, which keeps the array shape.

interview.q: Why do mask expressions need parentheses?
interview.answer: `&` binds tighter than comparison, so `a > 1 & a < 3` compares against the result of the bitwise operation. Parenthesise each comparison.

interview.q: What does `np.count_nonzero` count on a boolean mask?
interview.answer: The number of true entries.

interview.q: How do you replace negative values with zero?
interview.answer: `np.where(arr < 0, 0, arr)`, or clipping at zero when only that bound matters.

interview.q: Why does `arr > 1 and arr < 3` fail?
interview.answer: `and` needs one truth value, and a multi-element array does not have one.

interview.q: Customers with no purchases for 90 days must be flagged. Why is a boolean mask better than a loop that appends indices?
interview.answer: The mask is one vectorised comparison over the whole column, and it can be reused for counting, filtering and assignment. A Python loop grows a list and pays per-row overhead.

followUps.q: How do you reuse one mask for counting and assignment?
followUps.answer: Build it once (`mask = arr > threshold`), then `mask.sum()` for the count and `arr[mask] = value` for the update — same mask, one comparison pass.

followUps.q: What does the mask cost in memory?
followUps.answer: One byte per element (bool), which is why a mask over a huge float64 array is usually affordable.

interview.q: A codebase updates churn labels with `df[mask] = 1` then checks `df` and finds nothing changed. What kind of object was df likely to be?
interview.answer: A NumPy array's boolean assignment does mutate in place, so if nothing changed the value was probably a copy (advanced indexing on a pandas object, or a slice that was copied earlier). Verify with `base is`/`np.shares_memory`.

followUps.q: How do you detect an accidental copy in a chain of operations?
followUps.answer: Check `np.shares_memory` after each step, especially after advanced indexing or a pandas round trip, and look at `.base`.

followUps.q: Which assignment form avoids the chained-index copy trap?
followUps.answer: Assign into the array itself (`arr[mask] = 1`), not into a chained result like `df[mask][col] = 1`.

defense.q: Defend masking over an `if` loop when filtering a million rows.
defense.answer: The mask is computed once as one vectorised comparison and applied as a single gather, instead of a million interpreter iterations and list appends.

defense.q: Why must a mask match the length of the axis it filters?
defense.answer: It selects positions of that axis, so a shorter or longer mask has no defined mapping and NumPy raises rather than guessing.

defense.q: Defend `np.isin` for membership tests instead of a Python `in` loop.
defense.answer: `isin` sorts or hashes internally and answers for the whole array at once. A loop over `in` against a list is quadratic in the worst case.

defense.q: Defend `np.where` over assignment through a mask for three-way choices.
defense.answer: `where` returns a complete new array from two branches, so no element is left in an intermediate state and the intent is one expression.

defense.q: Explain why a mask of the wrong length raises.
defense.answer: The mask maps one-to-one onto positions of an axis, so a different length has no defined alignment. Failing is better than guessing.

defense.q: Defend `np.isin` for filtering against a whitelist.
defense.answer: It answers the whole array in one operation and stays fast for large lists, unlike a per-element Python membership loop.

defense.q: Defend a mask expression over a Python filter loop.
defense.answer: The comparison runs once over the buffer with no per-element call or list append.

defense.q: Explain why an empty mask selects nothing rather than everything.
defense.answer: It selects the positions it marks, and there are none.

defense.q: Defend `np.where` over mutating the input inside a helper.
defense.answer: It returns a new array, so the caller's data is untouched and the function stays predictable.
