learn.title: Structured arrays
learn.body: A structured dtype names each field and its type, so one array can hold an id and a score and you can select a column with a['field'].
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f4')])
print(a['score'])

learn.title: datetime64 arithmetic
learn.body: A datetime64 array with a unit such as [D] supports addition of whole days, so date maths stays integer arithmetic underneath.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.array(['2026-01-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]')
print(d + 1)

learn.title: Vectorised string operations
learn.body: np.char applies string methods elementwise; it is convenient for arrays of text but it is not a replacement for proper text tooling.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array(['num', 'py'])
print(np.char.upper(a))

learn.title: Fixed-width strings truncate
learn.body: A U2 dtype stores at most two characters per element, so longer text is cut on creation rather than at print time.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["abcd"], dtype="U2"))

learn.title: object dtype keeps Python objects
learn.body: dtype=object stores pointers to arbitrary Python values, which is flexible but loses the fast numeric paths that make arrays worthwhile.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, "x", None], dtype=object)
print(a.dtype, a[1])

learn.title: timedelta64 tells the gap
learn.body: Subtracting two datetime64 values returns a timedelta64, so date arithmetic reports an interval in the unit of the operands.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01'))

learn.title: Divide a timedelta to get a count
learn.body: Dividing a timedelta64 by a unit timedelta converts it to a plain number, which is how you get days, hours or seconds for analysis.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01')
print(d / np.timedelta64(1, 'D'))

learn.title: Fields are read by name
learn.body: A structured array indexes its fields by name, so a price column is a plain array you can sum without unpacking the records.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5), (2, 3.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('price', 'f4')])
print(a['price'].sum())

learn.title: char functions work elementwise on text
learn.body: The `np.char` namespace applies string methods to every element without a Python loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.upper(np.array(['np', 'ai'])).tolist())

learn.title: str_len counts characters
learn.body: Length is a property of the string, not the fixed-width buffer. Padding does not inflate the count.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.str_len(np.array(['ab', 'cde'])).tolist())

learn.title: Datetime differences are timedeltas
learn.body: Subtracting two `datetime64` values gives a `timedelta64`, which converts to a number by dividing by a unit.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

start = np.datetime64('2026-01-01')
end = np.datetime64('2026-01-11')
print((end - start) / np.timedelta64(1, 'D'))

learn.title: A structured array reads fields by name
learn.body: One row can hold several dtypes. Field access returns a normal array, so all the usual reductions apply.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

dtype = np.dtype([('name', 'U4'), ('score', 'i4')])
rows = np.array([('ada', 91)], dtype=dtype)
print(rows['score'].tolist())

learn.title: Dates as datetime64
learn.body: datetime64 stores an instant on a fixed unit, so subtraction gives a timedelta64 and comparison is a number comparison. No timezone is carried.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.array(['2026-01-01', '2026-03-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]')
print(d, d[1] - d[0])
print(d + np.timedelta64(10, 'D'))
learn.simple: Date bhi ek number hi hai, bas NumPy use khaas tarah se samajhta hai. Do dates ko minus karo to pata chal jata hai kitne din ka fark hai, aur plus karne par nayi date milti hai. Isme timezone nahi hota, sirf ek saaf unit (din, second) hota hai.
learn.pro: datetime64 stores an instant on a fixed unit, so subtraction yields timedelta64 and comparisons are integer comparisons. The unit is part of the dtype and a wrong unit shifts dates silently; no timezone is carried, so convert deliberately at the boundary.

learn.title: Structured arrays hold named fields
learn.body: A structured dtype gives every row named, typed fields, so a record stays one row instead of three parallel arrays.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rec = np.array([(1, 92.5), (2, 81.0)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f8')])
print(rec['score'].mean(), rec.dtype.names)
learn.simple: Socho har student ke liye ek line: id aur score. Structured array me har row ke andar naam wale khaane hote hain — `rec['score']` bol kar seedha score mil jata hai. Teen alag arrays rakhne ki zaroorat nahi.
learn.pro: A structured dtype gives each row named, typed fields stored contiguously, so a record stays one row and field access is a strided view. It suits records that travel together (sorting, saving, indexing); parallel arrays are simpler when columns are analysed independently.

learn.title: datetime64 carries its unit
learn.body: The unit (`D`, `s`, `ms`) is part of the dtype, so adding a number without a timedelta is refused while a timedelta keeps the unit explicit.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.datetime64('2026-01-01')
print(d.dtype, str(d + np.timedelta64(1, 'D')))
learn.simple: Date ke saath unit bhi dtype ka hissa hoti hai — din, second ya millisecond. Isliye number jodne se pehle batana padta hai ki woh kis unit me hai.
learn.pro: The unit is part of the `datetime64` dtype, so `2026-01-01` is stored as a day count while `2026-01-01T00:00:00` is a second count. Mixing units promotes to the finer one, and adding a bare number is refused because it has no unit.
steps: Create a date and print its dtype.
Add a one-day timedelta.
Print the result and confirm the unit.
learn.realWorld: Daily sales dates are stored as datetime64[D] so arithmetic stays in whole days.
mistakes: Adding a bare number without a unit.
revision: The unit is part of the dtype.

learn.title: astype converts integers to dates
learn.body: An integer array can become datetime64 with an explicit unit, which is how epoch seconds enter NumPy without string parsing.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
epochs = np.array([0, 86400])
print(epochs.astype('datetime64[s]').tolist())
learn.simple: Integer array ko unit bata kar date bana sakte ho. Isliye epoch seconds ya days seedha NumPy me aa jaate hain, string parse kiye bina.
learn.pro: Casting an integer array to `datetime64` with an explicit unit reinterprets each number as a count from the epoch. That is the direct route for timestamps coming out of a database, and the unit must match how the integers were recorded.
steps: Create an integer array of epoch seconds.
Cast it to datetime64 with seconds.
Print the dates.
learn.realWorld: Database timestamps arrive as integers and become dates at the boundary.
mistakes: Forgetting the unit and getting an unexpected interpretation.
revision: The integer counts from the epoch.

learn.title: sort a structured array by a field
learn.body: Passing `order=` sorts records by the named field, keeping id and score together.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(rec[np.argsort(rec, order='score')]['id'].tolist())

learn.title: string arrays have a fixed width
learn.body: The longest string sets the dtype width, and shorter values are padded. A longer value assigned later is truncated, not grown.
learn.code:

a = np.array(['ab', 'c'])
print(a.dtype, a.tolist())
learn.simple: Sabse lamba string dtype ki width set karta hai, chhote strings padding ke saath usi box me fit hote hain. Baad me lamba value daalne par woh kat jaata hai, box bada nahi hota.
learn.pro: The longest value determines the `<U<n>` width, and every element occupies that many bytes whether or not it fills them. Assigning a longer string later truncates to the declared width, because the fixed-width buffer cannot grow in place.
steps: Create a string array.
Print the dtype width.
Assign a longer value and observe truncation.
learn.realWorld: Country codes stored as <U2 reject or truncate longer input.
mistakes: Expecting the buffer to grow for a longer value.

learn.title: object arrays hold anything
learn.body: An object dtype stores Python references, so it can mix types but loses the compiled speed and needs pickle to save.

learn.simple: Object dtype Python ke references rakhta hai, isliye alag-alag types ek array me aa sakte hain. Par speed kam ho jaati hai aur save karne ke liye pickle chahiye.
learn.pro: An object array stores pointers to Python objects, so it can mix types at the cost of the compiled loops and a pickle requirement when saving. It is a container of references, not a numeric buffer, which is why vectorised arithmetic does not apply.

mistakes: Expecting vectorised numeric speed from object dtype.

interview.q: What is a structured dtype for?
interview.answer: It stores records with named, typed fields in one array, so a row can mix numbers and text without becoming a Python object.

interview.q: Why is `datetime64` not a Python `datetime`?
interview.answer: It is a fixed-width value with a declared unit, so it lives in a typed buffer and supports vectorised arithmetic and comparison.

interview.q: How do vectorised string operations help?
interview.answer: They run one compiled loop over a fixed-width string array instead of calling a Python method per element.

interview.q: How do you read one field of a structured array?
interview.answer: Index it by name, `arr["qty"]`, which returns a typed array for that field.

interview.q: What does a unit of `"M"` in a `datetime64` mean?
interview.answer: The value is stored as a count of whole months, so day-level information is not available at that unit.

interview.q: Why do string arrays have a fixed width?
interview.answer: The dtype fixes each element to a number of characters so the buffer can stay contiguous; longer strings are truncated.

interview.q: What does a structured array's dtype describe?
interview.answer: A list of named fields, each with its own dtype.

interview.q: How do you convert a `datetime64` to a coarser unit?
interview.answer: `astype("datetime64[D]")` for days, which changes the stored unit.

interview.q: Why is `np.char` more limited than Pandas string methods?
interview.answer: It works on fixed-width arrays with a small fixed set of operations.

interview.q: A dataset mixes dates as strings and timestamps as ints. Why is one datetime64 array better than two columns?
interview.answer: datetime64 gives one typed axis with real subtraction (timedelta64), ordering and comparison. Two representations force conversion at every use and invite silent unit mistakes (days vs seconds).

followUps.q: How do you convert integer epochs to `datetime64` correctly?
followUps.answer: State the unit: `epochs.astype('datetime64[s]')`; a wrong unit silently shifts every date instead of raising.

followUps.q: What breaks when units are mixed?
followUps.answer: Comparing day and second units truncates to the coarser unit, so two "different" timestamps can compare equal.

interview.q: A record has an id and a score. When is a structured array the right choice over two parallel arrays?
interview.answer: When rows are always used together — sorting, saving and indexing keep the fields aligned. Two parallel arrays are simpler when the fields are analysed separately and independently.

followUps.q: What does sorting a structured array sort by?
followUps.answer: The fields in declaration order unless you pass `order=[...]`, so field order is part of the record contract.

followUps.q: When do parallel arrays beat a structured array?
followUps.answer: When each column is analysed independently and vectorised as its own array; structured records win when rows travel together.

import numpy as np

# read the task, then store your answer in `result`
coding.solution:
import numpy as np
dtype = np.dtype([('name', 'U5'), ('qty', 'i4')])
rows = np.array([('a', 2), ('b', 3)], dtype=dtype)
result = int(rows['qty'].sum())
print(result)

defense.q: Defend structured arrays over a list of dicts for tabular data.
defense.answer: One contiguous typed block, vectorised field access, and no per-record dictionary overhead. A list of dicts costs an object per row and cannot be sorted by field cheaply.

defense.q: Explain the cost of a `<U10` string column.
defense.answer: Every element reserves ten characters regardless of content, so short strings waste memory and long ones truncate.

defense.q: Defend `datetime64` for time series before converting to pandas.
defense.answer: It keeps timestamps compact and arithmetic vectorised, and conversion is explicit at the boundary of the frame rather than implied by parsing.

defense.q: Defend parsing dates at the boundary rather than mid-pipeline.
defense.answer: One parse converts text to a typed value that arithmetic understands, and later stages never re-guess formats.

defense.q: Explain why a structured array is not a DataFrame.
defense.answer: It stores typed records but has no index, alignment, or per-column methods. It is the compact storage a frame may build on.

defense.q: Defend `object` dtype as a last resort.
defense.answer: It stores Python pointers, so it loses the buffer and vectorised speed. It is acceptable only for genuinely heterogeneous values.

defense.q: Defend keeping a timestamp as `datetime64` rather than a string.
defense.answer: It supports comparison and arithmetic and stays compact, where a string must be parsed first.

defense.q: Explain why a fixed-width string truncates silently.
defense.answer: The dtype reserves a fixed number of characters, so longer values lose their tail.

defense.q: Defend converting structured data to a frame at the analysis boundary.
defense.answer: Labels and alignment are the frame's job, while compact storage stays on the array side.

modules.title: Masked Arrays and Numerical Robustness
modules.goal: Detect and handle NaN and infinity honestly, and choose masked arrays or nan-aware functions deliberately.

topics.title: NaN is not equal to anything
topics.body: isnan locates missing values and nanmean ignores them; plain mean propagates NaN, so one missing reading can hide the whole summary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(np.isnan(a), np.nanmean(a))

topics.title: Infinity is a value, not a missing one
topics.body: isinf finds overflow and division-by-zero results; infinity is a real float value, so it must be filtered or clipped rather than treated as missing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf(np.array([1.0, np.inf])))

topics.title: Masked arrays carry their own mask
topics.body: A masked array stores a boolean mask beside the data, and reductions ignore masked positions — cleaner than overwriting values with NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.masked_array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 1, 0])
print(a.mean())

topics.title: isnan builds the mask
topics.body: NaN never equals itself, so isnan is the only reliable way to locate missing values before you decide to drop or fill them.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan])
print(np.isnan(a))

topics.title: nanmean ignores missing values
topics.body: mean propagates one NaN to the answer while nanmean skips those elements and averages the rest, so the two numbers differ on dirty data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan, 3.])
print(np.mean(a), np.nanmean(a))

topics.title: nan_to_num replaces NaN and infinity
topics.body: nan_to_num swaps non-finite values for finite defaults, which keeps a downstream model from receiving poisoning values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan_to_num(np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf])))

topics.title: allclose can treat NaN as equal
topics.body: By default two NaNs are not close, because allclose compares with ==; equal_nan=True is the switch that makes them match.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan], equal_nan=True), np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan]))

topics.title: nanargmax skips NaN
topics.body: argmax can return the position of a NaN, while nanargmax ignores them and returns the position of the largest real value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nanargmax([1., np.nan, 3.]))

topics.title: NaN never equals itself
topics.body: IEEE 754 defines `NaN != NaN`, so equality checks can never find missing values. Use `np.isnan` instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.nan == np.nan)

topics.title: isnan finds missing values
topics.body: The result is a boolean array, ready to be inverted with `~` or counted with `sum`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.isnan(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])).tolist())

topics.title: nanstd ignores the gaps
topics.body: The `nan`-prefixed reductions skip missing values. Plain `std` would return `nan` for the whole array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.nanstd(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0]))), 6))

topics.title: Mask NaN, then reduce
topics.body: Filtering with `~np.isnan(a)` is the explicit alternative to the `nan`-prefixed functions and works with any reduction.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(a[~np.isnan(a)].mean())

topics.title: Masked arrays ignore invalid cells
topics.body: A masked array carries a mask beside the data, so reductions skip the masked positions instead of returning NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[False, True, False])
print(a.mean(), a.filled(0))

topics.title: nan_to_num replaces non-finite values
topics.body: NaN and infinity break arithmetic and sorting. nan_to_num maps them to chosen finite values so downstream code has no special cases.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf, 2.0])
print(np.nan_to_num(a, nan=0.0, posinf=1e9, neginf=-1e9))

topics.title: masked_invalid masks NaN
topics.body: `np.ma.masked_invalid` masks NaN and infinity in one call, so a reduction skips the broken cells instead of returning NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.masked_invalid([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(float(m.mean()), int(m.count()))

topics.title: filled replaces masked values
topics.body: `filled(value)` materialises the masked array with the masked cells replaced, which is what a plotting or export step needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.masked_invalid([1.0, np.nan])
print(m.filled(0).tolist())

topics.title: count counts the unmasked cells
topics.body: `count()` reports how many values survive the mask, which is the denominator behind every masked mean.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[False, True, False])
print(int(m.count()))

topics.title: nanpercentile skips missing values
topics.body: `np.nanpercentile` computes a percentile over the valid values only, so one NaN does not destroy the whole answer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(float(np.nanpercentile([1.0, np.nan, 3.0], 50)))

topics.title: isinf finds infinities
topics.body: `np.isinf` isolates the infinite cells, which are a different problem from missing data and often come from a division by zero.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf([1.0, np.inf, -np.inf]).tolist())

topics.title: nan_to_num with chosen fill values
topics.body: Passing `nan=`, `posinf=` and `neginf=` keeps the replacement decision explicit instead of accepting the defaults.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan_to_num([np.nan, np.inf], nan=-1.0, posinf=999.0).tolist())

lab.title: Robust statistics
lab.brief: Compare mean, nanmean and masked mean on the same array with two missing values.
milestones: Explain which one you would ship

interviewBank.q: Why does NaN propagate through mean?
interviewBank.answer: NaN is not less than or greater than anything, so any comparison or sum involving it is undefined; the standard says the result is NaN.

interviewBank.q: When would you use `nanmean` and when a masked array?
interviewBank.answer: `nanmean` skips missing values in a numeric array; a masked array carries the mask with the data, which is better when missingness has meaning beyond NaN.

interviewBank.q: Why cannot an integer array hold NaN?
interviewBank.answer: NaN is a floating-point bit pattern with no integer representation, so an int dtype simply has no such value.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between NaN and None in an array?
interviewBank.answer: NaN is a float value that means "not a number" and propagates through arithmetic; None is a Python object that forces an object dtype and does not.

interviewBank.q: Why does `nanmean` warn on an all-NaN slice?
interviewBank.answer: There is no value left to average, so it returns NaN and warns that the result is not a real mean.

interviewBank.q: How do you detect infinity?
interviewBank.answer: Use `np.isinf`, optionally with `np.isfinite` to count only usable values.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.nan_to_num` replace by default?
interviewBank.answer: NaN becomes 0.0 and infinities become the largest and smallest finite values.

interviewBank.q: How do you drop rows containing NaN?
interviewBank.answer: Build `np.isnan(arr).any(axis=1)`, negate it, and index with that mask.

interviewBank.q: Why does the mean of an array with NaN return NaN?
interviewBank.answer: NaN propagates through the sum, and any value plus NaN is NaN.

interviewBank.q: Sensor data has -999 as a missing marker. What breaks if it is left in, and what are the two honest fixes?
interviewBank.answer: The marker drags every mean and histogram toward -999. Either replace it with np.nan and use nan-aware reductions, or mask it with numpy.ma so reductions skip it; both must be visible in the output.

followUps.q: How do you make the replacement auditable?
followUps.answer: Count what you changed (`(a == -999).sum()`) and surface that number in the report; a silent fill is indistinguishable from real data.

followUps.q: Which reductions silently ignore NaN?
followUps.answer: Only the `nan*` family (`nansum`, `nanmean`, `nanmedian`); plain `sum`/`mean` propagate NaN by design.

interviewBank.q: np.nanmean returns a number but np.mean returns nan on the same array. Is nanmean always safe?
interviewBank.answer: nanmean ignores NaN by reducing the effective count, so it is safe only when the missingness is random. If NaNs correlate with the value being measured, the mean is biased and that must be reported.

followUps.q: How do you report how much data was missing?
followUps.answer: Count `np.isnan(a).sum()` and its fraction, and attach it to every statistic derived from that column.

followUps.q: What is the risk of filling NaNs with the mean?
followUps.answer: It shrinks the variance and biases correlations toward zero; the filled value looks like data, so the distortion is invisible later.

defenseBank.q: Defend deciding a NaN policy at ingestion rather than mid-pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: Every later step must guess otherwise, and different guesses produce different numbers. One decision at the boundary is testable and documented.

defenseBank.q: Why is `nan == nan` false, and how do you test for it?
defenseBank.answer: IEEE defines NaN as unequal to everything, including itself, so use `np.isnan`.

defenseBank.q: Defend `nan_to_num` before a model that cannot accept NaN.
defenseBank.answer: The model would otherwise fail or silently produce NaN predictions, and choosing the replacement explicitly records what missing data became.

defenseBank.q: Defend failing loudly on unexpected NaN in a metric.
defenseBank.answer: A NaN silently poisons an average or a comparison, and a metric that reports NaN late is harder to trace than a guard at the start.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `nan_to_num` needs explicit replacement values.
defenseBank.answer: Any default is a modelling decision; stating the value records what missing data became instead of leaving it implicit.

defenseBank.q: Defend tracking missing-value counts as a metric.
defenseBank.answer: The count reveals ingestion problems that an imputed value would hide, and it is cheap to compute alongside the data.

defenseBank.q: Defend counting NaNs before choosing a fill value.
defenseBank.answer: The count shows whether imputation is reasonable at all, or whether the column is mostly empty.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `nanmean` warns on an all-NaN slice.
defenseBank.answer: The result is undefined, so it returns NaN and tells you the average was not over real values.

defenseBank.q: Defend `nan_to_num` only at the model boundary.
defenseBank.answer: Replacing earlier would hide missingness from checks that still need to know about it.

learn.title: NaN is not equal to anything
learn.body: isnan locates missing values and nanmean ignores them; plain mean propagates NaN, so one missing reading can hide the whole summary.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(np.isnan(a), np.nanmean(a))

learn.title: Infinity is a value, not a missing one
learn.body: isinf finds overflow and division-by-zero results; infinity is a real float value, so it must be filtered or clipped rather than treated as missing.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf(np.array([1.0, np.inf])))

learn.title: Masked arrays carry their own mask
learn.body: A masked array stores a boolean mask beside the data, and reductions ignore masked positions — cleaner than overwriting values with NaN.
learn.code:
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.masked_array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 1, 0])
print(a.mean())

learn.title: isnan builds the mask
learn.body: NaN never equals itself, so isnan is the only reliable way to locate missing values before you decide to drop or fill them.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan])
print(np.isnan(a))

learn.title: nanmean ignores missing values
learn.body: mean propagates one NaN to the answer while nanmean skips those elements and averages the rest, so the two numbers differ on dirty data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan, 3.])
print(np.mean(a), np.nanmean(a))

learn.title: nan_to_num replaces NaN and infinity
learn.body: nan_to_num swaps non-finite values for finite defaults, which keeps a downstream model from receiving poisoning values.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan_to_num(np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf])))

learn.title: allclose can treat NaN as equal
learn.body: By default two NaNs are not close, because allclose compares with ==; equal_nan=True is the switch that makes them match.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan], equal_nan=True), np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan]))

learn.title: nanargmax skips NaN
learn.body: argmax can return the position of a NaN, while nanargmax ignores them and returns the position of the largest real value.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nanargmax([1., np.nan, 3.]))

learn.title: NaN never equals itself
learn.body: IEEE 754 defines `NaN != NaN`, so equality checks can never find missing values. Use `np.isnan` instead.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.nan == np.nan)

learn.title: isnan finds missing values
learn.body: The result is a boolean array, ready to be inverted with `~` or counted with `sum`.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.isnan(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])).tolist())

learn.title: nanstd ignores the gaps
learn.body: The `nan`-prefixed reductions skip missing values. Plain `std` would return `nan` for the whole array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.nanstd(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0]))), 6))

learn.title: Mask NaN, then reduce
learn.body: Filtering with `~np.isnan(a)` is the explicit alternative to the `nan`-prefixed functions and works with any reduction.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(a[~np.isnan(a)].mean())

learn.title: Masked arrays ignore invalid cells
learn.body: A masked array carries a mask beside the data, so reductions skip the masked positions instead of returning NaN.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[False, True, False])
print(a.mean(), a.filled(0))
learn.simple: Kabhi data me kuch kharab numbers hote hain. Masked array un kharab khaanon par ek dhakkan laga deta hai — average nikaalo to NumPy unhe chhod deta hai, isliye jawab NaN nahi aata. Baad me `filled` se un khaanon me apna number bhar sakte ho.
learn.pro: A masked array carries a boolean mask beside the data, and reductions skip masked positions rather than propagating NaN. It distinguishes "missing" from "zero" explicitly; filled() materialises the mask as chosen values when an array without masks is required.

learn.title: nan_to_num replaces non-finite values
learn.body: NaN and infinity break arithmetic and sorting. nan_to_num maps them to chosen finite values so downstream code has no special cases.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf, 2.0])
print(np.nan_to_num(a, nan=0.0, posinf=1e9, neginf=-1e9))
learn.simple: NaN ka matlab hai "koi number nahi", aur infinity ka matlab hai "bahut bada". Ye dono aage ke hisaab ko kharab kar dete hain. `nan_to_num` unhe tumhare chune hue safe numbers se badal deta hai, taaki program chalta rahe.
learn.pro: nan_to_num maps NaN to zero by default and infinities to the dtype's largest finite magnitude, or to values you pass explicitly. It prevents NaN propagation into downstream arithmetic, but the choice of replacement is a modelling decision and should be reported.

learn.title: masked_invalid masks NaN
learn.body: `np.ma.masked_invalid` masks NaN and infinity in one call, so a reduction skips the broken cells instead of returning NaN.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.masked_invalid([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(float(m.mean()), int(m.count()))
learn.simple: `np.ma.masked_invalid` NaN aur infinity dono ko ek saath mask kar deta hai. Isliye mean ya sum kharab values ko chhod kar sahi answer deta hai.
learn.pro: `np.ma.masked_invalid` masks NaN and both infinities in one call, so reductions skip them instead of propagating NaN. The mask is stored beside the data, which keeps the original values available for inspection.
steps: Create a float vector with NaN.
Mask invalid values.
Compute the mean and print the count.
learn.visual:
masked NaN
mean ignores the gap
learn.realWorld: Sensor gaps are masked before a daily average is reported.
mistakes: Using a plain mean and getting NaN.

learn.title: filled replaces masked values
learn.body: `filled(value)` materialises the masked array with the masked cells replaced, which is what a plotting or export step needs.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.masked_invalid([1.0, np.nan])
print(m.filled(0).tolist())
learn.simple: `filled(value)` masked cells ki jagah tumhara diya hua number rakh deta hai. Plot ya export se pehle yeh zaroori hota hai.
learn.pro: `filled(value)` materialises the masked array with each masked cell replaced by the supplied value, returning a plain ndarray. The choice of fill value is a reporting decision, so it must be explicit rather than left to a default.
steps: Mask a value.
Fill it with zero.
Print the plain array.
learn.realWorld: Exporting a table requires a concrete fill value for missing cells.
mistakes: Filling with a value that is indistinguishable from real data.
revision: The fill value is a reporting choice.

learn.title: count counts the unmasked cells
learn.body: `count()` reports how many values survive the mask, which is the denominator behind every masked mean.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3], mask=[False, True, False])
print(int(m.count()))
learn.simple: `count()` batata hai kitni values mask se bach gayi hain. Masked mean ka denominator yahi hota hai.
learn.pro: `count()` reports how many cells survive the mask, which is the denominator behind every masked mean. It is not the array size, so printing it catches a mask that accidentally removed most of the data.
steps: Mask one value in a three-element array.
Print the count.
Compare with the array size.
learn.realWorld: The count is the denominator of every masked mean.
mistakes: Using the array length as the denominator.

learn.title: nanpercentile skips missing values
learn.body: `np.nanpercentile` computes a percentile over the valid values only, so one NaN does not destroy the whole answer.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(float(np.nanpercentile([1.0, np.nan, 3.0], 50)))
learn.simple: `np.nanpercentile` sirf valid numbers par percentile nikalta hai, isliye ek NaN poora answer kharab nahi karta. Percentile poochhne ka yahi safe version hai.
learn.pro: `np.nanpercentile` computes the percentile over the non-NaN values only, so a single missing cell does not force the result to NaN. It still interpolates between order statistics, and an all-NaN slice returns NaN with a warning.
steps: Create a vector containing NaN.
Compute the median with `nanpercentile`.
Compare with the plain percentile.
learn.realWorld: Latency percentiles must ignore failed requests recorded as NaN.
mistakes: Assuming an all-NaN slice returns 0.
revision: An all-NaN slice returns NaN with a warning.

learn.title: isinf finds infinities
learn.body: `np.isinf` isolates the infinite cells, which are a different problem from missing data and often come from a division by zero.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf([1.0, np.inf, -np.inf]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.isinf` sirf infinite values pakadta hai. Yeh missing data se alag problem hai, aur aksar zero se divide hone par aati hai.
learn.pro: `np.isinf` isolates the infinite cells, distinguishing them from NaN, which is a different failure. Infinite values usually come from a division by zero or an overflow, so finding them points at the arithmetic rather than the data source.
steps: Create a vector with both infinities.
Build the isinf mask.
Count the matches.
learn.realWorld: Ratios that divide by zero produce inf, which is a different bug from missing data.
mistakes: Treating inf as NaN and masking both blindly.
revision: They usually signal a zero denominator.

learn.title: nan_to_num with chosen fill values
learn.body: Passing `nan=`, `posinf=` and `neginf=` keeps the replacement decision explicit instead of accepting the defaults.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan_to_num([np.nan, np.inf], nan=-1.0, posinf=999.0).tolist())
learn.simple: `nan_to_num` me `nan`, `posinf` aur `neginf` ke liye apna replacement de sakte ho. Isliye default ke bharose nahi rehna padta.
learn.pro: Passing `nan=`, `posinf=` and `neginf=` keeps each replacement decision explicit instead of accepting NumPy's defaults. That matters when a fill value must be distinguishable from real data in a later aggregation.
steps: Create a vector with NaN and inf.
Replace each with an explicit value.
Print the cleaned array.
learn.realWorld: A model input must be finite, so each sentinel is chosen deliberately.
mistakes: Accepting defaults that collide with legitimate values.
revision: Each case takes its own fill.

interview.q: Why does NaN propagate through mean?
interview.answer: NaN is not less than or greater than anything, so any comparison or sum involving it is undefined; the standard says the result is NaN.

interview.q: When would you use `nanmean` and when a masked array?
interview.answer: `nanmean` skips missing values in a numeric array; a masked array carries the mask with the data, which is better when missingness has meaning beyond NaN.

interview.q: Why cannot an integer array hold NaN?
interview.answer: NaN is a floating-point bit pattern with no integer representation, so an int dtype simply has no such value.

interview.q: What is the difference between NaN and None in an array?
interview.answer: NaN is a float value that means "not a number" and propagates through arithmetic; None is a Python object that forces an object dtype and does not.

interview.q: Why does `nanmean` warn on an all-NaN slice?
interview.answer: There is no value left to average, so it returns NaN and warns that the result is not a real mean.

interview.q: How do you detect infinity?
interview.answer: Use `np.isinf`, optionally with `np.isfinite` to count only usable values.

interview.q: What does `np.nan_to_num` replace by default?
interview.answer: NaN becomes 0.0 and infinities become the largest and smallest finite values.

interview.q: How do you drop rows containing NaN?
interview.answer: Build `np.isnan(arr).any(axis=1)`, negate it, and index with that mask.

interview.q: Why does the mean of an array with NaN return NaN?
interview.answer: NaN propagates through the sum, and any value plus NaN is NaN.

interview.q: Sensor data has -999 as a missing marker. What breaks if it is left in, and what are the two honest fixes?
interview.answer: The marker drags every mean and histogram toward -999. Either replace it with np.nan and use nan-aware reductions, or mask it with numpy.ma so reductions skip it; both must be visible in the output.

followUps.q: How do you make the replacement auditable?
followUps.answer: Count what you changed (`(a == -999).sum()`) and surface that number in the report; a silent fill is indistinguishable from real data.

followUps.q: Which reductions silently ignore NaN?
followUps.answer: Only the `nan*` family (`nansum`, `nanmean`, `nanmedian`); plain `sum`/`mean` propagate NaN by design.

interview.q: np.nanmean returns a number but np.mean returns nan on the same array. Is nanmean always safe?
interview.answer: nanmean ignores NaN by reducing the effective count, so it is safe only when the missingness is random. If NaNs correlate with the value being measured, the mean is biased and that must be reported.

followUps.q: How do you report how much data was missing?
followUps.answer: Count `np.isnan(a).sum()` and its fraction, and attach it to every statistic derived from that column.

followUps.q: What is the risk of filling NaNs with the mean?
followUps.answer: It shrinks the variance and biases correlations toward zero; the filled value looks like data, so the distortion is invisible later.

projectLab.title: Robust statistics
projectLab.body: Compare mean, nanmean and masked mean on the same array with two missing values.
steps: Build the array
Print all three means
Explain which one you would ship

defense.q: Defend deciding a NaN policy at ingestion rather than mid-pipeline.
defense.answer: Every later step must guess otherwise, and different guesses produce different numbers. One decision at the boundary is testable and documented.

defense.q: Why is `nan == nan` false, and how do you test for it?
defense.answer: IEEE defines NaN as unequal to everything, including itself, so use `np.isnan`.

defense.q: Defend `nan_to_num` before a model that cannot accept NaN.
defense.answer: The model would otherwise fail or silently produce NaN predictions, and choosing the replacement explicitly records what missing data became.

defense.q: Defend failing loudly on unexpected NaN in a metric.
defense.answer: A NaN silently poisons an average or a comparison, and a metric that reports NaN late is harder to trace than a guard at the start.

defense.q: Explain why `nan_to_num` needs explicit replacement values.
defense.answer: Any default is a modelling decision; stating the value records what missing data became instead of leaving it implicit.

defense.q: Defend tracking missing-value counts as a metric.
defense.answer: The count reveals ingestion problems that an imputed value would hide, and it is cheap to compute alongside the data.

defense.q: Defend counting NaNs before choosing a fill value.
defense.answer: The count shows whether imputation is reasonable at all, or whether the column is mostly empty.

defense.q: Explain why `nanmean` warns on an all-NaN slice.
defense.answer: The result is undefined, so it returns NaN and tells you the average was not over real values.

defense.q: Defend `nan_to_num` only at the model boundary.
defense.answer: Replacing earlier would hide missingness from checks that still need to know about it.

modules.title: Performance and Vectorization
modules.goal: Replace Python loops with vectorised code, reuse buffers with out= and benchmark changes honestly.

topics.title: Vectorised reduction
topics.body: One NumPy expression runs in compiled loops over contiguous memory, so a million-element sum needs no Python iteration.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(1_000_000)
print(int((a * 2).sum()))

topics.title: Reuse a buffer with out=
topics.body: Passing out= writes the result into an existing array, avoiding a new allocation in hot loops where the shape is already known.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.multiply(a, 2, out=out)
print(out)

topics.title: Chunk large work
topics.body: array_split lets you process a big array in bounded pieces, which keeps peak memory predictable on datasets that do not fit comfortably.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(int(chunk.sum()) for chunk in np.array_split(a, 2)))

topics.title: einsum replaces a triple loop
topics.body: einsum writes the sum over indices in the subscript string, so a dot product, a trace or a batched contraction is one compiled call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3.)
print(np.einsum('i,i->', a, a))

topics.title: dot and @ agree
topics.body: np.dot and the @ operator compute the same matrix product, and proving it with allclose is a good habit before optimising either side.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.arange(4.).reshape(2, 2)
B = np.eye(2)
print(np.allclose(np.dot(A, B), A @ B))

topics.title: bincount counts integer categories
topics.body: bincount tallies non-negative integers in one pass, so labelled data is counted without a Python loop or a dictionary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])))

topics.title: vectorize wraps a Python function
topics.body: np.vectorize applies a scalar function elementwise for convenience, but it loops in Python underneath and is not a speed-up.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
f = np.vectorize(lambda x: x * x)
print(f(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

topics.title: sum in chunks instead of one huge temporary
topics.body: Adding slice sums keeps peak memory small, because each chunk is released instead of materialising a full-size intermediate array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(a[i:i + 4].sum() for i in range(0, 10, 4)))

topics.title: add.reduce sums along an axis
topics.body: Every ufunc has a `reduce` that applies it down an axis. It is the general form behind `sum`, `prod` and `max`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.add.reduce(np.arange(5)))

topics.title: einsum can read a diagonal
topics.body: Repeating an index in `einsum` means "same position on both axes", which extracts or sums the diagonal without a mask.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(np.einsum('ii->', A))

topics.title: bincount needs non-negative integers
topics.body: The output length is one more than the largest value, so position `i` counts how often `i` appeared. Floats raise a `TypeError`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])).tolist())

topics.title: dot on matrices is a matrix product
topics.body: On two 2-D arrays, `np.dot` and `@` agree. Confusing it with elementwise `*` is the classic shape bug.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dot(np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]]), np.array([2, 3])).tolist())

topics.title: Avoid temporaries with out=
topics.body: Every expression allocates a new array. Passing out= writes into an existing buffer, which matters when the arrays are large and the loop is repeated.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4.0)
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.multiply(a, 2, out=out)
print(out, out is a)

topics.title: In-place operations save memory
topics.body: Operators ending in = update the buffer instead of allocating, so a += 1 costs no new array. The trade-off is that aliased views see the change.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones(4, dtype=np.int64)
before = a
before += 1
print(a, before is a)

topics.title: Preallocate and assign
topics.body: Building an output array once and filling it by index is linear work. Growing with append copies the whole array on every step.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
out = np.empty(4, dtype=int)
for i in range(4):
    out[i] = i * i
print(out.tolist())

topics.title: Avoid repeated np.append
topics.body: `np.append` returns a new array, so calling it in a loop is quadratic. Collect in a list and convert once instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
values = [i * 2 for i in range(5)]
print(np.array(values).tolist())

topics.title: einsum for a dot product
topics.body: `np.einsum('i,i->', a, b)` states the contraction explicitly, which is a readable alternative to dot for simple index algebra.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(int(np.einsum('i,i->', np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4]))))

topics.title: bincount for integer counts
topics.body: `np.bincount` counts occurrences of non-negative integers in one pass and is much faster than a Python Counter over an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])).tolist())

topics.title: vectorize is convenience, not speed
topics.body: `np.vectorize` loops in Python under the hood, so it reads like a vectorised call without the performance. Prefer real ufuncs on hot paths.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
add_one = np.vectorize(lambda x: x + 1)
print(add_one([1, 2, 3]).tolist())

topics.title: Chunk a big reduction
topics.body: When a temporary would exceed memory, reduce each chunk and combine the partial results. The answer is identical, the peak memory is bounded.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
parts = [np.arange(i * 100, (i + 1) * 100).sum() for i in range(3)]
print(int(np.sum(parts)))

interviewBank.q: How do you replace a loop over rows with vectorised code?
interviewBank.answer: Express the row operation as whole-array arithmetic and reduce along `axis=1`, so the loop disappears into a compiled pass.

interviewBank.q: What does `out=` avoid, and when does it hurt?
interviewBank.answer: It avoids allocating a result buffer on every call. It hurts when the output aliases an input that is still needed, so check overlap.

interviewBank.q: Why is fancy indexing slower than slicing?
interviewBank.answer: A slice only changes metadata, while fancy indexing gathers arbitrary positions and always produces a copy.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.vectorize` actually do?
interviewBank.answer: It loops in Python and calls your function per element, adding broadcasting as a convenience. It does not compile anything.

interviewBank.q: Why is `np.einsum` often the clearest tensor operation?
interviewBank.answer: It names the indices once, so the contraction, transpose and sum are all visible in one short string instead of three calls.

interviewBank.q: How does `out=` interact with broadcasting?
interviewBank.answer: The output must already have the broadcast result shape; NumPy writes into it and never resizes it.

interviewBank.q: What does `np.einsum("ii->i", A)` return?
interviewBank.answer: The diagonal of A as a fresh result.

interviewBank.q: How do you replace a Python loop over two arrays?
interviewBank.answer: Express it as elementwise arithmetic, or as a matmul/einsum when axes are contracted.

interviewBank.q: Why is `np.vectorize` not a performance tool?
interviewBank.answer: It still calls the Python function once per element, so interpreter overhead stays.

interviewBank.q: A loop builds a 10,000-element array with np.append per iteration. Why is it slow, and what is the fix?
interviewBank.answer: np.append copies the whole array every call, so the total work is quadratic. Collect values in a Python list and call np.array once, or preallocate an output array and assign by index.

followUps.q: How do you preallocate when the final length is unknown?
followUps.answer: Collect into a Python list (amortised growth) and convert once, or count first and preallocate; avoid per-iteration `np.append`.

followUps.q: What is the real cost of `np.append` in a loop?
followUps.answer: Every call copies the whole existing array, so total work is quadratic in the number of iterations.

interviewBank.q: A hot path allocates a temporary at every step. When is `out=` the right optimisation and when is it a bug risk?
interviewBank.answer: out= is right when the destination is known and not aliased with the inputs; it avoids allocation churn. It is risky when the output is also an input or a view of one, because partial writes can corrupt the computation.

followUps.q: How do you check aliasing before using `out=`?
followUps.answer: `np.shares_memory(out, a)` and `np.shares_memory(out, b)`; any True means partial writes can corrupt the inputs.

followUps.q: Which kind of code benefits most from `out=`?
followUps.answer: A fixed-size ufunc repeated in a loop where the output buffer can be reused across iterations.

defenseBank.q: Defend `einsum` over nested Python loops for a tensor contraction.
defenseBank.answer: It states the index arithmetic once and runs a compiled loop with no intermediate arrays, which is both faster and easier to verify.

defenseBank.q: Explain why appending inside a loop is slow, and what to do instead.
defenseBank.answer: Each append may reallocate and copy the growing buffer. Preallocate to the known final size and fill by index.

defenseBank.q: Defend profiling before rewriting a loop that looks slow.
defenseBank.answer: The loop may not be the bottleneck, and an unmeasured rewrite can trade clarity for nothing. Measure, then optimise the part that dominates.

defenseBank.q: Defend choosing clarity over a hand-tuned ufunc.
defenseBank.answer: An unmeasured optimisation trades readability for an unknown gain. Clarity first, then profile and optimise the hot path.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `np.vectorize` does not make code fast.
defenseBank.answer: The Python call still happens once per element, so the interpreter overhead that dominated the loop remains.

defenseBank.q: Defend setting a memory budget when choosing a vectorised path.
defenseBank.answer: Several vectorised routes compute the same answer with very different peak memory, and the fastest one can still exhaust RAM.

defenseBank.q: Defend preallocating an output array over repeated appends.
defenseBank.answer: Growth reallocates and copies, while preallocation writes each result exactly once.

defenseBank.q: Explain why `out=` requires the exact result shape.
defenseBank.answer: NumPy writes into the supplied buffer and never resizes it.

defenseBank.q: Defend measuring before rewriting a loop with `einsum`.
defenseBank.answer: The loop may not dominate the runtime, and the rewrite trades clarity for an unmeasured gain.

learn.title: Vectorised reduction
learn.body: One NumPy expression runs in compiled loops over contiguous memory, so a million-element sum needs no Python iteration.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(1_000_000)
print(int((a * 2).sum()))

learn.title: Reuse a buffer with out=
learn.body: Passing out= writes the result into an existing array, avoiding a new allocation in hot loops where the shape is already known.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.multiply(a, 2, out=out)
print(out)

learn.title: Chunk large work
learn.body: array_split lets you process a big array in bounded pieces, which keeps peak memory predictable on datasets that do not fit comfortably.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(int(chunk.sum()) for chunk in np.array_split(a, 2)))

learn.title: einsum replaces a triple loop
learn.body: einsum writes the sum over indices in the subscript string, so a dot product, a trace or a batched contraction is one compiled call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3.)
print(np.einsum('i,i->', a, a))

learn.title: dot and @ agree
learn.body: np.dot and the @ operator compute the same matrix product, and proving it with allclose is a good habit before optimising either side.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.arange(4.).reshape(2, 2)
B = np.eye(2)
print(np.allclose(np.dot(A, B), A @ B))

learn.title: bincount counts integer categories
learn.body: bincount tallies non-negative integers in one pass, so labelled data is counted without a Python loop or a dictionary.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])))

learn.title: vectorize wraps a Python function
learn.body: np.vectorize applies a scalar function elementwise for convenience, but it loops in Python underneath and is not a speed-up.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
f = np.vectorize(lambda x: x * x)
print(f(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

learn.title: sum in chunks instead of one huge temporary
learn.body: Adding slice sums keeps peak memory small, because each chunk is released instead of materialising a full-size intermediate array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(a[i:i + 4].sum() for i in range(0, 10, 4)))

learn.title: add.reduce sums along an axis
learn.body: Every ufunc has a `reduce` that applies it down an axis. It is the general form behind `sum`, `prod` and `max`.

learn.title: einsum can read a diagonal
learn.body: Repeating an index in `einsum` means "same position on both axes", which extracts or sums the diagonal without a mask.

print(np.einsum('ii->', A))

learn.title: bincount needs non-negative integers
learn.body: The output length is one more than the largest value, so position `i` counts how often `i` appeared. Floats raise a `TypeError`.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])).tolist())

learn.title: dot on matrices is a matrix product
learn.body: On two 2-D arrays, `np.dot` and `@` agree. Confusing it with elementwise `*` is the classic shape bug.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dot(np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]]), np.array([2, 3])).tolist())

learn.title: Avoid temporaries with out=
learn.body: Every expression allocates a new array. Passing out= writes into an existing buffer, which matters when the arrays are large and the loop is repeated.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4.0)
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.multiply(a, 2, out=out)
print(out, out is a)
learn.simple: Har calculation ek naya dabba bana deti hai, aur bade data me yeh bahut jagah kha jata hai. `out=` bol kar tum NumPy ko bata sakte ho "jawab is purane dabbe me hi rakh do". Isse naya dabba nahi banta aur memory bachti hai.
learn.pro: Every expression allocates an output; out= writes into a caller-provided buffer and avoids that allocation churn. It is safe only when the destination does not alias an input, since partial writes during an aliased computation corrupt the result.

learn.title: In-place operations save memory
learn.body: Operators ending in = update the buffer instead of allocating, so a += 1 costs no new array. The trade-off is that aliased views see the change.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones(4, dtype=np.int64)
before = a
before += 1
print(a, before is a)
learn.simple: `a += 1` ka matlab hai usi dabbe ke andar numbers badal do — naya dabba nahi banta. Isliye memory bachti hai. Par dhyan rakho: agar kisi aur ne bhi wahi dabba dekha hua hai, uske numbers bhi badal jayenge.
learn.pro: Augmented assignment updates the existing buffer instead of allocating, with no extra array for large operands. The trade-off is aliasing: every view of that buffer observes the change, so in-place code must own its inputs.

learn.title: Preallocate and assign
learn.body: Building an output array once and filling it by index is linear work. Growing with append copies the whole array on every step.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
out = np.empty(4, dtype=int)
for i in range(4):
    out[i] = i * i
print(out.tolist())
learn.simple: Pehle poori array bana lo, phir index se values bharo. Yeh linear kaam hai, jabki baar-baar append karna har step par poora array copy karta hai.
learn.pro: Allocating the output once and filling it by index is linear work, while growing an array with `append` reallocates and copies on every step. Preallocation also fixes the dtype and shape up front, so no later conversion is needed.
steps: Allocate an empty output of known length.
Fill it by index in a loop.
Print the result.
learn.visual:
allocate once
fill by index (linear work)
learn.realWorld: A simulation writes each timestep into a preallocated trace array.
mistakes: Growing the array inside the loop instead.
revision: It fixes dtype and shape up front.

learn.title: Avoid repeated np.append
learn.body: `np.append` returns a new array, so calling it in a loop is quadratic. Collect in a list and convert once instead.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
values = [i * 2 for i in range(5)]
print(np.array(values).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.append` har baar naya array banata hai, isliye loop me woh quadratic ho jaata hai. List me collect karo aur aakhir me ek baar array banao.
learn.pro: `np.append` returns a new array, so calling it in a loop copies the accumulated data each iteration and turns linear work quadratic. Collecting values in a Python list and converting once keeps the number of allocations constant.
steps: Collect values in a Python list.
Convert the list to an array once.
Compare with appending inside a loop.
learn.visual:
list append is amortised
np.append copies every call
learn.realWorld: Reading a log line by line should collect first and convert once.
mistakes: Calling np.append in a hot loop.

learn.title: einsum for a dot product
learn.body: `np.einsum('i,i->', a, b)` states the contraction explicitly, which is a readable alternative to dot for simple index algebra.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(int(np.einsum('i,i->', np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4]))))
learn.simple: `np.einsum('i,i->', a, b)` index ka rule likh kar dot product nikalta hai. Yeh padhne me clear hota hai jab simple contraction ho.
learn.pro: `np.einsum('i,i->', a, b)` states the contraction explicitly: multiply matching indices and sum the repeated one. The notation makes the index algebra auditable, and the same string generalises to matrix products and traces.
steps: Create two vectors.
Compute their dot product with einsum.
Compare with `np.dot`.
learn.visual:
'i,i->' sums over i
same value as dot
learn.realWorld: Attention scores and contractions are often written with einsum for clarity.
mistakes: Writing an index that is neither output nor summed.

learn.title: bincount for integer counts
learn.body: `np.bincount` counts occurrences of non-negative integers in one pass and is much faster than a Python Counter over an array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.bincount` non-negative integers ki ginti ek pass me kar deta hai. Isliye Counter se bahut tez hai jab data already integer ho.
learn.pro: `np.bincount` counts occurrences of non-negative integers in one pass and returns an array indexed by value. Negative inputs raise, so a shift or a filtered mask is required before counting signed categories.
steps: Create a non-negative integer vector.
Call `bincount` and print the counts.
Try a negative value and read the error.
learn.realWorld: Class frequencies in a label array are a bincount.
mistakes: Passing negative labels.

learn.title: vectorize is convenience, not speed
learn.body: `np.vectorize` loops in Python under the hood, so it reads like a vectorised call without the performance. Prefer real ufuncs on hot paths.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
add_one = np.vectorize(lambda x: x + 1)
print(add_one([1, 2, 3]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.vectorize` dikhne me vectorised call jaisa hai, par andar se Python loop hi chalata hai. Isliye speed nahi badhti, sirf code chhota lagta hai.
learn.pro: `np.vectorize` is a convenience wrapper that applies a Python function element by element, so it keeps interpreter overhead and adds call costs. Use it for readability on small inputs, not on hot paths where a real ufunc or an array expression is available.
steps: Wrap a Python function with `vectorize`.
Apply it to an array.
Compare its runtime with a real ufunc.
learn.visual:
same values
extra Python call overhead
learn.realWorld: A one-off custom transform is fine to vectorize; a hot path is not.
mistakes: Assuming vectorize compiles the function.

learn.title: Chunk a big reduction
learn.body: When a temporary would exceed memory, reduce each chunk and combine the partial results. The answer is identical, the peak memory is bounded.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
parts = [np.arange(i * 100, (i + 1) * 100).sum() for i in range(3)]
print(int(np.sum(parts)))
learn.simple: Jab ek saath poora data process karne se memory bhar jaaye, to hisson me reduce karo aur partial totals jodo. Answer wahi aata hai, peak memory kam rehti hai.
learn.pro: Reducing chunk by chunk and combining the partial results gives the same answer with a bounded peak allocation. For sum and count the combination is addition; for mean it needs the chunk sizes, so the partials must carry them.
steps: Split a large array into chunks.
Reduce each chunk.
Combine the partial results.
learn.visual:
chunk sums → total
peak memory bounded
learn.realWorld: A dataset larger than memory is reduced in batches from disk.
mistakes: Combining means without carrying chunk sizes.

interview.q: How do you replace a loop over rows with vectorised code?
interview.answer: Express the row operation as whole-array arithmetic and reduce along `axis=1`, so the loop disappears into a compiled pass.

interview.q: What does `out=` avoid, and when does it hurt?
interview.answer: It avoids allocating a result buffer on every call. It hurts when the output aliases an input that is still needed, so check overlap.

interview.q: Why is fancy indexing slower than slicing?
interview.answer: A slice only changes metadata, while fancy indexing gathers arbitrary positions and always produces a copy.

interview.q: What does `np.vectorize` actually do?
interview.answer: It loops in Python and calls your function per element, adding broadcasting as a convenience. It does not compile anything.

interview.q: Why is `np.einsum` often the clearest tensor operation?
interview.answer: It names the indices once, so the contraction, transpose and sum are all visible in one short string instead of three calls.

interview.q: How does `out=` interact with broadcasting?
interview.answer: The output must already have the broadcast result shape; NumPy writes into it and never resizes it.

interview.q: What does `np.einsum("ii->i", A)` return?
interview.answer: The diagonal of A as a fresh result.

interview.q: How do you replace a Python loop over two arrays?
interview.answer: Express it as elementwise arithmetic, or as a matmul/einsum when axes are contracted.

interview.q: Why is `np.vectorize` not a performance tool?
interview.answer: It still calls the Python function once per element, so interpreter overhead stays.

interview.q: A loop builds a 10,000-element array with np.append per iteration. Why is it slow, and what is the fix?
interview.answer: np.append copies the whole array every call, so the total work is quadratic. Collect values in a Python list and call np.array once, or preallocate an output array and assign by index.

followUps.q: How do you preallocate when the final length is unknown?
followUps.answer: Collect into a Python list (amortised growth) and convert once, or count first and preallocate; avoid per-iteration `np.append`.

followUps.q: What is the real cost of `np.append` in a loop?
followUps.answer: Every call copies the whole existing array, so total work is quadratic in the number of iterations.

interview.q: A hot path allocates a temporary at every step. When is `out=` the right optimisation and when is it a bug risk?
interview.answer: out= is right when the destination is known and not aliased with the inputs; it avoids allocation churn. It is risky when the output is also an input or a view of one, because partial writes can corrupt the computation.

followUps.q: How do you check aliasing before using `out=`?
followUps.answer: `np.shares_memory(out, a)` and `np.shares_memory(out, b)`; any True means partial writes can corrupt the inputs.

followUps.q: Which kind of code benefits most from `out=`?
followUps.answer: A fixed-size ufunc repeated in a loop where the output buffer can be reused across iterations.

defense.q: Defend `einsum` over nested Python loops for a tensor contraction.
defense.answer: It states the index arithmetic once and runs a compiled loop with no intermediate arrays, which is both faster and easier to verify.

defense.q: Explain why appending inside a loop is slow, and what to do instead.
defense.answer: Each append may reallocate and copy the growing buffer. Preallocate to the known final size and fill by index.

defense.q: Defend profiling before rewriting a loop that looks slow.
defense.answer: The loop may not be the bottleneck, and an unmeasured rewrite can trade clarity for nothing. Measure, then optimise the part that dominates.

defense.q: Defend choosing clarity over a hand-tuned ufunc.
defense.answer: An unmeasured optimisation trades readability for an unknown gain. Clarity first, then profile and optimise the hot path.

defense.q: Explain why `np.vectorize` does not make code fast.
defense.answer: The Python call still happens once per element, so the interpreter overhead that dominated the loop remains.

defense.q: Defend setting a memory budget when choosing a vectorised path.
defense.answer: Several vectorised routes compute the same answer with very different peak memory, and the fastest one can still exhaust RAM.

defense.q: Defend preallocating an output array over repeated appends.
defense.answer: Growth reallocates and copies, while preallocation writes each result exactly once.

defense.q: Explain why `out=` requires the exact result shape.
defense.answer: NumPy writes into the supplied buffer and never resizes it.

defense.q: Defend measuring before rewriting a loop with `einsum`.
defense.answer: The loop may not dominate the runtime, and the rewrite trades clarity for an unmeasured gain.

modules.title: NumPy Ecosystem and Real-World Applications
modules.goal: Move arrays between NumPy, Pandas, plots and model inputs, and know which layer owns which job.

topics.title: Pandas is built on arrays
topics.body: Series.to_numpy() exposes the underlying values, which is how you hand a column to a NumPy routine and keep the data, not the labels.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, 2])
print(s.to_numpy(), s.to_numpy().mean())

topics.title: Feature matrices are 2-D arrays
topics.body: A model expects one row per sample and one column per feature; reducing along axis 0 gives one value per feature, which is the shape a scaler fits.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(axis=0).shape)

topics.title: Images are (height, width, channels)
topics.body: An RGB image is a 3-D uint8 array and its shape is the first thing to check before any filter or model input.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.zeros((2, 2, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
print(img.shape, img.dtype)

topics.title: Standardise each column
topics.body: Subtracting the column mean and dividing by the column standard deviation is broadcasting, and it is the step every model expects before training.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
print(Z.round(2))

topics.title: One-hot encode with eye
topics.body: Indexing an identity matrix with integer labels encodes a class vector into a matrix, no loop and no library needed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
labels = np.array([0, 2, 1])
print(np.eye(3, dtype=int)[labels])

topics.title: Images are uint8 arrays
topics.body: An image is just a (height, width, channels) array of unsigned bytes, so brightness is an addition clipped back into 0-255.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.array([[0, 128], [255, 64]], dtype=np.uint8)
bright = np.clip(img.astype(int) + 40, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
print(bright)

topics.title: A moving average is a convolution
topics.body: np.convolve with a window of 1/n computes a moving average, which is the array-only way to smooth a series without pandas.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4.])
print(np.convolve(v, np.ones(2) / 2, mode='valid'))

topics.title: Round only for display
topics.body: Rounding is a presentation choice: keep the full float for computation, and round only when the number is about to be shown.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round(2.675, 2), np.round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))

topics.title: Scale each row by its own maximum
topics.body: `keepdims=True` keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the division broadcasts back across the row without reshaping.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 6.0]])
print((a / a.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)).round(3).tolist())

topics.title: diff gives step-to-step change
topics.body: `np.diff` returns one fewer value than the input: the difference between each neighbouring pair.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.diff(np.array([100.0, 110.0, 99.0])).round(3).tolist())

topics.title: digitize buckets values into bins
topics.body: The output is the index of the bin each value falls into. By default the right edge is open, so `0.5` lands in the next bucket.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.digitize(np.array([0.1, 0.5, 1.5]), [0.5, 1.0]).tolist())

topics.title: Build a confusion matrix with bincount
topics.body: Encoding a pair of labels as `true * classes + predicted` turns the counts into a matrix with one reshape and no loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

truth = np.array([1, 0, 1])
predicted = np.array([1, 1, 1])
counts = np.bincount(truth * 2 + predicted, minlength=4)
print(counts.reshape(2, 2).tolist())

topics.title: An image is just an array
topics.body: A colour image is a (height, width, 3) array, so slicing a channel is plain indexing and brightness is multiplication by a scalar.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.arange(12).reshape(2, 2, 3)
print(img.shape)
print(img[..., 0])
print((img * 0).shape)

topics.title: Moving between NumPy and the rest of Python
topics.body: asarray accepts lists and tuples without copying when it can, and tolist returns plain lists for JSON or an API. That boundary is where dtype and shape must be checked.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
a = np.asarray(data)
print(a.shape, a.dtype, a.tolist())

topics.title: Standardise columns with broadcasting
topics.body: Subtract the column means and divide by the column standard deviations, both shaped (1, n), to standardise every feature in one expression.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1.0, 10.0], [3.0, 14.0]])
z = (a - a.mean(axis=0)) / a.std(axis=0)
print(np.round(z, 3).tolist())

topics.title: One-hot with eye indexing
topics.body: `np.eye(k)[labels]` turns integer labels into one-hot rows without a loop, which is the encoding most models expect.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(3)[[0, 2]].tolist())

topics.title: Moving average with convolve
topics.body: Convolving with a normalised window of ones smooths a series; `mode='valid'` drops the edges that are not fully covered.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.convolve([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], np.ones(2) / 2, mode='valid').tolist())

topics.title: diff subtracts neighbouring values
topics.body: `np.diff` subtracts neighbouring values, turning a level series into the changes between periods.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.diff([1, 4, 9, 16]).tolist())

topics.title: digitize assigns bin indices
topics.body: `np.digitize` returns the bin index for every value, which is how continuous measurements become categories.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.digitize([5, 15, 25], [10, 20]).tolist())

topics.title: Confusion matrix with bincount
topics.body: Encoding true/predicted pairs as `true * k + predicted` and calling bincount yields a flat confusion matrix in one pass.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
true = np.array([0, 1, 1])
pred = np.array([0, 1, 0])
print(np.bincount(true * 3 + pred, minlength=9).reshape(3, 3).tolist())

lab.title: Image array pipeline
lab.brief: Create a small image array, crop a region, and print the mean brightness per channel.

interviewBank.q: How does pandas relate to NumPy?
interviewBank.answer: A DataFrame stores its columns as NumPy arrays and adds labels, alignment and mixed dtypes on top. Numeric work still runs on the underlying arrays.

interviewBank.q: Why do scikit-learn estimators expect a 2-D array?
interviewBank.answer: The first axis is samples and the second is features, so the estimator can index rows and learn one coefficient per column.

interviewBank.q: What must you check before feeding an array to a model?
interviewBank.answer: Shape, dtype, missing values and scale, because a wrong shape fails, a wrong dtype is cast, and missing or unscaled data quietly degrades accuracy.

interviewBank.q: What does a model expect from `X.shape`?
interviewBank.answer: Two dimensions: `(n_samples, n_features)`, so each row is one example and each column one feature.

interviewBank.q: Why keep a validation split as an index array?
interviewBank.answer: The same positions can select from features, labels and any aligned table, so the split stays consistent without copying data.

interviewBank.q: Why might converting a DataFrame to an array copy?
interviewBank.answer: Columns with one dtype in one block can be viewed; mixed dtypes must be gathered into a new buffer, which is a copy.

interviewBank.q: What does `DataFrame.to_numpy()` return?
interviewBank.answer: The underlying values as one array, copying when the columns have different dtypes.

interviewBank.q: How do you standardise features before a model?
interviewBank.answer: Subtract the column means and divide by the column standard deviations.

interviewBank.q: Why split labels from features before fitting?
interviewBank.answer: The model expects features only, and labels must not be scaled or imputed as features.

interviewBank.q: An image analysis pipeline stores RGB as (height, width, 3). How do you compute per-channel means in one call?
interviewBank.answer: `img.mean(axis=(0, 1))` collapses height and width, leaving one mean per channel (shape (3,)).

followUps.q: How do you get per-channel standard deviation at the same time?
followUps.answer: `img.std(axis=(0, 1))` — same reduction axes, one more statistic, still a single pass over each channel.

followUps.q: What does `axis=(0, 1)` mean in words?
followUps.answer: Reduce over height and width, leaving the channel axis untouched, so the result has one value per channel.

interviewBank.q: A DataFrame column is converted to an array for arithmetic and back to a Series for the report. Where should the conversion live?
interviewBank.answer: At the boundary of the numerical function: take the array in, return an array, and let the caller wrap it back into a Series with the original index. Converting inside the hot path repeats work and loses index alignment.

followUps.q: How do you keep the index aligned after the array round trip?
followUps.answer: Carry the index alongside the array and reattach it on the way back; converting inside the hot function loses it.

followUps.q: When does `.to_numpy()` return a copy instead of a view?
followUps.answer: When the column has a non-NumPy-compatible dtype, is non-contiguous, or mixed types force an object array — pass `copy=False` only when you know the layout is compatible.

defenseBank.q: Defend keeping features as NumPy arrays between pipeline stages.
defenseBank.answer: The stages do numeric work, and a typed contiguous block is the cheapest representation with no label bookkeeping. Labels belong to the frame at the edges.

defenseBank.q: What copy happens when a DataFrame becomes a NumPy array?
defenseBank.answer: If the columns share one dtype and memory, the array can be a view; with mixed dtypes pandas must build a new block, which is a copy.

defenseBank.q: Defend keeping labels separate from the feature matrix.
defenseBank.answer: It prevents the label from being scaled or imputed as a feature, keeps shapes explicit, and makes the train/test split a slice rather than a column drop.

defenseBank.q: Defend NumPy arrays as the interchange format between pipeline stages.
defenseBank.answer: Every stage does numeric work and every framework accepts an array, so a typed contiguous block avoids conversions at each hop.

defenseBank.q: Explain why plotting code should receive arrays rather than frames.
defenseBank.answer: A plot needs x and y vectors, not labels or indexes; passing arrays makes the shape contract explicit and avoids re-parsing the frame.

defenseBank.q: Defend measuring end-to-end time before optimising one stage.
defenseBank.answer: A stage that looks slow may be dominated by loading or conversion elsewhere. Measurement prevents optimising the wrong thing.

defenseBank.q: Defend an array at the boundary between preprocessing and training.
defenseBank.answer: Both sides already speak arrays, so no conversion or label bookkeeping is needed there.

defenseBank.q: Explain why shape errors surface late in a pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: Many steps broadcast or tolerate extra axes, so the mismatch survives until a model rejects it.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing a validation split as indices.
defenseBank.answer: The same indices select features and labels, keeping them aligned without copying either.
