learn.title: Pandas is built on arrays
learn.body: Series.to_numpy() exposes the underlying values, which is how you hand a column to a NumPy routine and keep the data, not the labels.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, 2])
print(s.to_numpy(), s.to_numpy().mean())

learn.title: Feature matrices are 2-D arrays
learn.body: A model expects one row per sample and one column per feature; reducing along axis 0 gives one value per feature, which is the shape a scaler fits.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(axis=0).shape)

learn.title: Images are (height, width, channels)
learn.body: An RGB image is a 3-D uint8 array and its shape is the first thing to check before any filter or model input.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.zeros((2, 2, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
print(img.shape, img.dtype)

learn.title: Standardise each column
learn.body: Subtracting the column mean and dividing by the column standard deviation is broadcasting, and it is the step every model expects before training.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
print(Z.round(2))

learn.title: One-hot encode with eye
learn.body: Indexing an identity matrix with integer labels encodes a class vector into a matrix, no loop and no library needed.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
labels = np.array([0, 2, 1])
print(np.eye(3, dtype=int)[labels])

learn.title: Images are uint8 arrays
learn.body: An image is just a (height, width, channels) array of unsigned bytes, so brightness is an addition clipped back into 0-255.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.array([[0, 128], [255, 64]], dtype=np.uint8)
bright = np.clip(img.astype(int) + 40, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
print(bright)

learn.title: A moving average is a convolution
learn.body: np.convolve with a window of 1/n computes a moving average, which is the array-only way to smooth a series without pandas.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4.])
print(np.convolve(v, np.ones(2) / 2, mode='valid'))

learn.title: Round only for display
learn.body: Rounding is a presentation choice: keep the full float for computation, and round only when the number is about to be shown.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round(2.675, 2), np.round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))

learn.title: Scale each row by its own maximum
learn.body: `keepdims=True` keeps the reduced axis as length 1, so the division broadcasts back across the row without reshaping.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 6.0]])
print((a / a.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)).round(3).tolist())

learn.title: diff gives step-to-step change
learn.body: `np.diff` returns one fewer value than the input: the difference between each neighbouring pair.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.diff(np.array([100.0, 110.0, 99.0])).round(3).tolist())

learn.title: digitize buckets values into bins
learn.body: The output is the index of the bin each value falls into. By default the right edge is open, so `0.5` lands in the next bucket.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.digitize(np.array([0.1, 0.5, 1.5]), [0.5, 1.0]).tolist())

learn.title: Build a confusion matrix with bincount
learn.body: Encoding a pair of labels as `true * classes + predicted` turns the counts into a matrix with one reshape and no loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

truth = np.array([1, 0, 1])
predicted = np.array([1, 1, 1])
counts = np.bincount(truth * 2 + predicted, minlength=4)
print(counts.reshape(2, 2).tolist())

learn.title: An image is just an array
learn.body: A colour image is a (height, width, 3) array, so slicing a channel is plain indexing and brightness is multiplication by a scalar.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
img = np.arange(12).reshape(2, 2, 3)
print(img.shape)
print(img[..., 0])
print((img * 0).shape)
learn.simple: Photo bhi asal me numbers ka table hai — height, width aur teen colour channels. Isliye image ka ek channel nikalna bas indexing hai, aur brightness badhana bas har number ko multiply karna. NumPy ke liye photo aur koi data alag nahi.
learn.pro: A colour image is a (height, width, 3) array, so channel selection is indexing and brightness is scalar multiplication over the whole buffer. The same operations that work on any ndarray apply unchanged, which is why image pipelines are NumPy-shaped.

learn.title: Moving between NumPy and the rest of Python
learn.body: asarray accepts lists and tuples without copying when it can, and tolist returns plain lists for JSON or an API. That boundary is where dtype and shape must be checked.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
a = np.asarray(data)
print(a.shape, a.dtype, a.tolist())
learn.simple: Jab tumhe list se array chahiye, `np.asarray` use karo — wo jitna ho sake copy nahi banata. Jab JSON ya API ke liye wapas list chahiye, `tolist()` use karo. Is border par type aur shape check karna mat bhoolo.
learn.pro: asarray accepts lists and tuples and avoids copying when the input is already a compatible ndarray; tolist converts back to Python lists for JSON or an API. The boundary is where dtype and shape must be asserted, because a silent promotion or a copy changes both behaviour and memory.

learn.title: Standardise columns with broadcasting
learn.body: Subtract the column means and divide by the column standard deviations, both shaped (1, n), to standardise every feature in one expression.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1.0, 10.0], [3.0, 14.0]])
z = (a - a.mean(axis=0)) / a.std(axis=0)
print(np.round(z, 3).tolist())
learn.simple: Har column ka mean ghatao aur standard deviation se divide karo. Dono cheezein `(1, n)` shape me banane se poora table ek saath standardise ho jaata hai.
learn.pro: Subtracting the `(1, n)` column means and dividing by the `(1, n)` standard deviations standardises every feature in one broadcast expression. Keeping the reduced axis as length 1 is what makes the shapes align with the data instead of a transposed result.
steps: Create a small feature matrix.
Compute column means and standard deviations.
Subtract and divide using broadcasting.
learn.visual:
each column → mean 0, std 1
shapes (rows, cols)
learn.realWorld: Standardisation is a required preprocessing step for many models.
mistakes: Using the population std when the sample std was intended.
revision: Keep the reduced axis as length 1.

learn.title: One-hot with eye indexing
learn.body: `np.eye(k)[labels]` turns integer labels into one-hot rows without a loop, which is the encoding most models expect.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(3)[[0, 2]].tolist())
learn.simple: `np.eye(k)[labels]` integer labels ko one-hot rows me badal deta hai. Isliye loop likhne ki zarurat nahi padti.
learn.pro: `np.eye(k)[labels]` gathers the matching identity row for each label, producing a one-hot matrix without a loop. The label dtype must be an integer index, and an out-of-range label raises rather than silently producing a zero row.
steps: Create integer labels.
Index an identity matrix with them.
Print the one-hot rows.
learn.realWorld: Categorical labels become model-ready one-hot rows in one gather.
mistakes: Using labels outside 0…k-1.
revision: Eye indexing gathers a row per label.

learn.title: Moving average with convolve
learn.body: Convolving with a normalised window of ones smooths a series; `mode='valid'` drops the edges that are not fully covered.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.convolve([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], np.ones(2) / 2, mode='valid').tolist())
learn.simple: `convolve` ko normalised ones ke window se chalane par series smooth ho jaati hai. `mode='valid'` sirf woh hisse rakhta hai jahan poora window fit ho.
learn.pro: Convolving with a normalised window of ones computes a moving average, and `mode='valid'` keeps only the positions where the whole window fits. The output length shrinks by the window length minus one, which is why the edge values have no average.
steps: Create a series.
Convolve it with a normalised window.
Compare the output length with the input.
learn.realWorld: Smoothing a noisy metric for a dashboard uses a moving average.
mistakes: Forgetting to normalise the window.

learn.title: diff subtracts neighbouring values
learn.body: `np.diff` subtracts neighbouring values, turning a level series into the changes between periods.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.diff([1, 4, 9, 16]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.diff` har value se uske pehle wali value ghata deta hai, isliye level series badlav ki series ban jaati hai. Output ek element chhoti hoti hai.
learn.pro: `np.diff` subtracts adjacent values along an axis, turning a level series into period-over-period changes. The output is one element shorter per step, and a second `diff` gives the change of the change.
steps: Create a series of levels.
Take the first difference.
Print the shorter output and check one value by hand.
learn.realWorld: Daily change in a cumulative count is a diff.
mistakes: Expecting the output to keep the input length.

learn.title: digitize assigns bin indices
learn.body: `np.digitize` returns the bin index for every value, which is how continuous measurements become categories.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.digitize([5, 15, 25], [10, 20]).tolist())
learn.simple: `np.digitize` har number ko batata hai woh kaunse bin me girta hai. Isliye continuous measurement seedha category ban jaata hai.
learn.pro: `np.digitize` returns the index of the bin each value falls into, using the supplied bin edges and a right-open convention by default. The result is an integer category array, so the edges must be sorted for the indices to mean anything.
steps: Define sorted bin edges.
Digitize a few values.
Check which edge convention the indices follow.
learn.realWorld: Age bands and score buckets are produced with digitize.
mistakes: Passing unsorted edges.

learn.title: Confusion matrix with bincount
learn.body: Encoding true/predicted pairs as `true * k + predicted` and calling bincount yields a flat confusion matrix in one pass.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
true = np.array([0, 1, 1])
pred = np.array([0, 1, 0])
print(np.bincount(true * 3 + pred, minlength=9).reshape(3, 3).tolist())
learn.simple: True aur predicted label ko `true * k + predicted` se ek number banao, phir `bincount` chalao. Poora confusion matrix ek pass me ban jaata hai.
learn.pro: Encoding each `(true, predicted)` pair as `true * k + predicted` and calling `bincount` with `minlength=k*k` yields the flattened confusion matrix in one pass. Reshaping to `(k, k)` puts the true class on rows and the predicted class on columns.
steps: Encode true and predicted labels as pairs.
Count the encoded pairs with bincount.
Reshape to a k×k matrix.
learn.realWorld: A classifier report starts from the confusion matrix built this way.
mistakes: Reshaping with the wrong class count.

interview.q: How does pandas relate to NumPy?
interview.answer: A DataFrame stores its columns as NumPy arrays and adds labels, alignment and mixed dtypes on top. Numeric work still runs on the underlying arrays.

interview.q: Why do scikit-learn estimators expect a 2-D array?
interview.answer: The first axis is samples and the second is features, so the estimator can index rows and learn one coefficient per column.

interview.q: What must you check before feeding an array to a model?
interview.answer: Shape, dtype, missing values and scale, because a wrong shape fails, a wrong dtype is cast, and missing or unscaled data quietly degrades accuracy.

interview.q: What does a model expect from `X.shape`?
interview.answer: Two dimensions: `(n_samples, n_features)`, so each row is one example and each column one feature.

interview.q: Why keep a validation split as an index array?
interview.answer: The same positions can select from features, labels and any aligned table, so the split stays consistent without copying data.

interview.q: Why might converting a DataFrame to an array copy?
interview.answer: Columns with one dtype in one block can be viewed; mixed dtypes must be gathered into a new buffer, which is a copy.

interview.q: What does `DataFrame.to_numpy()` return?
interview.answer: The underlying values as one array, copying when the columns have different dtypes.

interview.q: How do you standardise features before a model?
interview.answer: Subtract the column means and divide by the column standard deviations.

interview.q: Why split labels from features before fitting?
interview.answer: The model expects features only, and labels must not be scaled or imputed as features.

interview.q: An image analysis pipeline stores RGB as (height, width, 3). How do you compute per-channel means in one call?
interview.answer: `img.mean(axis=(0, 1))` collapses height and width, leaving one mean per channel (shape (3,)).

followUps.q: How do you get per-channel standard deviation at the same time?
followUps.answer: `img.std(axis=(0, 1))` — same reduction axes, one more statistic, still a single pass over each channel.

followUps.q: What does `axis=(0, 1)` mean in words?
followUps.answer: Reduce over height and width, leaving the channel axis untouched, so the result has one value per channel.

interview.q: A DataFrame column is converted to an array for arithmetic and back to a Series for the report. Where should the conversion live?
interview.answer: At the boundary of the numerical function: take the array in, return an array, and let the caller wrap it back into a Series with the original index. Converting inside the hot path repeats work and loses index alignment.

followUps.q: How do you keep the index aligned after the array round trip?
followUps.answer: Carry the index alongside the array and reattach it on the way back; converting inside the hot function loses it.

followUps.q: When does `.to_numpy()` return a copy instead of a view?
followUps.answer: When the column has a non-NumPy-compatible dtype, is non-contiguous, or mixed types force an object array — pass `copy=False` only when you know the layout is compatible.

defense.q: Defend keeping features as NumPy arrays between pipeline stages.
defense.answer: The stages do numeric work, and a typed contiguous block is the cheapest representation with no label bookkeeping. Labels belong to the frame at the edges.

defense.q: What copy happens when a DataFrame becomes a NumPy array?
defense.answer: If the columns share one dtype and memory, the array can be a view; with mixed dtypes pandas must build a new block, which is a copy.

defense.q: Defend keeping labels separate from the feature matrix.
defense.answer: It prevents the label from being scaled or imputed as a feature, keeps shapes explicit, and makes the train/test split a slice rather than a column drop.

defense.q: Defend NumPy arrays as the interchange format between pipeline stages.
defense.answer: Every stage does numeric work and every framework accepts an array, so a typed contiguous block avoids conversions at each hop.

defense.q: Explain why plotting code should receive arrays rather than frames.
defense.answer: A plot needs x and y vectors, not labels or indexes; passing arrays makes the shape contract explicit and avoids re-parsing the frame.

defense.q: Defend measuring end-to-end time before optimising one stage.
defense.answer: A stage that looks slow may be dominated by loading or conversion elsewhere. Measurement prevents optimising the wrong thing.

defense.q: Defend an array at the boundary between preprocessing and training.
defense.answer: Both sides already speak arrays, so no conversion or label bookkeeping is needed there.

defense.q: Explain why shape errors surface late in a pipeline.
defense.answer: Many steps broadcast or tolerate extra axes, so the mismatch survives until a model rejects it.

defense.q: Defend storing a validation split as indices.
defense.answer: The same indices select features and labels, keeping them aligned without copying either.

capstone.title: Capstone: a year of sales, answered with arrays
capstone.brief: You are handed twelve months of unit sales across six products and a price list. Build one NumPy pipeline that answers the questions a manager actually asks — which month earned most, which product carries the year, how volatile each product is, and what next quarter looks like if the current trend holds. No loops for the arithmetic, no pandas, no hand-typed totals.
capstone.dataset: Generated in code so it is reproducible: `default_rng(7).integers(20, 120, size=(12, 6))` gives units per month per product, and the price list is `[249, 199, 349, 149, 299, 179]`. Shape (12, 6) means months are rows and products are columns — decide that once and keep it everywhere.

starter.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
units = rng.integers(20, 120, size=(12, 6))
price = np.array([249, 199, 349, 149, 299, 179])
revenue = units * price
monthly = revenue.sum(axis=1)
print("units shape:", units.shape)
print("monthly revenue:", monthly.tolist())
print("best month:", int(monthly.argmax()) + 1)
print("mean per month:", round(float(monthly.mean()), 2))

tiers.name: Beginner
tiers.goal: Answer the four manager questions with reductions and one comparison.
requirements: Compute per-month revenue with broadcasting, not a loop over products.
Report the best month with argmax and the worst month with argmin.
Report total units and total revenue for the year.
Print the shape of every array you create and say what each axis means.
deliverables: A script that prints six labelled numbers with their units.
One sentence per number explaining which axis was collapsed.
stretch: Express the same monthly totals with `@ price` and confirm the numbers match.

tiers.name: Intermediate
tiers.goal: Add per-product analysis, shares and a fair comparison across products.
requirements: Per-product yearly revenue and its share of the total, sorted descending.
Per-product mean and standard deviation across the twelve months.
The month × product cell with the highest revenue, reported as (month, product) using unravel_index.
A boolean mask that selects months above the yearly monthly mean.
deliverables: A printed table whose ordering is explained (sorted by revenue).
A mask whose True count matches the number you print.
stretch: Normalise each product to its own first month and compare growth in percent.

tiers.name: Advanced
tiers.goal: Turn the table into a defensible forecast and a written recommendation.
requirements: Fit a straight-line trend per product with `np.polyfit` over the twelve months.
Project the next three months per product and total them.
Quantify uncertainty honestly: report the residual standard deviation and say what the projection assumes.
State one decision the data supports and one it does not.
deliverables: A projection array of shape (3, 6) plus its monthly totals.
A short written recommendation with the numbers it rests on.
A limitations paragraph naming at least two assumptions.
stretch: Compare the linear projection against a simple 3-month moving average and explain which is more honest for this data.

milestones.title: 1 · Fix the shape contract
milestones.detail: Write down months × products before any arithmetic. Print units.shape and verify (12, 6); every later axis choice depends on it.

milestones.title: 2 · Broadcasting, not looping
milestones.detail: Multiply units by price to get revenue. Confirm revenue.sum(axis=1) matches a manual total for one month.

milestones.title: 3 · Ask the manager questions
milestones.detail: Best and worst month, per-product share, per-product volatility, and the mask of above-average months. Each answer is one reduction or one comparison.

milestones.title: 4 · Project and defend
milestones.detail: Fit the trend, project three months, then write what the projection assumes and what would break it.

rubric.evidence: Every reduction names the axis it collapses, and printed shapes match the claim.
No Python loop performs the revenue or aggregation work; broadcasting is used where it belongs.
Numbers carry units, the mask count matches the printed count, and the projection states its assumptions.
The recommendation is supported by the computed numbers, and the limitations paragraph names real risks.

assessment.pass: All four milestones produce numbers you can explain, and the rubric totals at least 70.
assessment.excellent: 90 or more, with the advanced tier's projection and limitations written so a non-programmer could act on them.
